statements.text: There are principles in human nature that interest a person in the fortune of others.
These principles render the happiness of others necessary to a person, even if they derive nothing from it except the pleasure of seeing it.
Pity or compassion is the emotion felt for the misery of others when it is seen or vividly conceived.
People often derive sorrow from the sorrow of others.
The sentiment of pity or compassion is not confined to virtuous and humane people.
Even the greatest ruffian or most hardened violator of laws is not altogether without pity or compassion.
We have no immediate experience of what other men feel.
We can form no idea of how others are affected except by conceiving what we ourselves would feel in the same situation.
Our senses never inform us of what others suffer as long as we ourselves are at ease.
Our imagination is the only faculty that can form any conception of another person's sensations.
The imagination represents to us what would be our own sensations if we were in another person's case.
By imagination, we place ourselves in another's situation and conceive ourselves enduring the same torments.
By imagining another's suffering, we become in some measure the same person with them and form some idea of their sensations.
When we adopt another's agonies as our own through imagination, they begin to affect us.
Conceiving or imagining being in pain or distress excites some degree of the same emotion as actually being in it.
The degree of emotion excited by imagination is proportional to the vivacity or dulness of the conception.
When we see a stroke aimed at another person's limb, we naturally shrink and draw back our own corresponding limb.
When the stroke falls on another person, we feel it in some measure and are hurt by it as well as the sufferer.
A mob watching a dancer on a slack rope naturally writhe, twist, and balance their own bodies as they see the dancer do.
Persons with delicate fibers and weak constitutions complain of feeling itching or uneasy sensations in parts of their own bodies corresponding to sores and ulcers they see on beggars.
The horror conceived at the misery of others affects the corresponding part in oneself more than any other part.
The force of the conception of another's misery can produce physical sensations in a person's own body.
Men of robust make often feel soreness in their own eyes when looking upon sore eyes of others.
The soreness felt in one's own eyes when looking at sore eyes of others is due to the delicacy of that organ.
Our fellow-feeling is not only called forth by circumstances that create pain or sorrow.
Whatever passion arises from any object in the person principally concerned, an analogous emotion arises in the breast of every attentive spectator.
Our joy for the deliverance of heroes in tragedy or romance is as sincere as our grief for their distress.
Our fellow-feeling with the misery of others is not more real than that with their happiness.
We enter into the gratitude of others towards faithful friends who did not desert them in difficulties.
We heartily go along with the resentment of others against perfidious traitors who injured, abandoned, or deceived them.
In every passion of which the mind of man is susceptible, the emotions of the bystander correspond to what he imagines should be the sentiments of the sufferer.
Pity and compassion signify our fellow-feeling with the sorrow of others.
Sympathy may be used to denote our fellow-feeling with any passion whatever.
On some occasions, sympathy may arise merely from the view of a certain emotion in another person.
Passions may sometimes be transfused from one man to another instantaneously and before any knowledge of what excited them.
Grief and joy strongly expressed in the look and gestures of a person at once affect the spectator with some degree of like emotion.
A smiling face is a cheerful object to everyone who sees it.
A sorrowful countenance is a melancholy object to everyone who sees it.
Some passions' expressions excite no sympathy and may provoke disgust or anger before the cause is known.
The furious behavior of an angry man is more likely to exasperate observers against himself than against his enemies.
Sympathy arises more from the view of the situation that excites a passion than from the view of the passion itself.
People sometimes feel sympathy for a passion in another person that the other person seems incapable of experiencing.
When we put ourselves in another's case, a passion may arise in us from imagination even if it does not arise in the other person from reality.
We blush for the impudence and rudeness of another even if that person shows no sense of impropriety.
We feel embarrassment for another's behavior because we imagine how confused we would be if we behaved similarly.
The loss of reason is considered the most dreadful calamity to mankind by those with some humanity.
People with humanity feel deeper commiseration for the loss of reason than for any other human wretchedness.
A person who has lost reason may laugh and sing and be insensible to their own misery.
The anguish felt by humanity at the sight of someone who has lost reason is not a reflection of the sufferer's own sentiment.
Compassion for someone who has lost reason arises from imagining what one would feel if placed in the same situation with present reason and judgment.
A mother hears the moanings of her infant during disease and cannot know exactly what the infant feels.
A mother combines the infant's real helplessness with her own consciousness of helplessness and fears for the infant's future.
From these combined feelings, the mother forms a complete image of misery and distress for her own sorrow.
The infant feels only the uneasiness of the present instant, which is never great.
The infant is perfectly secure regarding the future and lacks fear and anxiety due to thoughtlessness and lack of foresight.
Fear and anxiety are great tormentors of the human breast that reason and philosophy cannot fully defend against in adulthood.
People sympathize even with the dead, focusing on circumstances that affect their senses but not their happiness.
People think it is miserable for the dead to be deprived of sunlight, life, conversation, and to be laid in the grave.
People imagine the dead are miserable because they are forgotten by friends and relations over time.
People feel that sympathy is especially due to the dead when they are in danger of being forgotten.
People pay vain honors to the memory of the dead to artificially keep alive their melancholy remembrance.
People's sympathy cannot console the dead, which adds to the perceived calamity of death.
The regret, love, and lamentations of friends cannot yield comfort to the dead.
The happiness of the dead is not affected by deprivation of sunlight, life, conversation, or being forgotten.
The idea of endless melancholy after death arises from people projecting their own consciousness onto the dead.
People imagine their own emotions in the situation of being dead by placing their living souls in inanimate bodies.
The terror of one's own dissolution arises from this illusion of imagination.
The idea of circumstances that cannot cause pain after death makes people miserable while alive.
The dread of death is a significant principle in human nature.
The dread of death is a great poison to individual happiness.
The dread of death acts as a great restraint upon the injustice of mankind.
While the dread of death afflicts and mortifies the individual, it guards and protects society.
Nothing pleases us more than to observe in other men a fellow-feeling with all the emotions of our own breast.
We are shocked by the appearance of the contrary of fellow-feeling.
Some think that pleasure and pain from sympathy can be explained by self-love and the need for assistance from others.
Man rejoices when others adopt his passions because he is then assured of their assistance.
Man grieves when others show contrary passions because he is then assured of their opposition.
Pleasure and pain from sympathy are often felt instantaneously and on frivolous occasions.
The instantaneous nature of pleasure and pain from sympathy suggests they cannot be derived from self-interested considerations.
A man is mortified when he tries to divert company but nobody laughs except himself.
The mirth of the company is highly agreeable to a man and regarded as the greatest applause.
Pleasure from sympathy does not arise solely from the additional vivacity that mirth receives from others' mirth.
Pain from lack of sympathy does not arise solely from the disappointment of missing the pleasure of shared mirth.
Reading a book or poem to a companion can be pleasurable even if one no longer finds amusement in reading it alone.
We enter into the surprise and admiration which a companion naturally feels when reading a book or poem.
We consider ideas in a book or poem in the light in which they appear to a companion rather than in our own light.
We are amused by sympathy with a companion's amusement which enlivens our own.
We would be vexed if a companion did not seem entertained by a book or poem we read to him.
Sympathy enlivens joy and alleviates grief.
Sympathy enlivens joy by presenting another source of satisfaction.
Sympathy alleviates grief by insinuating into the heart an agreeable sensation.
We are more anxious to communicate our disagreeable passions to friends than our agreeable passions.
We derive more satisfaction from friends' sympathy with our disagreeable passions than with our agreeable passions.
We are more shocked by the lack of sympathy with our disagreeable passions than with our agreeable passions.
The unfortunate are relieved when they find a person to whom they can communicate the cause of their sorrow.
Upon the sympathy of another, the unfortunate seem to disburden themselves of part of their distress.
The unfortunate say that the person sympathizing shares their sorrow with them.
The person who sympathizes seems to derive a part of the sorrow to himself.
The sorrow felt by the sympathizer seems to alleviate the weight of the sorrow felt by the unfortunate.
Relating misfortunes renews the grief of the unfortunate by awakening the memory of afflicting circumstances.
The tears of the unfortunate flow faster after relating their misfortunes.
The unfortunate are apt to abandon themselves to all the weakness of sorrow when relating their misfortunes.
The unfortunate take pleasure in the sympathy of another despite the renewal of their grief.
The sweetness of sympathy more than compensates the bitterness of sorrow enlivened and renewed by relating it.
The cruelest insult to the unfortunate is to appear to make light of their calamities.
Not being affected by the joy of companions is considered want of politeness.
Not wearing a serious countenance when companions tell us their afflictions is real and gross inhumanity.
Love is an agreeable passion; resentment is a disagreeable passion.
We are less anxious that friends adopt our friendships than that they enter into our resentments.
We can forgive friends who seem little affected by favours but lose patience if they seem indifferent to injuries done to us.
We are more angry if friends do not sympathize with our resentment than if they do not enter into our gratitude.
Friends can easily avoid being friends to our friends but can hardly avoid being enemies to those with whom we are at variance.
When the original passions of the person principally concerned are in perfect concord with the sympathetic emotions of the spectator, they appear just and proper to the spectator.
When the passions of another do not coincide with what the spectator feels, they appear unjust and improper to the spectator.
To approve of the passions of another as suitable to their objects is the same as observing that we entirely sympathize with them.
Not to approve of the passions of another as suitable to their objects is the same as observing that we do not entirely sympathize with them.
A man who resents injuries done to me and observes that I resent them as he does necessarily approves of my resentment.
A man whose sympathy keeps time to my grief cannot but admit the reasonableness of my sorrow.
A person who admires the same poem or picture exactly as I do must allow the justness of my admiration.
A person who laughs at the same joke and laughs along with me cannot well deny the propriety of my laughter.
A person who feels no such emotion as I feel or feels none that bears proportion to mine cannot avoid disapproving my sentiments due to their dissonance with his own.
If my animosity goes beyond what the indignation of my friend can correspond to, I incur a degree of his disapprobation.
If my grief exceeds what my friend's most tender compassion can go along with, I incur a degree of his disapprobation.
If my admiration is either too high or too low to tally with my friend's own admiration, I incur a degree of his disapprobation.
If I laugh loud and heartily when my friend only smiles, or only smile when he laughs loud and heartily, I incur a degree of his disapprobation.
A person's own sentiments are the standards and measures by which he judges the sentiments of others.
To approve of another man's opinions is to adopt those opinions.
To adopt another man's opinions is to approve of them.
If the same arguments convince you and me, I necessarily approve of your conviction.
If the same arguments do not convince me, I necessarily disapprove of your conviction.
To approve or disapprove of the opinions of others means to observe their agreement or disagreement with our own.
Approving or disapproving the sentiments or passions of others is the same as observing their agreement or disagreement with our own.
Sometimes we approve without any sympathy or correspondence of sentiments.
Even in cases where we seem to approve without sympathy, our approbation is ultimately founded upon a sympathy or correspondence of sentiments.
We may approve of a jest and the laughter of the company though we ourselves do not laugh because we are in a grave humour or have attention engaged elsewhere.
We have learned from experience what sort of pleasantry usually makes us laugh and observe that a particular jest is of that kind.
We approve of the laughter of the company and feel it is natural and suitable to its object because we know we would usually join in it.
We often approve of the grief of a stranger who shows marks of deep affliction upon hearing of a death.
We may not enter into the violence of a stranger's sorrow or conceive concern for him if he and his father are unknown to us or we are occupied with other things.
We have learned from experience that such a misfortune naturally excites such a degree of sorrow.
We know that if we took time to consider the stranger's situation fully, we would sincerely sympathize with him.
Our approbation of sorrow is founded on the consciousness of conditional sympathy even when that sympathy does not actually take place.
General rules derived from experience correct the impropriety of our present emotions on many occasions.
The sentiment or affection of the heart from which any action proceeds can be considered in relation to the cause which excites it or the motive which gives occasion to it.
The sentiment or affection of the heart can also be considered in relation to the end it proposes or the effect it tends to produce.
The propriety or impropriety of an action consists in the suitableness or unsuitableness, proportion or disproportion, which the affection bears to the cause or object which excites it.
The merit or demerit of an action consists in the beneficial or hurtful nature of the effects which the affection aims at or tends to produce.
Philosophers have recently considered chiefly the tendency of affections and have given little attention to their relation to the cause which excites them.
In common life, when judging a person's conduct and sentiments, we consider both the relation to the cause and the tendency to produce effects.
When we blame excesses of love, grief, or resentment, we consider both the ruinous effects they tend to produce and the little occasion given for them.
We say the merit of a person or the provocation is not sufficient to justify violent passion.
If the cause of an affection were proportioned to it, we might approve of the violence of the emotion.
When judging an affection as proportioned or disproportioned to its cause, we use the correspondent affection in ourselves as the rule.
If upon bringing the case home to ourselves, the sentiments coincide with ours, we approve them as proportioned and suitable.
If the sentiments do not coincide with ours, we disapprove them as extravagant and out of proportion.
Every faculty in one man is the measure by which he judges the like faculty in another.
I judge of your sight by my sight, your ear by my ear, your reason by my reason, your resentment by my resentment, and your love by my love.
I neither have nor can have any other way of judging about the faculties of others.
We may judge the propriety or impropriety of another person's sentiments by their correspondence or disagreement with our own.
This judgment can be made either when the objects exciting the sentiments are considered without any peculiar relation to ourselves or the other person.
Alternatively, the judgment can be made when the objects are considered as peculiarly affecting one or the other of us.
When objects are considered without any peculiar relation to either person, and the sentiments entirely correspond, we ascribe to the other person qualities of taste and good judgment.

Examples of such objects include the beauty of a plain, the greatness of a mountain, the ornaments of a building, the expression of a picture, the composition of a discourse, the conduct of a third person, proportions of quantities and numbers, and appearances of the universe.
We and our companion look at these objects from the same point of view and do not require sympathy or an imaginary change of situation to produce harmony of sentiments.
Differences in sentiment about these objects arise from different degrees of attention or natural acuteness in the mind's faculty.
When a companion's sentiments coincide with our own on obvious and easy matters, he deserves no special praise or admiration.
When a companion's sentiments not only coincide but lead and direct our own, showing attention to overlooked details and adjustment to circumstances, we approve and admire them.
Approbation heightened by wonder and surprise constitutes admiration, and applause is its natural expression.
A man who judges that exquisite beauty is preferable to gross deformity is approved by all but not much admired.
The man of taste who distinguishes minute differences of beauty and deformity excites admiration.
The experienced mathematician who easily unravels intricate proportions excites admiration.
The great leader in science and taste who directs our sentiments and whose talents astonish us excites admiration and deserves applause.
Most praise bestowed on intellectual virtues is grounded on this foundation of admiration.
The utility of qualities like good judgment and taste is an afterthought and not what first recommends them to our approbation.
We originally approve another man's judgment as right, accurate, and agreeable to truth because it agrees with our own.
Taste is originally approved not as useful but as just, delicate, and precisely suited to its object.
With regard to objects that affect either ourselves or the person whose sentiments we judge, it is more difficult to preserve harmony and correspondence of sentiments.
Misfortunes or injuries that befall a person affect that person more nearly than a companion who does not share the same situation.
We do not view personal misfortunes from the same station as we do a picture, poem, or system of philosophy.
It is easier to overlook lack of correspondence of sentiments about indifferent objects than about objects that particularly interest either person.
Opposite judgments in matters of speculation or taste can be overlooked without damaging conversation if neither person is deeply interested.
If a companion has no fellow-feeling or proportionate sympathy for one's misfortunes or injuries, conversation becomes intolerable.
Lack of sympathy leads to mutual intolerance and inability to support each other's company.
To have correspondence of sentiments in such cases, the spectator must endeavor to put himself in the situation of the sufferer.
The spectator must adopt the whole case of the companion with all its minutest incidents.
The spectator must strive to render as perfect as possible the imaginary change of situation upon which sympathy is founded.
The emotions of the spectator often fall short of the violence of what is felt by the sufferer.
Mankind is naturally sympathetic but does not conceive the same degree of passion for another's suffering as the person principally concerned.
The imaginary change of situation upon which sympathy is founded is momentary.
The thought of their own safety and that they are not the sufferers continually intrudes upon spectators.
This intrusion hinders spectators from conceiving any passion that approaches the same degree of violence as the sufferer feels.
The person principally concerned passionately desires a more complete sympathy from spectators.
The sufferer's sole consolation is to see the emotions of spectators' hearts beat in concord with his own violent and disagreeable passions.
The sufferer can only hope to obtain this consolation by lowering his passion to a level that spectators can follow.
The sufferer must flatten the sharpness of his passion's natural tone to harmonize with the emotions of those around him.
What spectators feel will always be different in some respects from what the sufferer feels.
Compassion can never be exactly the same as original sorrow.
The secret consciousness that the change of situations is imaginary lowers the degree and varies the kind of sympathy.
The two sentiments of original sorrow and compassion may have sufficient correspondence for the harmony of society.
Though original sorrow and compassion will never be unisons, they may be concords.
Nature teaches spectators to assume the circumstances of the person principally concerned.
Nature also teaches the sufferer to assume, in some measure, the circumstances of the spectators.
Spectators continually place themselves in the sufferer's situation and conceive emotions similar to his.
The sufferer constantly places himself in the spectators' situation and conceives some degree of coolness about his own fortune.
Spectators consider what they would feel if they were the sufferers.
The sufferer imagines how he would be affected if he were only one of the spectators of his own situation.
The sufferer's sympathy makes him look at his situation in some measure with the spectators' eyes.
The reflected passion the sufferer conceives is much weaker than the original passion.
This reflected passion abates the violence of what the sufferer felt before coming into the presence of spectators.
The mind is rarely so disturbed that the company of a friend will not restore some degree of tranquillity and sedateness.
The breast is calmed and composed the moment we come into the presence of a friend.
We are immediately reminded of the light in which a friend will view our situation.
We begin to view our situation in the same light as a friend does because the effect of sympathy is instantaneous.
We expect less sympathy from a common acquaintance than from a friend.
We cannot open to a common acquaintance all the little circumstances we can unfold to a friend.
We assume more tranquillity before a common acquaintance and focus on general outlines of our situation.
We expect still less sympathy from an assembly of strangers than from a common acquaintance.
We assume still more tranquillity before strangers and bring down our passion to a pitch they can follow.
If we are masters of ourselves, the presence of a mere acquaintance will compose us more than that of a friend.
The presence of an assembly of strangers composes us more than that of an acquaintance.
Society and conversation are the most powerful remedies for restoring the mind to tranquillity.
Society and conversation are the best preservatives of an equal and happy temper necessary for self-satisfaction and enjoyment.
Men of retirement and speculation often have more humanity, generosity, and a nicer sense of honour than men of the world.
Men of retirement and speculation seldom possess the equality of temper common among men of the world.

Two different sets of virtues are founded upon two different efforts: the effort of the spectator to enter into the sentiments of the person principally concerned, and the effort of the person principally concerned to bring down his emotions to what the spectator can go along with.

The amiable virtues, which include softness, gentleness, candid condescension, and indulgent humanity, are founded upon the effort of the spectator to enter into the sentiments of the person principally concerned.

The respectable virtues, which include self-denial, self-government, and command of the passions, originate from the effort of the person principally concerned to bring down his emotions to what the spectator can go along with.
A person whose sympathetic heart re-echoes all the sentiments of those with whom he converses appears amiable.
A person who grieves for the calamities of others, resents their injuries, and rejoices at their good fortune is considered amiable.
Those who feel only for themselves and are insensible to the happiness or misery of others appear disagreeable.
The presence of a person who is hard and obdurate and feels only for himself causes pain to those who converse with him.
Noble propriety and grace are felt in the conduct of those who exert recollection and self-command, which constitute the dignity of every passion.
Clamorous grief that calls upon compassion with sighs, tears, and importunate lamentations is regarded with disgust.
Reserved, silent, and majestic sorrow that shows itself in swelling eyes, quivering lips and cheeks, and distant coldness of behavior is revered.
Silent and majestic sorrow imposes silence and respectful attention upon observers.
The insolence and brutality of anger indulged without check or restraint is the most detestable of all objects.
Noble and generous resentment governs pursuit of injuries by the indignation of the impartial spectator rather than by rage of the sufferer.
Generous resentment allows no word or gesture beyond what the impartial spectator would dictate.
Generous resentment never desires to inflict greater punishment than what every indifferent person would rejoice to see executed.
To feel much for others and little for ourselves, to restrain selfish affections and indulge benevolent affections, constitutes the perfection of human nature.
The harmony of sentiments and passions among mankind consists in loving ourselves only as we love our neighbour.
The great precept of nature is to love ourselves only as we love our neighbour or as our neighbour is capable of loving us.
Virtues of sensibility and self-command are not found in ordinary degrees but in uncommon degrees of delicacy and understanding.
The amiable virtue of humanity requires a sensibility much beyond what is possessed by the rude vulgar of mankind.
The great and exalted virtue of magnanimity demands much more self-command than the weakest mortals can exert.
In common degrees of intellectual qualities there is no ability, and in common degrees of moral qualities there is no virtue.
Virtue is excellence, something uncommonly great and beautiful, rising far above what is vulgar and ordinary.
Amiable virtues consist in a degree of sensibility that surprises by its exquisite and unexpected delicacy and tenderness.
Respectable virtues consist in a degree of self-command that astonishes by its amazing superiority over the most ungovernable passions of human nature.
There is a considerable difference between virtue and mere propriety.
Qualities and actions that deserve to be admired and celebrated differ from those that simply deserve to be approved of.
To act with perfect propriety often requires only a common and ordinary degree of sensibility or self-command.
Eating when hungry is perfectly right and proper on ordinary occasions and is approved by everybody but is not virtuous.
Actions that fall short of perfect propriety may still have considerable virtue if they approach nearer to perfection than expected in difficult occasions.
Great exertions of self-command may not completely stifle human weakness or reduce passions to perfect moderation.
Behavior that falls short of perfect propriety in difficult situations may still deserve applause and be denominated virtuous.
Such behavior may manifest generosity and magnanimity beyond what most men are capable of.
When judging actions, two standards are often used: the idea of complete propriety and perfection, and the idea of the common degree of excellence attained by most men.
No human conduct ever did or can come up to the idea of complete propriety and perfection.
Actions that go beyond the common degree of excellence, even if far from absolute perfection, deserve applause.
Actions that fall short of the common degree of excellence deserve blame.
Critics may judge works of great masters by an idea of perfection which no human work can reach, seeing only faults and imperfections.
When critics compare great works to the common degree of excellence in the art, such works often deserve the highest applause.
The highest applause is given to works that approach much nearer to perfection than the greater part of works in the same category.
The propriety of every passion excited by objects peculiarly related to ourselves lies in a certain mediocrity.
If the passion is too high or too low, the spectator cannot enter into it.
Grief and resentment for private misfortunes and injuries may easily be too high in the greater part of mankind.
Grief and resentment for private misfortunes and injuries may be too low, though this more rarely happens.
The excess of passion is denominated weakness and fury.
The defect of passion is called stupidity, insensibility, and want of spirit.
People cannot enter into passions that are either excessive or deficient but are astonished and confounded to see them.
The mediocrity in which the point of propriety consists is different in different passions.
The mediocrity is high in some passions and low in others.
Some passions are indecent to express very strongly even on occasions where they are felt in the highest degree.
Other passions have the strongest expressions that are extremely graceful on many occasions, even if the passions themselves do not arise so necessarily.
Passions with little or no sympathy are those which it is indecent to express very strongly.
Passions with the greatest sympathy have the strongest expressions that are extremely graceful.
Passions are regarded as decent or indecent in proportion to how much mankind are disposed to sympathize with them.
It is indecent to express any strong degree of passions arising from a certain situation or disposition of the body.
The company, not being in the same disposition, cannot be expected to sympathize with strong bodily passions.
Violent hunger is often natural and unavoidable but is always indecent to express strongly.
Eating voraciously is universally regarded as a piece of ill manners.
There is some degree of sympathy with hunger.
It is agreeable to see companions eat with a good appetite.
Expressions of loathing towards food are offensive.
A healthy man's habitual bodily disposition makes his stomach keep time with agreeable food and not with loathsome food.
We can sympathize with the distress caused by excessive hunger when reading descriptions of sieges or sea-voyages.
We imagine ourselves in the situation of sufferers of hunger and conceive their grief, fear, and consternation.
We feel some degree of the passions described in such accounts and therefore sympathize with them.
We do not grow hungry by reading descriptions of hunger and thus cannot properly sympathize with the hunger itself.
The passion by which Nature unites the two sexes is naturally the most furious of all passions.
All strong expressions of the passion uniting the sexes are indecent on every occasion.
This indecency applies even between persons in whom the passion's indulgence is acknowledged as innocent by human and divine laws.
There is some degree of sympathy with the passion uniting the sexes.
Talking to a woman as to a man is improper.
The company of women is expected to inspire more gaiety, pleasantry, and attention.
A man entirely insensitive to the fair sex is somewhat contemptible even to other men.
There is aversion for all appetites originating from the body.
All strong expressions of bodily appetites are loathsome and disagreeable.
Some ancient philosophers considered bodily appetites as passions shared with brutes and beneath human dignity.
Other passions shared with brutes, such as resentment, natural affection, and gratitude, do not appear brutal.
The true cause of disgust for bodily appetites in others is that we cannot enter into them.
Once bodily appetites are gratified, the object that excited them ceases to be agreeable to the person.
The presence of the object of bodily appetite often becomes offensive to the person after gratification.
The person who has gratified bodily appetites can no longer enter into his own passion.
After dining, people order the covers to be removed.
We should treat the objects of the most ardent bodily desires as we treat food after dining.
Temperance is the virtue that consists in the command of bodily appetites.
Prudence restrains bodily appetites within bounds prescribed by regard to health and fortune.
Temperance confines bodily appetites within limits required by grace, propriety, delicacy, and modesty.
Crying out with bodily pain, however intolerable, appears unmanly and unbecoming.
There is a good deal of sympathy with bodily pain.
Seeing a stroke aimed at another person causes a natural shrinking and drawing back of one's own limb.
When the stroke falls, one feels it in some measure and is hurt as well as the sufferer.
The hurt felt by the observer is excessively slight compared to the sufferer.
If the sufferer makes a violent outcry, the observer who cannot sympathize despises him.
Passions originating from the body excite either no sympathy or a degree of sympathy disproportionate to the sufferer's violence.
Passions originating from the imagination excite more sympathy than bodily passions.
In some Greek tragedies, there is an attempt to excite compassion by representing the agonies of bodily pain.
Philoctetes cries out and faints from the extremity of his sufferings.
Hippolytus and Hercules are introduced as expiring under the severest tortures.
The fortitude of Hercules was incapable of supporting the severest tortures.
In these cases, it is not the pain which interests the audience, but some other circumstance.
It is not the sore foot, but the solitude of Philoctetes which affects the audience.
The solitude of Philoctetes diffuses a romantic wildness over the tragedy.
The agonies of Hercules and Hippolytus are interesting only because death is foreseen as the consequence.
If the heroes were to recover, the representation of their sufferings would be considered ridiculous.
A tragedy consisting of distress from a colic would be considered absurd despite the pain's exquisiteness.
Attempts to excite compassion by representing bodily pain are among the greatest breaches of decorum in Greek theatre.
There is little sympathy felt with bodily pain.
The little sympathy with bodily pain is the foundation of the propriety of constancy and patience in enduring it.
A man who endures the severest tortures without weakness, groaning, or passion commands the highest admiration.
The firmness of a man enduring pain enables him to keep time with the audience's indifference and insensibility.
The magnanimous effort of a man to endure pain without weakness is admired and approved.
From experience of common human weakness, people are surprised when someone acts with admirable constancy under pain.
Approbation mixed with wonder and surprise constitutes the sentiment called admiration.
Applause is the natural expression of admiration.
Passions derived from a peculiar turn or habit of the imagination are perfectly natural but little sympathized with.
The imaginations of mankind not having acquired a particular turn cannot enter into the passions derived from that turn.
Passions derived from a peculiar turn of imagination are always, in some measure, ridiculous.
A strong attachment naturally grows up between two persons of different sexes who have long fixed their thoughts upon one another.
People do not sympathize with the eagerness of emotions of a lover because their imagination has not run in the same channel.
If a friend has been injured, people readily sympathize with his resentment and grow angry with the person he is angry with.
If a friend has received a benefit, people readily enter into his gratitude and have a high sense of the merit of his benefactor.
People do not feel bound to conceive a passion of the same kind or for the same person as their friend who is in love.
Love appears disproportioned to the value of the object to every person except the lover.
Love is pardoned in a certain age because it is natural but is always laughed at because others cannot enter into it.
All serious and strong expressions of love appear ridiculous to a third person.
A lover may be good company to his mistress but is good company to nobody else.
A lover, while in sober senses, endeavors to treat his own passion with raillery and ridicule.
People prefer to hear of love in a style of raillery and ridicule rather than in a grave, pedantic, and long-sentenced style.

Our sympathy with sorrow is generally a more lively sensation than our sympathy with joy.

The benefits of the rich and powerful can extend but to a few, but their fortunes interest almost everybody.
People are eager to assist the rich and powerful in completing a system of happiness that approaches perfection.
People desire to serve the rich and powerful for their own sake, without any other recompense but vanity or honor.
Deference to the inclinations of the rich and powerful is not chiefly founded on regard to the utility of submission or the order of society.
Even when society's order seems to require opposition to superiors, people can hardly bring themselves to oppose them.
The doctrine that kings are servants of the people to be obeyed, resisted, deposed, or punished as public convenience requires is a doctrine of reason and philosophy, not of Nature.
Nature teaches submission to kings for their own sake, to tremble and bow before their exalted station.
People regard the smile of kings as a sufficient reward for any services.
People dread the displeasure of kings as the severest of all mortifications, even if no other evil follows.
Treating kings as ordinary men and reasoning or disputing with them requires great resolution and is supported by familiarity and acquaintance.
Strong motives and passions like fear, hatred, and resentment are rarely sufficient to overcome the natural disposition to respect kings.
Kings' conduct must have excited the highest degree of passions before the bulk of the people oppose them with violence or desire their punishment or deposition.
Even after opposing kings violently, people are apt to relent and relapse into habitual deference to their natural superiors.
People cannot stand the mortification of their monarch and compassion soon replaces resentment.
People forget past provocations and their old principles of loyalty revive after opposing their monarch.
People run to re-establish the ruined authority of their old masters with the same violence with which they had opposed it.
The death of Charles I brought about the Restoration of the royal family.
Compassion for James II when seized by the populace almost prevented the Revolution and made it proceed more heavily.
The great may seem insensible to the easy price at which they may acquire public admiration.
The young nobleman is instructed to support the dignity of his rank by habitual regard to every circumstance of ordinary behavior.
The young nobleman studies to perform small duties with exact propriety because he is conscious of being observed.
The young nobleman acts with freedom and elevation inspired by the thought that mankind favors his inclinations.
The young nobleman's air, manner, and deportment mark an elegant and graceful sense of his own superiority.
Those born to inferior stations can hardly ever arrive at the elegant and graceful sense of superiority shown by the young nobleman.
The young nobleman uses arts supported by rank and preeminence to make mankind submit to his authority and govern their inclinations.
These arts, supported by rank and preeminence, are usually sufficient to govern the world on ordinary occasions.
Lewis XIV was regarded during most of his reign as the most perfect model of a great prince in France and all Europe.
Lewis XIV acquired his great reputation not by scrupulous justice, dangers, difficulties, or unrelenting application.
Lewis XIV did not acquire his reputation by extensive knowledge, exquisite judgment, or heroic valor.
Lewis XIV was first of all the most powerful prince in Europe and held the highest rank among kings.
Lewis XIV surpassed all his courtiers in the gracefulness of his shape and majestic beauty of his features.
The sound of Lewis XIV's voice was noble and affecting and gained hearts which his presence intimidated.
Lewis XIV had a step and deportment suitable only to him and his rank, which would have been ridiculous in any other person.
The embarrassment of those who spoke to Lewis XIV flattered his secret satisfaction with his own superiority.
An old officer confessed trembling before Lewis XIV, saying he did not tremble before his enemies.
Lewis XIV's frivolous accomplishments, supported by his rank and some talents and virtues, established him in the esteem of his age.
Lewis XIV's reputation has drawn respect from posterity.
In Lewis XIV's times and presence, no other virtue appeared to have merit compared to his accomplishments.
Politeness is considered a virtue of the great and does little honor to anyone but themselves.
A coxcomb who imitates the manner of the great and tries to appear eminent by superior propriety is rewarded with contempt for folly and presumption.
A man of inferior rank is unlikely to distinguish himself by politeness or mannerisms.
A private man should exhibit perfect modesty and plainness, with as much negligence as is consistent with respect to company.
A private man must acquire dependents to balance those of the great, relying on the labor of his body and activity of his mind.
A private man must cultivate superior knowledge in his profession and superior industry in its exercise.
A private man must be patient in labor, resolute in danger, and firm in distress.
A private man must bring his talents into public view through difficult, important, and judicious undertakings pursued with severe and unrelenting application.
Probity, prudence, generosity, and frankness must characterize a private man's behavior on ordinary occasions.
A private man must be forward to engage in situations requiring great talents and virtues to act with propriety and gain honor.
A man of spirit and ambition who is depressed by his situation looks impatiently for great opportunities to distinguish himself.
Such a man looks forward with satisfaction to foreign war or civil dissension as occasions to gain attention and admiration.
A man of rank and distinction whose glory consists in propriety of ordinary behavior is content with humble renown and has no talents to acquire others.
The man of rank is unwilling to embarrass himself with situations attended with difficulty or distress.
To figure at a ball is the great triumph of a man of rank, and succeeding in an intrigue of gallantry is his highest exploit.
The man of rank has an aversion to public confusions, not from love of mankind or lack of courage, but from consciousness of lacking required virtues.
The man of rank may expose himself to some little danger and make a campaign when it is fashionable.
The man of rank shudders at situations demanding continual and long exertion of patience, industry, fortitude, and application of thought.
Virtues like patience, industry, fortitude, and application of thought are hardly ever met with in men born to high stations.
In all governments, even monarchies, highest offices and administration are generally held by men educated in middle and inferior ranks who advanced by industry and abilities.
These men who advanced by industry and abilities face jealousy and resentment from those born their superiors.
The great first regard these men with contempt, then envy, and finally truckle to them with abject meanness.
The loss of easy empire over the affections of mankind makes the fall from greatness insupportable.
When the family of the king of Macedon was led in triumph by Paulus Æmilius, their misfortunes divided the attention of the Roman people with their conqueror.
The sight of the royal children, tender in age and insensible of their situation, struck spectators with sorrow and compassion.
The king appeared confounded, astonished, and bereft of all sentiment by the greatness of his calamities.
The king's friends and ministers often looked at him and burst into tears, showing they thought of his greatness of calamities rather than their own misfortunes.
The generous Romans regarded the fallen king with disdain and indignation, considering him unworthy of compassion for bearing to live under such calamities.
According to most historians, the king was to spend his remaining days under protection of a powerful and humane people in a state of plenty, ease, leisure, and security.
The king was no longer surrounded by an admiring mob of fools, flatterers, and dependents.
The king was no longer gazed upon by multitudes nor able to render himself the object of their respect, gratitude, love, or admiration.
The passions of nations were no longer molded by the king's inclinations.
This loss of public attention and influence was the insupportable calamity that bereaved the king of all sentiment.
Lord Rochefoucault said that love is commonly succeeded by ambition, but ambition is hardly ever succeeded by love.
Ambition, when it possesses the breast entirely, admits neither a rival nor a successor.
Those accustomed to possession or hope of public admiration find all other pleasures sicken and decay.
Most discarded statesmen who tried to overcome ambition and despise honors they could no longer attain spent their time in listless and insipid indolence.
These statesmen were chagrined at thoughts of their own insignificance and incapable of interest in private life occupations.
They found enjoyment only when talking of former greatness and satisfaction only when engaged in vain projects to recover it.

To live free, fearless, and independent and never barter liberty for servitude, one should never enter the place of ambition or compare oneself with masters of the earth who have already engrossed public attention.
People imagine it is very important to be in a situation that attracts general sympathy and attention.
Place is a great object that divides the wives of aldermen.
Place is the end of half the labors of human life.
Place is the cause of all the tumult, bustle, rapine, and injustice introduced by avarice and ambition.
People of sense despise place, meaning they despise sitting at the head of the table.
People of sense are indifferent about who is pointed out to the company by small advantages.
No man despises rank, distinction, or preeminence unless he is raised far above or sunk far below the ordinary standard of human nature.
A man who is confirmed in wisdom and real philosophy is satisfied with propriety of conduct and does not care about being attended to or approved of.
A man habituated to the idea of his own meanness may be so indifferent as to forget the desire for superiority.
Becoming the natural object of joyous congratulations and sympathetic attentions gives prosperity its dazzling splendor.
Nothing darkens the gloom of adversity more than feeling that misfortunes are objects of contempt and aversion.
The most dreadful calamities are not always the most difficult to support.
It is often more mortifying to appear in public under small disasters than under great misfortunes.
Small disasters excite no sympathy, but great misfortunes call forth lively compassion.
The sentiments of spectators are closer to those of the sufferer in great misfortunes than in small disasters.
Imperfect fellow-feeling lends some assistance in supporting misery.
A gentleman would be more mortified to appear covered with filth and rags than with blood and wounds before a gay assembly.
Blood and wounds would interest the pity of a gay assembly.
Filth and rags would provoke laughter from a gay assembly.
A judge who orders a criminal to be set in the pillory dishonors him more than if he had condemned him to the scaffold.
A great prince who caned a general officer at the head of his army disgraced him irrecoverably.
The punishment of caning is considered more dishonoring than shooting through the body.
By the laws of honor, to strike with a cane dishonors, but to strike with a sword does not.
Slighter punishments inflicted on a gentleman are regarded as the most dreadful by a humane and generous people.
European governments, except Russia, do not scourge or set persons of quality in the pillory for any crime.
A brave man is not rendered contemptible by being brought to the scaffold.
A brave man is rendered contemptible by being set in the pillory.
A brave man's behavior at the scaffold may gain him universal esteem and admiration.
No behavior at the pillory can render a man agreeable.
The sympathy of spectators supports a man at the scaffold.
There is no sympathy for a man in the pillory, or if any, it is not with his pain but with his consciousness of lack of sympathy.
Those who pity a man in the pillory blush and hang down their heads.
A man in the pillory feels irrecoverably degraded by the punishment, not by the crime.
A man who dies with resolution is regarded with esteem and approbation.
A man who dies with resolution wears an undaunted countenance.
If a crime does not deprive a man of respect, the punishment never will.
A man who dies with resolution has no suspicion that his situation is the object of contempt or derision.
A man who dies with resolution can assume an air of perfect serenity, triumph, and exultation.
Cardinal de Retz said great dangers have charms because there is some glory even when we miscarry.
Cardinal de Retz said moderate dangers have nothing but what is horrible because loss of reputation always attends lack of success.
Human virtue is superior to pain, poverty, danger, and death.
Human virtue does not require its utmost efforts to despise pain, poverty, danger, and death.
Having misery exposed to insult and derision is a situation in which human virtue's constancy is more apt to fail.
Compared with the contempt of mankind, all other external evils are easily supported.
There is a disposition to admire and almost worship the rich and powerful.
There is a disposition to despise or neglect persons of poor and mean condition.
This disposition is necessary to establish and maintain the distinction of ranks and the order of society.
This disposition is the great and most universal cause of the corruption of our moral sentiments.
Wealth and greatness are often regarded with respect and admiration due only to wisdom and virtue.
Contempt is often unjustly bestowed upon poverty and weakness.
Moralists in all ages have complained about the unjust admiration of wealth and greatness and contempt of poverty and weakness.
People desire both to be respectable and to be respected.
People dread both to be contemptible and to be contemned.
Upon coming into the world, people find that wisdom and virtue are not the sole objects of respect.
The respectful attentions of the world are more strongly directed towards the rich and great than towards the wise and virtuous.
The vices and follies of the powerful are much less despised than the poverty and weakness of the innocent.
To deserve, acquire, and enjoy the respect and admiration of mankind are great objects of ambition and emulation.
Two roads lead to respect and admiration: the study of wisdom and practice of virtue, and the acquisition of wealth and greatness.
Two different characters are presented for emulation: one of proud ambition and ostentatious avidity, and one of humble modesty and equitable justice.
Two different models are held out to fashion character and behavior: one gaudy and glittering, the other correct and exquisitely beautiful.
The gaudy and glittering model forces itself upon the notice of every wandering eye.
The correct and exquisitely beautiful model attracts the attention of scarce anybody but the most studious and careful observer.
The wise and virtuous are a select, though small, party who are the real and steady admirers of wisdom and virtue.
The great mob of mankind are admirers and worshippers of wealth and greatness.
Most frequently, the admirers and worshippers of wealth and greatness are disinterested.
The respect felt for wisdom and virtue is different from that conceived for wealth and greatness.
The sentiments of respect for wisdom and virtue and for wealth and greatness bear a considerable resemblance.
In some particular features, the sentiments of respect for wisdom and virtue and for wealth and greatness are different.
In the general air of the countenance, the sentiments of respect for wisdom and virtue and for wealth and greatness seem very nearly the same.
Inattentive observers are very apt to mistake the respect for wealth and greatness for respect for wisdom and virtue.
In equal degrees of merit, scarce any man respects the poor and humble more than the rich and great.
Most men admire the presumption and vanity of the rich and great more than the real and solid merit of the poor and humble.
It is not agreeable to good morals or good language to say that mere wealth and greatness, abstracted from merit and virtue, deserve respect.
Mere wealth and greatness almost constantly obtain respect.
Wealth and greatness may be considered as, in some respects, natural objects of respect.
Exalted stations may be completely degraded by vice and folly.
Vice and folly must be very great to completely degrade exalted stations.
The profligacy of a man of fashion is looked upon with much less contempt and aversion than that of a man of meaner condition.
In a man of meaner condition, a single transgression of rules of temperance and propriety is more resented than the constant and avowed contempt of them in a man of fashion.
In the middling and inferior stations of life, the road to virtue and the road to fortune are very nearly the same.
In the middling and inferior professions, real and solid professional abilities joined to prudent, just, firm, and temperate conduct can very seldom fail of success.
Abilities sometimes prevail where conduct is not correct.
Habitual imprudence, injustice, weakness, or profligacy will always cloud and sometimes depress the most splendid professional abilities.
Men in inferior and middling stations can never be great enough to be above the law.
People have a disposition to admire and imitate the rich and the great.
The rich and the great are able to set or lead what is called the fashion.
The dress of the rich and great is considered the fashionable dress.
The language of conversation of the rich and great is considered the fashionable style.
The air and deportment of the rich and great are considered the fashionable behaviour.
Even the vices and follies of the rich and great are considered fashionable.
Many men are proud to imitate and resemble the rich and great in qualities that dishonour and degrade them.
Vain men often give themselves airs of fashionable profligacy which they do not approve of in their hearts.
Some vain men are not guilty of the profligacy they pretend to have.
Vain men desire to be praised for things they do not think praise-worthy.
Vain men are ashamed of unfashionable virtues which they sometimes practise in secret.
There are hypocrites of wealth and greatness as well as of religion and virtue.
A vain man is as apt to pretend to be what he is not in wealth and greatness as a cunning man is in religion and virtue.
A vain man assumes the equipage and splendid way of living of his superiors without considering the suitability to their situation and fortune.
Praise-worthy qualities derive their merit and propriety from their suitableness to the situation and fortune of the person.
Many poor men place their glory in being thought rich.
Poor men who pretend to be rich often do not consider that the duties imposed by that reputation can reduce them to beggary.
Candidates for fortune too frequently abandon the paths of virtue.
The road to fortune and the road to virtue sometimes lie in very opposite directions.
Ambitious men flatter themselves that in a splendid situation they will command respect and admiration.
Ambitious men believe they will act with superior propriety and grace in their elevated situation.
Ambitious men believe the lustre of their future conduct will cover or efface the foulness of the steps by which they arrived at elevation.
In many governments, candidates for the highest stations are above the law.
Candidates for the highest stations who attain their ambition have no fear of being called to account for the means by which they acquired it.
Candidates for greatness often use fraud and falsehood, intrigue and cabal to supplant and destroy those who oppose them.
Candidates for greatness sometimes perpetrate enormous crimes such as murder, assassination, rebellion, and civil war to achieve their aims.
Candidates for greatness more frequently miscarry than succeed.
Those who miscarry in their ambitions commonly gain disgraceful punishment due to their crimes.
Those who attain wished-for greatness are often miserably disappointed in the happiness they expect to enjoy.
Ambitious men pursue honour rather than ease or pleasure.
The honour of an exalted station appears polluted and defiled by the baseness of the means through which it was attained.
Ambitious men may try to efface the remembrance of their past deeds by profuse liberal expense, indulgence in profligate pleasure, public business, or war.
The remembrance of past deeds never fails to pursue ambitious men.
Ambitious men remember what they have done and believe others remember it as well.
Amidst pomp, adulation, acclamations, pride of conquest, and triumph of war, ambitious men are secretly pursued by shame and remorse.
Ambitious men imagine black and foul infamy pursuing them and ready to overtake them.
Even great Caesar could not dismiss his suspicions despite dismissing his guards.
The remembrance of Pharsalia haunted and pursued Caesar.
Caesar pardoned Marcellus at the request of the senate.
Caesar told the senate he was aware of designs against his life but was content to die and despised conspiracies.
Caesar had perhaps lived long enough for nature but had lived too long for real glory or happiness in the love and esteem of his equals.
Part II is titled 'Of Merit and Demerit; or, Of the Objects of Reward and Punishment.'
Part II consists of three sections.
There is a set of qualities ascribed to the actions and conduct of mankind that are distinct from propriety or impropriety, and from decency or ungracefulness.
These distinct qualities are called Merit and Demerit.

statements.59-3: Merit is the quality of deserving reward.

statements.text: Demerit is the quality of deserving punishment.
The sentiment or affection of the heart from which any action proceeds is the basis of the action's virtue or vice.
The sentiment or affection can be considered in two different relations: first, in relation to the cause or object which excites it.
The sentiment or affection can also be considered in relation to the end it proposes or the effect it tends to produce.
The propriety or impropriety, decency or ungracefulness of an action depends on the suitableness or unsuitableness of the affection to the cause or object which excites it.
The merit or demerit, the good or ill desert of an action depends on the beneficial or hurtful effects which the affection proposes or tends to produce.
The sense of the propriety or impropriety of actions has been explained in the former part of the discourse.
The current section aims to consider the sense of the good or ill desert of actions.
Whatever appears to be the proper object of gratitude appears to deserve reward.
Whatever appears to be the proper object of resentment appears to deserve punishment.
An action must appear to deserve reward if it appears to be the proper and approved object of the sentiment that most immediately and directly prompts us to reward.
An action must appear to deserve punishment if it appears to be the proper and approved object of the sentiment that most immediately and directly prompts us to punish.
The sentiment that most immediately and directly prompts us to reward is gratitude.
The sentiment that most immediately and directly prompts us to punish is resentment.
An action must appear to deserve reward if it appears to be the proper and approved object of gratitude.
An action must appear to deserve punishment if it appears to be the proper and approved object of resentment.
To reward is to recompense, remunerate, or return good for good received.
To punish is to recompense or remunerate in a different manner; it is to return evil for evil that has been done.
There are other passions besides gratitude and resentment that interest us in the happiness or misery of others.
No other passions so directly excite us to be the instruments of either happiness or misery as gratitude and resentment.
Love and esteem that grow upon acquaintance and habitual approbation lead us to be pleased with the good fortune of the person who is the object of such emotions.
Love and esteem make us willing to lend a hand to promote the good fortune of the person we love or esteem.
Love is satisfied if the good fortune of the person we love is brought about without our assistance.
Gratitude is not satisfied if the person to whom we owe obligations is made happy without our assistance.
Gratitude feels a debt until we have recompensed the person to whom we owe obligations.
Hatred and dislike that grow upon habitual disapprobation can lead us to take malicious pleasure in the misfortune of the person who excites such passions.
Dislike and hatred harden us against sympathy and sometimes dispose us to rejoice at another's distress.
If there is no resentment, dislike and hatred would not naturally lead us to wish to be instrumental in bringing about another's misfortune.
Even if we could fear no punishment, we would rather that the misfortune of a disliked person happen by other means than by our own hand.
A person under violent hatred might find it agreeable to hear that the person he abhors was killed by accident.
If a person had the least spark of justice, it would hurt him excessively to have been the occasion of the misfortune of a person he dislikes.
The thought of voluntarily contributing to the misfortune of a disliked person would shock a person beyond all measure.
A person would reject with horror the imagination of designing to cause misfortune to a disliked person.
If a person could imagine himself capable of causing such misfortune, he would regard himself as odious as the person he dislikes.
If a person who had done us a great injury dies of a fever or is executed for another crime, it might soothe our hatred but not fully gratify our resentment.
Resentment prompts us to desire that the person who injured us be punished by our means and for that particular injury.
Resentment cannot be fully gratified unless the offender grieves for the particular wrong he caused us.
The offender must be made to repent and be sorry for the specific action that caused harm.
Others may be terrified from committing the same offense through fear of like punishment.
The natural gratification of resentment tends to produce the political ends of punishment, including correction of the criminal and example to the public.
Gratitude and resentment are the sentiments that most immediately and directly prompt reward and punishment.
A person must appear to deserve reward if he appears to be the proper and approved object of gratitude.
A person must appear to deserve punishment if he appears to be the proper and approved object of resentment.
To be the proper and approved object of gratitude or resentment means to be the object of gratitude or resentment that naturally seems proper and is approved of.
Passions of human nature seem proper and are approved of when the heart of every impartial spectator entirely sympathizes with them.
Passions of human nature seem proper and are approved of when every indifferent by-stander entirely enters into and goes along with them.
A person deserves reward if they are the natural object of gratitude which every human heart is disposed to applaud.
A person deserves punishment if they are the natural object of resentment which every reasonable man is ready to adopt and sympathize with.
An action deserves reward if everybody who knows of it wishes to reward it and delights to see it rewarded.
An action deserves punishment if everybody who hears of it is angry with it and rejoices to see it punished.
We sympathize with the joy of our companions when they are in prosperity.
We join with our companions in the complacency and satisfaction with which they naturally regard the cause of their good fortune.
We enter into the love and affection our companions conceive for the cause of their good fortune and begin to love it too.
We would be sorry if the cause of our companions' good fortune was destroyed or placed too far from them, even if they lost no pleasure except seeing it.

If a man has been the fortunate instrument of the happiness of his brethren, our sympathy with the joy of the person who receives the benefit animates our fellow-feeling with his gratitude towards the benefactor.
When we look upon the benefactor with the eyes we imagine the recipient must look upon him, the benefactor appears in an engaging and amiable light.
We readily sympathize with the grateful affection the recipient conceives for the benefactor.
We applaud the returns the recipient is disposed to make for the good offices conferred upon him.
As we enter into the affection from which these returns proceed, the returns seem proper and suitable to their object.
We sympathize with the sorrow of our fellow-creature whenever we see his distress.
We enter into the abhorrence and aversion our fellow-creature has for whatever caused his distress.
Our heart adopts and beats time to the grief of the sufferer and is animated with the spirit by which he endeavors to drive away or destroy the cause of it.

The indolent and passive fellow-feeling by which we accompany the sufferer in his sufferings gives way to a more vigorous and active sentiment to go along with him in repelling or gratifying his aversion to the cause.
When one man is oppressed or injured by another, our sympathy with the distress of the sufferer animates our fellow-feeling with his resentment against the offender.
We are rejoiced to see the sufferer attack his adversary in his turn.
We are eager and ready to assist the sufferer whenever he exerts himself for defense or vengeance within a certain degree.
If the injured person perishes in the quarrel, we sympathize with the real resentment of his friends and relations.
We sympathize with the imaginary resentment we lend to the dead who is no longer capable of feeling any human sentiment.
We put ourselves in the situation of the dead, entering into his body and animating anew his deformed and mangled carcass in our imagination.
When we bring the case of the dead home to our own bosoms, we feel an emotion which the person principally concerned is incapable of feeling.
The sympathetic tears we shed for the immense and irretrievable loss of the dead seem to be a small part of the duty we owe him.
The injury suffered by the dead demands a principal part of our attention.
We feel the resentment which we imagine the dead ought to feel and would feel if there remained any consciousness in his body.
We think the blood of the dead calls aloud for vengeance.
The very ashes of the dead seem disturbed at the thought that his injuries are to pass unrevenged.
The horrors supposed to haunt the bed of the murderer and the ghosts imagined to rise from graves to demand vengeance originate from natural sympathy with the imaginary resentment of the slain.
Nature has stamped upon the human heart an immediate and instinctive approbation of the sacred and necessary law of retaliation, antecedent to all reflections upon the utility of punishment.
Where there is no approbation of the conduct of the person who confers the benefit, there is little sympathy with the gratitude of the person who receives it.
Where there is no disapprobation of the motives of the person who causes harm, there is no sympathy with the resentment of the person who suffers.
If the motives of the agent appear improper, we have little sympathy with the gratitude of the beneficiary.
If the motives of the agent appear proper and we enter into the affections influencing the conduct, we have no sympathy with the resentment of the sufferer.
Little gratitude seems due when the agent's motives lack propriety.
All sorts of resentment seem unjust when the agent's motives are proper.
An action with improper motives seems to merit little reward.
An action with proper motives seems to deserve no punishment.
Where we cannot sympathize with the agent's affections, we are less disposed to enter into the gratitude of the beneficiary.
Foolish and profuse generosity conferring great benefits from trivial motives demands a very small return.
Giving an estate to a man merely because his name is the same as the giver's does not demand proportionate recompense.
Contempt for the folly of the agent hinders sympathy with the gratitude of the beneficiary.
A benefactor who acts from trivial motives seems unworthy of gratitude.
When placing ourselves in the situation of the person obliged, we feel no great reverence for a benefactor with trivial motives.
We easily absolve a foolish benefactor from much submissive veneration and esteem.
If a benefactor treats a weak friend with kindness and humanity, we excuse him from many attentions and regards demanded of a worthier patron.
Princes who have profusely given wealth, power, and honours to favourites have seldom excited strong attachment.
James the First of Great Britain was well-natured but injudiciously prodigal and seems to have attached nobody to his person.
James the First appears to have lived and died without a friend.
The gentry and nobility of England exposed their lives and fortunes for James the First's more frugal and distinguishing son.
The son of James the First had a cold and distant severity in his ordinary deportment.
Where the agent's conduct is directed by motives and affections we approve of, we cannot sympathize with the resentment of the sufferer.
When two people quarrel, adopting the resentment of one makes it impossible to enter into the resentment of the other.
Sympathy with the person whose motives we approve hardens us against sympathy with the other party.
We regard the person whose motives we disapprove as in the wrong.
Whatever the person regarded as in the wrong suffers, if it is what we would have wished him to suffer, it cannot displease or provoke us.
When an inhuman murderer is brought to the scaffold, we may have compassion for his misery.
We cannot sympathize with the resentment of a murderer against his prosecutor or judge.
The just indignation of prosecutor and judge against a vile criminal is fatal and ruinous to the criminal.
We cannot be displeased with a sentiment whose tendency we ourselves adopt when we bring the case home to ourselves.
We do not thoroughly and heartily sympathize with the gratitude of one man towards another merely because the other has caused his good fortune.
We must adopt the principles of the agent and go along with all the affections which influenced his conduct before we can entirely sympathize with the gratitude of the person who has been benefited.
If there has been no propriety in the conduct of the benefactor, no matter how beneficial its effects, it does not necessarily require any proportionable recompense.
When the beneficent tendency of the action is joined with the propriety of the affection from which it proceeds, we entirely sympathize and go along with the motives of the agent.
The love conceived for the benefactor on his own account enhances and enlivens our fellow-feeling with the gratitude of those who owe their prosperity to his good conduct.
Actions that have beneficent tendencies and proper affections seem to demand and call aloud for a proportionable recompense.
We entirely enter into the gratitude which prompts to bestow a reward when we entirely sympathize with and approve of the sentiment prompting the reward.
The benefactor is the proper object of reward when we entirely sympathize with and approve of the sentiment prompting to reward him.
When we approve of and go along with the affection from which the action proceeds, we must necessarily approve of the action.
When we approve of the affection from which the action proceeds, we regard the person towards whom it is directed as its proper and suitable object.
We cannot sympathize with the resentment of one man against another merely because the other has caused his misfortune.
We cannot sympathize with resentment unless the cause of misfortune acted from motives which we cannot enter into.
Before adopting the resentment of the sufferer, we must disapprove of the motives of the agent.
We must feel that our heart renounces all sympathy with the affections which influenced the conduct of the agent before we can adopt the resentment.
If there is no impropriety in the motives of the agent, no matter how fatal the tendency of the action, it does not deserve punishment or resentment.
When the hurtfulness of the action is joined with the impropriety of the affection from which it proceeds, our heart rejects all fellow-feeling with the motives of the agent.
When our heart rejects all fellow-feeling with the motives of the agent, we heartily and entirely sympathize with the resentment of the sufferer.
Actions that are hurtful and proceed from improper affections seem to deserve and call aloud for a proportionable punishment.
We entirely enter into and approve of the resentment which prompts to inflict punishment when we sympathize with it.
The offender seems to be the proper object of punishment when we entirely sympathize with and approve of the sentiment prompting to punish.
When we approve and go along with the affection from which the action proceeds, we must necessarily approve of the action.
When we approve of the affection from which the action proceeds, we regard the person against whom it is directed as its proper and suitable object.
Our sense of the propriety of conduct arises from a direct sympathy with the affections and motives of the person who acts.
Our sense of merit arises from an indirect sympathy with the gratitude of the person who is acted upon.
We cannot thoroughly enter into the gratitude of the person who receives the benefit unless we beforehand approve of the motives of the benefactor.

The sense of merit is a compounded sentiment made up of two distinct emotions: a direct sympathy with the sentiments of the agent and an indirect sympathy with the gratitude of those who receive the benefit.
When reading history about actions of proper and beneficent greatness of mind, we enter eagerly into such designs and are animated by the generosity which directs them.
We become keen for the success of such actions and grieved at their disappointment.
In imagination, we transport ourselves to the scenes of distant and forgotten adventures and imagine ourselves acting the part of historical benefactors.
These sentiments are founded upon direct sympathy with the person who acts.
Indirect sympathy with those who receive the benefit of such actions is also sensibly felt.
When placing ourselves in the situation of beneficiaries, we enter with warm and affectionate fellow-feeling into their gratitude towards their benefactors.
Our heart sympathizes with the highest transports of grateful affection of those who receive benefits.
We think no honors or rewards can be too great for those who bestow such benefits.
We heartily applaud and go along with proper returns made by beneficiaries to their benefactors.
We are shocked beyond measure if beneficiaries appear to have little sense of the obligations conferred upon them.
Our whole sense of merit, good desert, propriety of recompense, and making the benefactor rejoice arises from sympathetic emotions of gratitude and love.
Our sense of the impropriety of conduct arises from a want of sympathy or a direct antipathy to the affections and motives of the agent.
Our sense of demerit arises from an indirect sympathy with the resentment of the sufferer.
We cannot enter into the resentment of the sufferer unless our heart beforehand disapproves the motives of the agent and renounces all fellow-feeling with them.
The sense of demerit is a compounded sentiment made up of two distinct emotions: a direct antipathy to the sentiments of the agent and an indirect sympathy with the resentment of the sufferer.
When reading history about perfidy and cruelty of persons like Borgia or Nero, our heart rises against the detestable sentiments influencing their conduct.
Our sentiments in such cases are founded upon direct antipathy to the affections of the agent.
Indirect sympathy with the resentment of sufferers is more sensibly felt.
When we bring home to ourselves the situation of persons insulted, murdered, or betrayed by oppressors, we feel indignation against such oppressors.
Our sympathy with the unavoidable distress of innocent sufferers is as real and lively as our fellow-feeling with their just and natural resentment.
The sympathy with the distress of sufferers heightens our animosity against those who caused it.
The idea of the sufferers' distress inflames and intensifies our animosity against their oppressors.
When thinking of the anguish of sufferers, we take part with them more earnestly against their oppressors.
We enter with eagerness into the schemes of vengeance of sufferers.
We imagine wreaking punishment upon violators of the laws of society.
Our sense of the horror and atrocity of such conduct arises from sympathetic indignation.
We take delight in hearing that such conduct was properly punished.
We feel indignation when such conduct escapes due retaliation.
