Our whole sense of ill desert, propriety of inflicting evil on the guilty, and making them grieve arises from sympathetic indignation.
Sympathetic indignation naturally arises in the breast of the spectator when he brings home to himself the case of the sufferer.
The section is titled 'OF JUSTICE AND BENEFICENCE.'
This is Section II of the text.
Actions of a beneficent tendency that proceed from proper motives seem alone to require reward.
Actions of a beneficent tendency are the approved objects of gratitude or excite the sympathetic gratitude of the spectator.
Actions of a hurtful tendency that proceed from improper motives seem alone to deserve punishment.
Actions of a hurtful tendency are the approved objects of resentment or excite the sympathetic resentment of the spectator.
Beneficence is always free and cannot be extorted by force.
The mere want of beneficence exposes to no punishment.
The mere want of beneficence tends to do no real positive evil.
The mere want of beneficence may disappoint of the good which might reasonably have been expected.
The mere want of beneficence may justly excite dislike and disapprobation.
The mere want of beneficence cannot provoke any resentment which mankind will go along with.
A man who does not recompense his benefactor when he has the power and the benefactor needs assistance is guilty of the blackest ingratitude.
The heart of every impartial spectator rejects all fellow-feeling with the selfishness of such motives.
A man who is selfish in gratitude is the proper object of the highest disapprobation.
A man who is selfish in gratitude does no positive hurt to anybody.
A man who is selfish in gratitude only does not do that good which in propriety he ought to have done.
Hatred is a passion naturally excited by impropriety of sentiment and behaviour.
Resentment is a passion never properly called forth but by actions which tend to do real and positive hurt to some particular persons.
The want of gratitude cannot be punished.
To oblige a man by force to perform what in gratitude he ought to perform would be more improper than his neglecting to perform it.
A benefactor would dishonour himself if he attempted by violence to constrain a man to gratitude.
It would be impertinent for any third person who was not the superior of either to intermeddle in compelling gratitude.
Duties of beneficence recommended by gratitude approach nearest to what is called a perfect and complete obligation.
Friendship, generosity, and charity prompt us to do with universal approbation what is more free and less extorted by force than duties of gratitude.
We talk of the debt of gratitude, not of charity, generosity, or friendship when friendship is mere esteem without gratitude for good offices.
Resentment seems to have been given by nature for defence and for defence only.
Resentment is the safeguard of justice and the security of innocence.
Resentment prompts us to beat off mischief attempted to be done to us and to retaliate that which is already done.
Resentment aims that the offender may repent of his injustice and that others may be terrified from committing the like offence.
Resentment must be reserved for defence and justice purposes.
The spectator cannot approve resentment when it is exerted for any other purpose than defence or justice.
The mere want of beneficent virtues may disappoint us of good but neither does nor attempts to do mischief from which we can defend ourselves.
Justice is a virtue of which observance is not left to the freedom of our own wills.
Justice may be extorted by force.
Violation of justice exposes to resentment and consequently to punishment.
Violation of justice is injury.
Injustice does real and positive hurt to some particular persons from motives naturally disapproved of.
Injustice is the proper object of resentment and punishment.
Mankind approve of violence employed to avenge hurt done by injustice.
Mankind approve of violence employed to prevent and beat off injury and to restrain offenders from hurting neighbors.
A person who meditates injustice feels that force may be properly used by the person he is about to injure and by others to obstruct or punish the crime.
A superior may sometimes oblige those under his jurisdiction to behave with a certain degree of propriety to one another with universal approbation.
The laws of all civilized nations oblige parents to maintain their children.
The laws of all civilized nations oblige children to maintain their parents.
The laws of civilized nations impose upon men many other duties of beneficence.
The civil magistrate is entrusted with the power of preserving the public peace by restraining injustice.
The civil magistrate is entrusted with the power of promoting the prosperity of the commonwealth by establishing good discipline.
The civil magistrate is entrusted with the power of discouraging every sort of vice and impropriety.
The civil magistrate may prescribe rules that prohibit mutual injuries among fellow-citizens.
The civil magistrate may prescribe rules that command mutual good offices to a certain degree.
When the sovereign commands what is merely indifferent and could have been omitted without blame, it becomes blameable and punishable to disobey him.
When the sovereign commands what could not have been omitted without the greatest blame, it becomes more punishable to be wanting in obedience.
The duty of a law-giver to command obedience requires great delicacy and reserve to execute with propriety and judgment.
Neglecting the duty of commanding obedience exposes the commonwealth to many gross disorders and shocking enormities.
Pushing the duty of commanding obedience too far is destructive of liberty, security, and justice.
The mere want of beneficence seems to merit no punishment from equals.
Greater exertions of beneficence appear to deserve the highest reward.
Greater exertions of beneficence are the natural and approved objects of the liveliest gratitude.
The breach of justice exposes to punishment.
The observance of the rules of justice seems scarcely to deserve any reward.
Justice merits all the approbation which is due to propriety.
Justice does no real positive good and is entitled to very little gratitude.
Mere justice is, on most occasions, a negative virtue that only hinders us from hurting our neighbour.
A man who abstains from violating the person, estate, or reputation of his neighbours has very little positive merit.
A man who abstains from violating his neighbours fulfils all the rules of justice.
A man who fulfils all the rules of justice does everything his equals can force him to do or punish him for not doing.
We may often fulfil all the rules of justice by sitting still and doing nothing.
Retaliation is the great law dictated to us by Nature expressed as 'As every man doth, so shall it be done to him.'
Beneficence and generosity are due to the generous and beneficent.
Those whose hearts never open to the feelings of humanity should be shut out from the affections of all their fellow-creatures.
Those whose hearts never open to humanity should be allowed to live in society as in a great desert where nobody cares for them or inquires after them.
The violator of the laws of justice ought to be made to feel the evil he has done to another.
If no regard to the sufferings of others restrains a violator of justice, he ought to be overawed by the fear of his own sufferings.
A man who is barely innocent and only observes the laws of justice can merit only that his neighbours respect his innocence.
A man who is barely innocent can merit that the same laws of justice be religiously observed with regard to him.
There can be no proper motive for hurting our neighbour except just indignation for evil which that other has done to us.
To disturb another's happiness merely because it stands in the way of our own is something no impartial spectator can accept.
Taking from another what is of real use to him merely because it may be of equal or more use to us is not acceptable.
Every man is by nature first and principally recommended to his own care.
It is fit and right that every man should be more deeply interested in whatever immediately concerns himself than in what concerns any other man.
Hearing of the death of another person with whom we have no particular connection will give us less concern than a very insignificant disaster that has befallen ourselves.
We must not ruin our neighbour to prevent a small misfortune to ourselves.
We must view ourselves not only as we appear to ourselves but also as we appear to others.
Though every man may prefer himself to all mankind, he dares not avow that he acts according to this principle to mankind.
Others will never go along with a man acting solely according to his natural preference for himself.
When a man views himself as others view him, he sees that to them he is but one of the multitude, no better than any other.
To act so that the impartial spectator may enter into the principles of one's conduct requires humbling the arrogance of self-love.
Others will allow a man to be more anxious about and pursue his own happiness more earnestly than that of any other person.
In the race for wealth, honours, and preferments, a man may strive hard to outstrip competitors.
If a man justles or throws down any competitor, the indulgence of the spectators ends.
Violating fair play is not admitted by spectators.
Spectators consider all men as equally good in every respect.
Spectators do not enter into the self-love by which a man prefers himself so much to another.
Spectators sympathize with the natural resentment of the injured.
The offender becomes the object of hatred and indignation from spectators.
The greater and more irreparable the evil done, the higher the resentment of the sufferer.
The sympathetic indignation of the spectator and the sense of guilt in the agent increase with the severity of the evil done.
Death is the greatest evil one man can inflict upon another.
Murder is the most atrocious of all crimes affecting individuals in the sight of mankind and the person who committed it.
Being deprived of what we possess is a greater evil than being disappointed of what we only expect.
Theft and robbery, which take from us what we possess, are greater crimes than breach of contract, which disappoints us of what we expected.
The most sacred laws of justice guard the life and person of our neighbour.
Next in sacredness are laws guarding property and possessions.
Last come laws guarding personal rights or what is due from promises of others.
Violators of the more sacred laws of justice feel agonies of shame, horror, and consternation.
When reflecting coolly on past conduct, the violator can enter into none of the motives which influenced it.
The violator sympathizes with the hatred and abhorrence others have for him.
The violator becomes in some measure the object of his own hatred and abhorrence.
The situation of the person who suffered by the violator's injustice calls upon the violator's pity.
The violator regrets the unhappy effects of his own conduct.
The violator feels that his conduct has rendered him the proper object of resentment and indignation of mankind.
The violator is haunted by the thought of vengeance and punishment.
The violator dares no longer look society in the face and imagines himself rejected by all mankind.
The violator cannot hope for the consolation of sympathy in his greatest distress.
The remembrance of the violator's crimes has shut out all fellow-feeling from the hearts of his fellow-creatures.
A man who performs a generous action from proper motives feels himself to be the natural object of love and gratitude from those he has served.
The man who has performed a generous action feels sympathy with those he has served.
The man who has performed a generous action feels the esteem and approbation of all mankind by sympathy with those he has served.
When the man looks backward to the motive from which he acted, he surveys it in the light in which an indifferent spectator would survey it.
The man continues to enter into the motive from which he acted and applauds himself by sympathy with the approbation of an impartial judge.
In both points of view, the man's own conduct appears to him agreeable.
The man's mind is filled with cheerfulness, serenity, and composure at the thought of his conduct.
The man is in friendship and harmony with all mankind.
The man looks upon his fellow-creatures with confidence and benevolent satisfaction.
The man is secure that he has rendered himself worthy of the most favourable regards of others.
The consciousness of merit or deserved reward consists in the combination of the sentiments described.
Man can subsist only in society and was fitted by nature to that situation.
All members of human society stand in need of each other's assistance and are exposed to mutual injuries.
When necessary assistance is reciprocally afforded from love, gratitude, friendship, and esteem, society flourishes and is happy.
Members of society are bound together by agreeable bands of love and affection, drawing them to a common center of mutual good offices.
Society may subsist without mutual love or affection if necessary assistance is given from a sense of utility.
Society can be upheld by a mercenary exchange of good offices according to an agreed valuation even if no man owes obligation or gratitude to another.
Society cannot subsist among those who are always ready to hurt and injure one another.
The moment injury begins and mutual resentment and animosity take place, all the bands of society are broken asunder.
If there is any society among robbers and murderers, they must abstain from robbing and murdering one another.
Beneficence is less essential to the existence of society than justice.
Society may subsist without beneficence but the prevalence of injustice must utterly destroy it.
Nature exhorts mankind to acts of beneficence by the pleasing consciousness of deserved reward.
Nature has not thought it necessary to enforce beneficence by the terrors of merited punishment if it is neglected.
Beneficence is the ornament which embellishes society, not the foundation which supports it.
Justice is the main pillar that upholds the whole edifice of human society.
If justice is removed, the fabric of human society must crumble into atoms.
Nature has implanted in the human breast a consciousness of ill desert and terrors of merited punishment to enforce justice.
These terrors of merited punishment serve as safeguards of the association of mankind to protect the weak, curb the violent, and chastise the guilty.
Men feel much less for another with whom they have no particular connection than for themselves.
The misery of a fellow-creature is of little importance to men compared to a small convenience of their own.
Men have much power to hurt others and many temptations to do so.
Without the principle of justice standing up in defense of innocence, men would be ready to attack one another like wild beasts.
In the universe, means are adjusted with the nicest artifice to the ends they are intended to produce.
In plants and animal bodies, every operation is contrived for advancing the support of the individual and propagation of the species.
Efficient causes and final causes are distinguished in the operations of bodies.
Digestion, circulation of blood, and secretion are necessary operations for animal life.
We do not ascribe desire or intention to bodily operations like digestion or blood circulation.
The wheels of a watch are adjusted to produce the effect of pointing the hour.
The wheels of a watch are put into motion by a spring which does not intend the effect it produces.
In accounting for mental operations, people often confuse efficient and final causes.
People tend to impute to reason the efficient cause of sentiments and actions that advance ends recommended by reason.
This leads to imagining that the wisdom of man is the cause of certain effects, when it is actually the wisdom of God.
The system of human nature seems simpler and more agreeable when all operations are deduced from a single principle.
Society cannot subsist unless the laws of justice are tolerably observed.
No social intercourse can take place among men who do not generally abstain from injuring one another.
It has been thought that the necessity of justice is the ground for approving enforcement of laws of justice by punishment.
Man has a natural love for society and desires the union of mankind to be preserved for its own sake.
Man takes delight in contemplating the orderly and flourishing state of society.
Man is chagrined at whatever tends to produce disorder and confusion in society.
Man is sensible that his own interest and possibly his preservation depend on the preservation of society.
Man has an abhorrence of whatever tends to destroy society and is willing to use every means to prevent it.
Injustice necessarily tends to destroy society.
Every appearance of injustice alarms man and he tries to stop its progress.
If injustice cannot be restrained by gentle means, man must suppress it by force and violence.
Man often approves enforcement of laws of justice by capital punishment of violators.
The disturber of the public peace is removed from the world by capital punishment.
Others are terrified by the fate of the punished disturber from imitating his example.
We frequently confirm our natural sense of the propriety and fitness of punishment by reflecting on its necessity for preserving the order of society.
When the guilty suffer just retaliation, the natural indignation of mankind tells them it is due to their crimes.
The terror of approaching punishment breaks and humbles the insolence of injustice.
When the guilty cease to be objects of fear, generous and humane people begin to pity them.
The thought of the guilty's suffering extinguishes resentment for the sufferings of others caused by them.
People are disposed to pardon and forgive the guilty and to save them from punishment they had considered due.
People call to their assistance the consideration of the general interest of society to counterbalance partial humanity.
Mercy to the guilty is considered cruelty to the innocent.
People oppose compassion for a particular person with a more enlarged compassion for mankind.
We sometimes defend the propriety of observing general rules of justice by their necessity to support society.
The young and licentious sometimes ridicule sacred rules of morality and profess abominable maxims of conduct.
Our indignation rouses us to refute and expose detestable principles.
We do not assign hatred and detestation as the sole reason for condemning detestable principles.
We think the reason for condemning detestable principles would not be conclusive if it were only because we hate them.
When asked why we should not act in certain manners, it is supposed that such manners are not naturally objects of hatred.
We generally argue that disorder and confusion of society would result from the universal prevalence of licentious practices.
It commonly requires no great discernment to see the destructive tendency of licentious practices to society's welfare.
All men, even the most stupid and unthinking, abhor fraud, perfidy, and injustice and delight to see them punished.
Few men have reflected upon the necessity of justice to the existence of society.
Concern for the fortune and happiness of individuals does not commonly arise from concern for society's fortune and happiness.
We are no more concerned for the destruction of a single man because he is part of society than for the loss of a single guinea because it is part of a thousand guineas.
Our regard for the multitude is made up of the particular regards we feel for the individuals composing it.
When a small sum is unjustly taken, we prosecute the injury from regard to that particular sum, not the whole fortune.
When a single man is injured or destroyed, we demand punishment not from concern for society's interest but for that individual.
This concern for individuals does not necessarily include love, esteem, or affection.
The concern requisite is the general fellow-feeling we have with every man as a fellow-creature.
We enter into the resentment of an odious person when he is injured by those who have given him no provocation.
Disapproval of a person's ordinary character does not altogether prevent fellow-feeling with his natural indignation.
People who are not extremely candid or accustomed to regulate natural sentiments by general rules tend to have their fellow-feeling damped.
Sometimes we punish and approve punishment from a view to the general interest of society which cannot otherwise be secured.
Punishments for breaches of civil police or military discipline do not immediately hurt any particular person.
The remote consequences of breaches of civil police or military discipline are supposed to produce considerable inconvenience or great disorder in society.
A sentinel who falls asleep on watch suffers death by the laws of war because such carelessness might endanger the whole army.
Such severity in punishment may appear necessary, just, and proper.
When the preservation of an individual is inconsistent with the safety of a multitude, it is just that the many be preferred to the one.
This punishment, though necessary, appears excessively severe.
The natural atrocity of the crime of a sentinel falling asleep is little, and the punishment is great.
It is difficult for the heart to reconcile itself to the punishment of a sentinel who falls asleep.
A man of humanity must exert firmness and resolution to inflict or accept such punishment.
The just punishment of an ungrateful murderer or parricide is viewed with ardour and transport by the heart.
If a murderer escapes punishment, it would excite highest indignation and calls for divine vengeance.
The different sentiments towards the punishment of a sentinel and a murderer prove that approbation of the one is not founded on the same principles as the other.
The centinel is viewed as an unfortunate victim devoted to the safety of numbers.
One would be glad to save the centinel, but the interest of the many opposes it.
If the murderer escapes punishment, it would cause great disappointment and anger.
Praise or blame due to any action must belong either to the intention or affection of the heart, the external action or movement of the body, or the good or bad consequences that proceed from it.
The three circumstances of an action—intention, external action, and consequences—constitute the whole nature and circumstances of the action.
The external action or movement of the body cannot be the foundation of any praise or blame.
The same external movement of the body can be present in both innocent and blameable actions.
For example, both a person who shoots a bird and a person who shoots a man perform the same external movement of drawing the trigger of a gun.
The consequences that actually proceed from any action are more indifferent to praise or blame than the external movement of the body.
Consequences depend on fortune and not on the agent.
Consequences cannot be the proper foundation for any sentiment regarding the character and conduct of the agent.
The only consequences for which an agent can be answerable are those that were intended or that show some agreeable or disagreeable quality in the intention of the heart.
All praise or blame, approbation or disapprobation, must ultimately belong to the intention or affection of the heart.
The maxim that praise or blame belongs to intention is self-evident and acknowledged by all mankind.
No one dissents from the maxim that the merit or demerit of actions depends on the intentions or affections from which they arose.
If intentions or affections are equally proper and beneficent, or equally improper and malevolent, the merit or demerit of the actions is the same.
The agent is equally the suitable object of gratitude or resentment if intentions are equally proper or improper.
In particular cases, actual consequences have a great effect on our sentiments concerning the merit or demerit of actions.
Actual consequences almost always either enhance or diminish our sense of merit or demerit.
Scarce any instance exists where our sentiments are entirely regulated by the rule that only intention determines merit or demerit.
This irregularity of sentiment is felt by everybody.
Scarce anybody is sufficiently aware of this irregularity of sentiment.
Nobody is willing to acknowledge this irregularity of sentiment.
The author proceeds to explain the cause of this irregularity of sentiment.
The author will consider the cause, the extent of influence, and the purpose intended by nature regarding this irregularity.
The causes of pain and pleasure immediately excite the passions of gratitude and resentment in all animals.
Gratitude and resentment are excited by both inanimated and animated objects.
People can be angry at inanimated objects, such as a stone that hurts them.
Reflection corrects the sentiment of anger towards inanimated objects, making us realize they are improper objects of revenge.
When the mischief caused by an object is very great, the object becomes disagreeable to us and we may take pleasure in destroying it.
We might treat an instrument that accidentally caused a friend's death with vengeance, feeling guilty if we neglect to do so.
People conceive a sort of gratitude for inanimated objects that have caused them great or frequent pleasure.
A sailor who escaped a shipwreck on a plank would likely preserve the plank with care and affection.
People can grow fond of objects like a snuff-box, pen-knife, or staff that they have long used.
Losing or breaking such cherished objects causes vexation disproportionate to the value of the damage.
Houses and trees that have been long enjoyed are looked upon with respect as benefactors.
The decay of a house or the ruin of a tree affects people with melancholy even if they sustain no loss.
The ancients' belief in Dryads and Lares, genii of trees and houses, was probably suggested by affection for such objects.
Before anything can be a proper object of gratitude or resentment, it must be the cause of pleasure or pain and capable of feeling them.
Gratitude and resentment cannot be satisfactorily vented on objects without sensibility.
Animals are less improper objects of gratitude and resentment than inanimated objects because they can feel pleasure and pain.
Animals that cause harm, such as a dog that bites or an ox that gores, are punished.
If animals cause the death of a person, they are often put to death to satisfy the relations of the slain and the public.
Animals that have been remarkably serviceable to their masters become objects of lively gratitude.
The brutality of an officer who stabbed his horse to prevent it from serving another person is shocking.
Animals are not complete and perfect objects of gratitude or resentment because something is still lacking for entire gratification.
Gratitude desires to make the benefactor feel pleasure in return and to make him conscious that he receives this reward because of his past conduct.
Gratitude aims to make the benefactor pleased with his conduct and satisfied that the recipient was worthy of his good offices.
We are charmed by the concord between our benefactor's sentiments and our own regarding the worth of our character and the esteem due to us.
We delight in finding a person who values us as we value ourselves and distinguishes us from others with similar attention.
One chief end of returns made to a benefactor is to maintain and increase his esteem.
A generous mind often disdains the thought of extorting new favors from a benefactor through importunities of gratitude.
When we cannot approve of the motives or character of our benefactor, our gratitude is diminished regardless of the services rendered.
We are less flattered by distinction from a weak or worthless patron and do not pursue preserving his esteem for its own sake.
Resentment aims not only to make the enemy feel pain but to make him conscious that he feels it because of his past conduct.
Resentment seeks to make the enemy repent of his conduct and realize that the injured person did not deserve such treatment.
What enrages us most against an injurer is the little account he makes of us and the unreasonable preference he gives to himself.
The absurd self-love of an injurer, imagining others may be sacrificed to his convenience or humor, shocks and exasperates us more than the mischief suffered.
A principal end of revenge is to bring the injurer back to a just sense of what is due to others and the wrong he has done.
Revenge is imperfect if it cannot make the injurer sensible of his wrong.
If the enemy acted properly and the injury was deserved, a person with candor or justice can entertain no resentment.
For an object to be a complete and proper object of gratitude or resentment, it must have three qualifications.
The first qualification is that the object must be the cause of pleasure in gratitude or pain in resentment.
The second qualification is that the object must be capable of feeling those sensations.
The third qualification is that the object must have produced those sensations from design, approved in gratitude and disapproved in resentment.
Pleasure or pain is the sole exciting cause of gratitude and resentment.
The intentions of a person can be proper and beneficent or improper and malevolent.
If a person fails to produce the good or evil they intended, less gratitude or resentment is due to them.
The absence of the exciting cause (pleasure or pain) results in less gratitude or resentment.
If a person's intentions lack benevolence or malice, but their actions produce great good or evil, some gratitude or resentment may still arise.
Producing great good without laudable benevolence results in a shadow of merit.
Producing great evil without blameable malice results in a shadow of demerit.
The consequences of actions are under the empire of Fortune.
Fortune influences the sentiments of mankind regarding merit and demerit.
The influence of fortune diminishes our sense of the merit or demerit of actions that arise from laudable or blameable intentions when they fail to produce their proposed effects.
The influence of fortune increases our sense of the merit or demerit of actions beyond what is due to the motives or affections when they accidentally cause extraordinary pleasure or pain.
If a person's proper and beneficent intentions fail to produce their effects, his merit seems imperfect.
If a person's improper and malevolent intentions fail to produce their effects, his demerit seems incomplete.
The irregularity of sentiment about merit and demerit is felt not only by those immediately affected but also by the impartial spectator.
A man who solicits an office for another without obtaining it is regarded as a friend and seems to deserve love and affection.
A man who solicits and procures an office for another is more peculiarly considered as a patron and benefactor and is entitled to respect and gratitude.
The person obliged may think himself on a level with the friend who fails to procure an office but feels inferior to the friend who succeeds.
It is common to say that we are equally obliged to the man who has endeavored to serve us as to him who actually did so, but this must be understood with allowance.
A generous person may entertain nearly the same sentiments for a friend who fails as for one who succeeds.
For the truly generous, being beloved and esteemed by those they think worthy gives more pleasure and excites more gratitude than all advantages from those sentiments.
When generous people lose advantages from a friend's success, they seem to lose but a trifle, which is scarcely worth regarding.
Even generous people lose some pleasure and consequently some gratitude when a friend fails compared to when he succeeds.
Between a friend who fails and a friend who succeeds, all other circumstances equal, there is some little difference of affection in favor of the one who succeeds.
People are unjust in thinking that less gratitude is due to a man who intended a benefit but could only help it a little forward if the benefit was not procured by him.
Gratitude is divided among different persons who contributed to a pleasure, so a smaller share seems due to any one.
People commonly say that a person intended to serve and exerted himself to the utmost, but they are not obliged to him for the benefit if it depended on others' concurrence.
The person who unsuccessfully endeavored to confer a benefit has less dependency on the gratitude of the man he meant to oblige than if he had succeeded.
The merit of talents and abilities hindered by accident from producing effects seems imperfect even to those convinced of the capacity.
A general hindered by envy from gaining a great advantage regrets the loss of the opportunity forever.
The general laments being hindered from performing an action that would have added lustre to his character in his own eyes and those of others.
It does not satisfy the general or others to reflect that the plan depended on him and that success was infallible if permitted to proceed.
The general did not execute the plan and thus lacks the actual merit of having performed a great action.
Taking the management of a public affair from a man who almost brought it to conclusion is regarded as the most invidious injustice.
A man who has done much in an affair should be allowed to acquire the complete merit of finishing it.
Pompey was objected to for coming in upon the victories of Lucullus and gathering laurels due to another's fortune and valor.
The glory of Lucullus was less complete in the opinion of his friends when he was not permitted to finish the conquest.
An architect is mortified when his plans are not executed or are altered to spoil the building's effect.
The plan is all that depends upon the architect.
The architect's genius is as completely discovered in the plan as in the actual execution to good judges.
A plan does not give the same pleasure as a noble and magnificent building, even to the most intelligent.
The effects and amusement derived from a building are vastly different and greater than from a plan.
Many men may have talents superior to those of Caesar and Alexander and might perform greater actions in the same situations.
We do not behold men with superior talents with the same astonishment and admiration as Caesar and Alexander.
Calm judgments may approve men with superior talents more, but they lack the splendor of great actions to dazzle and transport the mind.
The superiority of virtues and talents does not have the same effect as the superiority of achievements, even on those who acknowledge that superiority.
The merit of an unsuccessful attempt to do good is diminished in the eyes of ungrateful mankind by the miscarriage.
The demerit of an unsuccessful attempt to do evil is likewise diminished.
The design to commit a crime is rarely punished with the same severity as the actual commission of it.
Treason is an exception where the design to commit the crime is punished severely.
Treason immediately affects the being of the government itself.
The government is more jealous of treason than of any other crime.
In punishing treason, the sovereign resents injuries done to himself.
In punishing other crimes, the sovereign resents injuries done to other men.
The sovereign's resentment in treason cases is his own, while in other crimes it is by sympathy with his subjects.
The sovereign is apt to be more violent and sanguinary in punishing treason than an impartial spectator would approve.
The sovereign's resentment in treason rises on smaller occasions and does not always wait for the crime or attempt.
A treasonable concert or conversation is punished in many countries as severely as the actual commission of treason.
For all other crimes, the mere design without an attempt is seldom punished and never severely.
A criminal design and a criminal action do not necessarily imply the same degree of depravity.
The man who fires a pistol at his enemy but misses is rarely punished with death by the laws of any country.
Under old Scottish law, an assassin who wounds but does not cause death within a certain time is not liable to death.
The mere attempt to commit murder ought to be capital in all countries due to high resentment and terror.
The attempt to commit smaller crimes is almost always punished lightly or not at all.
A thief caught with his hand in a neighbor's pocket before taking anything is punished with ignominy only.
If the thief had taken a handkerchief, he would have been put to death.
A house-breaker found setting a ladder to a neighbor's window but not entering is not exposed to capital punishment.
The attempt to ravish is not punished as a rape.
The attempt to seduce a married woman is not punished, though seduction is punished severely.
Resentment against a person who only attempted mischief is seldom strong enough to justify the same punishment as if the crime was done.
The joy of deliverance lessens the sense of atrocity of the conduct of an unsuccessful criminal.
The grief of misfortune increases the sense of atrocity of a committed crime.
The real demerit is the same in both cases of attempted and committed crime since intentions were equally criminal.
There is an irregularity in the sentiments of all men and a relaxation of discipline in laws regarding attempts versus completed crimes.
Civilized peoples tend to dispense with or mitigate punishments when natural indignation is not increased by consequences of the crime.
Barbarians are not delicate or inquisitive about motives when no actual consequence has happened from an action.
A person who resolved and took measures to commit a crime but was prevented by accident regards this as a great deliverance.
Such a person thanks Heaven for saving him from guilt and a life of horror, remorse, and repentance.
Though his hands are innocent, the person is conscious that his heart is equally guilty as if he had executed the crime.
Considering the crime was not executed gives great ease to the conscience of the person.
The person considers himself less deserving of punishment and resentment due to the failure to execute the crime.
This good fortune diminishes or removes all sense of guilt.
Remembering the resolution to commit the crime makes the person regard his escape as greater and more miraculous.
The person looks back on the danger to his peace of mind with terror, like one safe remembering a hazard.
The second effect of fortune's influence is to increase the sense of merit or demerit of actions beyond what is due to motives when they cause extraordinary pleasure or pain.
The agreeable or disagreeable effects of an action often cast a shadow of merit or demerit on the agent, even if intentions do not deserve it.
The messenger of bad news is disagreeable to us.
We feel gratitude for the man who brings good tidings.
For a moment, we regard both messengers as authors of our good or bad fortune.
The first author of our joy is the object of transitory gratitude and affection.
Courts customarily reward officers who bring news of victory with considerable preferments.
Generals choose principal favorites to deliver agreeable news.
The first author of our sorrow is the object of transitory resentment.
We look upon the bearer of bad news with chagrin and uneasiness.
The rude and brutal may vent spleen on the bearer of bad news.
Tigranes, king of Armenia, struck off the head of the man who brought him the first account of an approaching enemy.
Punishing the bearer of bad news is barbarous and inhuman.
Rewarding the messenger of good news is agreeable and considered suitable to the bounty of kings.
The difference in treatment of messengers arises because social and benevolent affections are easily exerted, but malevolent affections require more solid reasons.
In general, people are averse to entering into unsocial and malevolent affections.

It is a rule that people ought never to approve of the gratification of unsocial and malevolent affections unless the malicious and unjust intention of the person against whom they are directed renders him their proper object.
On some occasions, people relax the severity of not approving unsocial and malevolent affections.

When the negligence of one man causes unintended damage to another, people generally approve of the sufferer inflicting punishment on the offender beyond what the offence would have deserved without the damage.
There is a degree of negligence that deserves some chastisement even if it causes no damage.
Throwing a large stone over a wall into a public street without warning is an example of negligence deserving chastisement.
A very accurate police would punish throwing a stone into a street without causing mischief.
A person who throws a stone carelessly shows insolent contempt for the happiness and safety of others.
Such conduct is a real injustice and wantonly exposes neighbors to danger.
Gross negligence is said in law to be almost equal to malicious design.
When unlucky consequences happen from carelessness, the person guilty is often punished as if they intended those consequences.
Conduct that was thoughtless and insolent but deserving some chastisement is considered atrocious and liable to severe punishment if it causes damage.
If a person accidentally kills a man by throwing a stone carelessly, many countries' laws, including old Scottish law, make them liable to the last punishment.
This severe punishment is not altogether inconsistent with natural sentiments.
Just indignation against folly and inhumanity is exasperated by sympathy with the sufferer.
Bringing a man to the scaffold merely for throwing a stone carelessly without hurting anyone is shocking to natural sense of equity.
The folly and inhumanity of careless conduct is the same whether or not it causes harm.
Sentiments differ depending on whether careless conduct causes harm.
Indignation of spectators is often animated by the actual consequences of an action.
Laws of almost all nations show great severity in cases where negligence causes harm.
There is a general relaxation of discipline in laws of an opposite kind.
Another degree of negligence involves no injustice.
A person guilty of this negligence treats neighbors as he treats himself and means no harm.
Such a person is not as careful as he ought to be and deserves some blame and censure but no punishment.
If this negligence causes damage, the person is obliged by law to compensate the damage.
Compensation for damage caused by blamable negligence is approved by natural sentiments of mankind.
It is considered just that one man should not suffer by the carelessness of another.
There is a species of negligence that consists in a lack of anxious timidity and circumspection about possible consequences.
Lack of excessive care when no bad consequences follow is not regarded as blamable.
Excessive timid circumspection is not regarded as a virtue but as a quality that incapacitates for action and business.
When lack of excessive care causes damage, the person is often obliged by law to compensate it.
Under Aquilian law, a man who cannot manage a frightened horse and causes damage must compensate the damage.
People think a person who rides a dangerous horse and causes damage ought not to have ridden it and regard it as unpardonable levity.
Without an accident, refusing to ride a dangerous horse would be regarded as timid weakness and unnecessary anxiety.
A person who involuntarily hurts another by accident often feels a sense of ill desert toward the sufferer.
Such a person naturally expresses concern and makes acknowledgments to the sufferer.
If the person has sensibility, he desires to compensate the damage and appease the resentment of the sufferer.
Making no apology or offering no atonement after causing damage is regarded as the highest brutality.
The task of making amends is imposed because the impartial spectator feels indulgence for the unjust resentment of the sufferer.
The good or bad consequences of actions affect the sentiments of both the person who performs them and others.
Fortune has some influence on the sentiments of mankind regarding character and conduct.
The world judges actions by their outcomes rather than by their intentions.
There is a general maxim that the event of an action should not influence our sentiments about the merit or propriety of the conduct.
In practice, people's sentiments rarely conform exactly to the maxim that outcomes should not affect judgments of merit.
The success or failure of an action influences opinions about the prudence of how it was conducted.
The success or failure of an action also animates gratitude or resentment and affects the sense of merit or demerit of the design.
Nature implanted the seeds of irregularity in human sentiments to promote the happiness and perfection of the species.
If resentment were caused only by hurtful designs or malevolent affections, people would feel intense passion against those harboring such intentions even without action.
If thoughts and intentions were punished as actions are, every court would become an inquisition.
Actions that produce or attempt to produce actual evil and put others in fear are the only proper objects of human punishment and resentment.
Sentiments, designs, and affections are beyond the limits of human jurisdiction and reserved for divine judgment.
The rule that men are liable to punishment only for actions, not for designs or intentions, is founded on the irregularity of human sentiments.
The irregularity of sentiments that appears absurd is actually a demonstration of providential care.
The merit of an unsuccessful attempt to serve and of good inclinations and kind wishes appears imperfect.
Man was made for action to promote changes favorable to the happiness of himself and others.
Man should not be satisfied with indolent benevolence or mere good wishes.
Nature teaches that neither man nor mankind can be fully satisfied with conduct unless it produces actual good outcomes.
Praise of good intentions without good actions is insufficient to excite the highest degree of self-applause or public acclaim.
A man who has no important actions but expresses noble sentiments cannot demand a high reward.
We can esteem and love a man with good sentiments but owe him nothing if he has done no actual service.
Rewarding latent virtue that has been useless only for lack of opportunity is an effect of divine benevolence.
Punishing for affections of the heart alone, where no crime has been committed, is insolent and barbarous tyranny.
Benevolent affections deserve most praise when they do not wait until it becomes almost a crime not to exert themselves.
Malevolent affections can scarcely be too slow or deliberate.
It is important that evil done without design is regarded as a misfortune to both the doer and the sufferer.
Man is taught to reverence the happiness of others and to dread causing harm even unknowingly.
In ancient heathen religion, holy ground consecrated to a god was not to be trod upon except on solemn occasions.
A man who unknowingly violated consecrated ground became piacular and incurred the vengeance of the god until atonement was made.
Nature renders the happiness of every innocent man holy and protected against wanton or ignorant violation.
Ignorant and involuntary violation of another's happiness requires some expiation proportional to the offense.
A man who accidentally causes another's death without negligence feels piacular though not guilty.
Such a man considers the accident one of the greatest misfortunes that could befall him.
If the family of the slain is poor and the man is in tolerable circumstances, he takes them under his protection.
If the family of the slain is better off, the man tries to atone by submission, sorrow, and good offices.
The distress of an innocent person who unknowingly does something blameworthy has inspired scenes in ancient and modern drama.
The fallacious sense of guilt constitutes the distress of characters like Œdipus, Jocasta, Monimia, and Isabella.
These characters are piacular but not guilty.
If a man causes evils unintentionally or fails to produce intended good, Nature provides consolation for his innocence.
Nature provides reward for a man's virtue even if his intended good is not achieved.
There is a maxim that events not dependent on our conduct should not diminish the esteem due to us.
A man calls upon his magnanimity and firmness of soul to regard himself as he ought to appear.
A man strives to see himself as he would have appeared if his generous designs had succeeded.
A man strives to see himself as he would still appear despite the miscarriage of his designs.
The ideal regard for a man depends on sentiments of mankind being candid and equitable or consistent.
The more candid and humane part of mankind supports a man's effort to maintain a good opinion of himself.
The candid and humane exert generosity and greatness of mind to correct irregularity in human nature.
The candid and humane endeavor to regard a man's unfortunate magnanimity as they would if it had been successful.
Without generous exertion, people would naturally consider successful magnanimity positively.
Part III is titled 'Of the Foundation of Our Judgments Concerning Our Own Sentiments and Conduct, and of the Sense of Duty.'
The principle by which we approve or disapprove of our own conduct is the same as that by which we judge the conduct of others.
We approve or disapprove of another person's conduct based on whether we can sympathize with the sentiments and motives behind it when imagining ourselves in their place.
We approve or disapprove of our own conduct by imagining ourselves in the situation of another person and viewing our conduct from their perspective.
We cannot judge our own sentiments and motives unless we remove ourselves from our natural standpoint and view them from a distance.
The only way to view our own sentiments and motives from a distance is by imagining how other people would view them.
Any judgment we form about our own conduct always refers to what we believe others' judgments are or would be.
We examine our own conduct as we imagine a fair and impartial spectator would examine it.
If we can fully sympathize with the passions and motives influencing our conduct from the spectator's viewpoint, we approve of it.
If we cannot sympathize with the spectator's disapproval of our conduct, we condemn it.
A human being raised in complete isolation without communication with others could not think about the propriety or demerit of their own sentiments and conduct.
Without society, a person cannot judge the beauty or deformity of their own mind or character.
Society provides a mirror for self-judgment through the countenance and behavior of others.
The reactions of others mark when they approve or disapprove of our sentiments.
A person unfamiliar with society would focus entirely on external objects that please or hurt them, not on their own passions.
In isolation, a person’s passions would rarely become objects of their own thoughts or consideration.
Bringing a person into society causes their own passions to become causes of new passions.
In society, a person observes that some of their passions are approved by others and some are disapproved.
Approval by others elevates a person, while disapproval casts them down.
A person’s desires, aversions, joys, and sorrows become causes of new desires, aversions, joys, and sorrows in society.
Our first ideas of personal beauty and deformity come from the shape and appearance of others, not from ourselves.
We become aware that others judge our appearance and feel pleased when they approve and displeased when they disapprove.
We examine our own appearance by placing ourselves before a mirror or by other means to view ourselves as others do.
If we are satisfied with our own appearance after examination, we can better endure negative judgments from others.
If we feel naturally unattractive, any disapproval from others mortifies us greatly.
A person who is tolerably handsome can tolerate jokes about minor irregularities, but a truly deformed person cannot.
We care about our own beauty or deformity only because of its effect on others.
Without connection to society, we would be indifferent to our own beauty or deformity.
Our first moral judgments are made about the characters and conduct of others.
We are quick to observe how others' characters and conduct affect us.
We learn that others are equally frank in judging our own character and conduct.
We become anxious to know how much we deserve others' censure or applause.
We examine our own passions and conduct by imagining how they appear to others.
We imagine ourselves as spectators of our own behavior to judge its effect.
This imagined spectator viewpoint is the only way to scrutinize the propriety of our own conduct.
If we approve of our conduct from the spectator's viewpoint, we feel satisfied and can be indifferent to others' opinions.
If we doubt our conduct's approval, we become anxious to gain others' approval and fear their censure.
When judging our own conduct, we divide ourselves into two persons: the examiner (judge) and the agent (person judged).
The examiner represents a different character from the person whose conduct is judged.
The judge is the spectator who tries to enter into the sentiments about the conduct by imagining the situation.
The person judged is the agent whose conduct is being evaluated.
It is impossible for the judge and the person judged to be exactly the same in every respect.
To be amiable and to be meritorious are the great characters of virtue.
To be odious and punishable are the great characters of vice.
The characters of virtue and vice have an immediate reference to the sentiments of others.
Virtue is said to be amiable and meritorious because it excites love and gratitude in other men.
Virtue is not said to be amiable or meritorious because it is the object of its own love or gratitude.
The consciousness of being the object of favorable regards is the source of inward tranquillity and self-satisfaction.
The suspicion of not being the object of favorable regards gives occasion to the torments of vice.
Being beloved and knowing that one deserves to be beloved is a source of great happiness.
Being hated and knowing that one deserves to be hated is a source of great misery.
Man naturally desires to be loved and to be lovely, meaning to be the natural and proper object of love.
Man naturally dreads not only to be hated but to be hateful, meaning to be the natural and proper object of hatred.
Man desires not only praise but praise-worthiness, meaning to be the natural and proper object of praise even if praised by nobody.
Man dreads not only blame but blame-worthiness, meaning to be the natural and proper object of blame even if blamed by nobody.
The love of praise-worthiness is not entirely derived from the love of praise.
The love of praise and the love of praise-worthiness resemble each other, are connected, and often blended, but are distinct and independent in many respects.
Admiration for those whose character and conduct we approve disposes us to desire to become objects of similar agreeable sentiments.
Emulation, the anxious desire to excel, is originally founded in admiration of the excellence of others.
We cannot be satisfied with being admired only for what others are admired for; we must believe ourselves admirable for the same qualities.
To attain satisfaction in admiration, we must become impartial spectators of our own character and conduct.
Viewing our character and conduct as others would view them leads to happiness and contentment if they appear as we wish.
Finding that others view our character and conduct in the same favorable light confirms our happiness and contentment.
Others' approbation confirms our self-approbation and strengthens our sense of praise-worthiness.
The love of praise seems to be derived in great measure from the love of praise-worthiness.
Sincere praise gives little pleasure if it cannot be considered proof of praise-worthiness.
Esteem and admiration bestowed from ignorance or mistake do not provide complete satisfaction if we know we do not deserve them.
Applause for actions not performed or for motives not influencing our conduct is not applause for us but for another person.
We derive no satisfaction from praise that is not deserved and should find it mortifying.
Being pleased with groundless applause is a proof of superficial levity and weakness and is called vanity.
Vanity is the foundation of the vices of affectation and common lying.
Foolish liars who invent adventures and coxcombs who claim false rank are pleased with the applause they imagine they receive.
Their vanity arises from a gross illusion of the imagination.
Such persons admire themselves in the light they believe others view them, not in the light they ought to be viewed.
Their superficial weakness and folly prevent them from seeing themselves as their conscience knows they truly appear.
Ignorant and groundless praise gives no solid joy or satisfaction that can bear serious examination.
It often gives real comfort to reflect that our conduct deserves praise even if no praise is actually bestowed.
We are pleased with having done what is praise-worthy, not only with receiving praise.
We are mortified to reflect that we have justly merited blame even if that blame is never actually exerted against us.
A man conscious of having observed proper conduct reflects with satisfaction on the propriety of his behavior.
He views his conduct as the impartial spectator would and enters into all motives influencing it.
He looks back on his conduct with pleasure and approbation even if mankind never learns what he has done.
He regards himself according to the light in which he would be regarded if others were better informed.
He anticipates applause and admiration that would be bestowed if the public were properly informed.
He applauds and admires himself by sympathy with sentiments that do not actually take place but ought to.
Men have voluntarily thrown away life to acquire after death a renown they could no longer enjoy.
Their imagination anticipates fame and admiration they will never hear or feel.
There is little difference between approbation bestowed after death and approbation never bestowed but deserved.
If posthumous approbation produces violent effects, deserved but unbestowed approbation should be highly regarded.
Nature endowed man with an original desire to please and an original aversion to offend his brethren.
Man feels pleasure in favorable regard and pain in unfavorable regard from others.
Man finds others' approbation flattering and agreeable for its own sake.
Man finds others' disapprobation mortifying and offensive.
Nature has endowed man with a desire of being approved of by his brethren.
Nature has also endowed man with a desire of being what ought to be approved of.
The desire to be approved of alone would only make a man wish to appear fit for society.
The desire to be what ought to be approved of is necessary to make a man anxious to be really fit for society.
The desire to be approved of alone could prompt a man to affect virtue and conceal vice.
The desire to be what ought to be approved of inspires a real love of virtue and abhorrence of vice.
In every well-formed mind, the desire to be what ought to be approved of is stronger than the desire to be approved of.
The weakest and most superficial people can be delighted with praise they know is unmerited.
A wise man rejects praise on all occasions when he knows it is unmerited.
A wise man often feels the highest pleasure in doing what he knows to be praise-worthy even if no praise is bestowed.
Obtaining approbation where no approbation is due is never an important object for a wise man.
Obtaining approbation where it is really due may sometimes be of no great importance to a wise man.
Being that which deserves approbation must always be an object of the highest importance.
Desiring or accepting praise where no praise is due is the effect of the most contemptible vanity.
Desiring praise where it is really due is desiring an essential act of justice.
The love of just fame and true glory for its own sake is not unworthy of a wise man.
A wise man sometimes neglects or despises just fame and true glory.
A wise man is most apt to neglect just fame when he has perfect assurance of the propriety of his conduct.
A wise man's self-approbation can be sufficient without confirmation from others.
Self-approbation is at least the principal object about which a wise man can or ought to be anxious.
The love of self-approbation is the love of virtue.
Love and admiration for some characters dispose us to wish to become objects of such sentiments.
Hatred and contempt for others dispose us to dread resembling them.
We dread being hateful and despicable more than the thought of being hated and despised.
We dread doing anything that can render us just objects of hatred and contempt even if those sentiments are never exerted against us.
A man who breaks measures of conduct to be agreeable to mankind feels shame when reflecting on his actions.
Such a man imagines contempt and derision as if from an impartial spectator.
He feels he is the natural object of hatred and contempt and trembles at the thought of actual exertion of those sentiments.
If the guilt involves enormous crimes, the man feels horror and remorse even if assured no one will know.
Even if he believes there is no God to revenge it, he still feels hatred and indignation from fellow-creatures.
These pangs of conscience are like daemons or avenging furies that haunt the guilty.
These pangs allow no quiet or repose and often drive the guilty to despair and distraction.
No assurance of secrecy or principles of irreligion can entirely deliver the guilty from these pangs.
Only complete insensibility to honour and infamy, vice and virtue can free a man from these pangs.
Men who have committed dreadful crimes sometimes reveal their guilt voluntarily due to horror of their situation.
By acknowledging guilt and submitting to resentment, they hope to reconcile themselves to natural sentiments of mankind.
They hope to be objects of compassion rather than horror and to die in peace with forgiveness.
Compared to their feelings before discovery, even the thought of confession seems happiness.
In such cases, horror of blame-worthiness can conquer the dread of blame.
To allay horror and pacify remorse, they voluntarily submit to reproach and punishment due to their crimes.
Only the most frivolous and superficial people can be much delighted with praise they know to be unmerited.
Unmerited reproach can severely mortify even men of more than ordinary constancy.
Men of ordinary constancy easily learn to despise foolish tales circulated in society.
Foolish tales in society often die away in a few days or weeks due to their absurdity and falsehood.
An innocent man of more than ordinary constancy is often severely mortified by a serious but false imputation of a crime.
False imputations supported by circumstances that give them an air of probability shock and mortify innocent men.
An innocent man is humbled to find that anyone thinks him capable of a crime he did not commit.
Even when conscious of innocence, the imputation of a crime can cast a shadow of disgrace and dishonor on a man's character.
Just indignation at a gross injury can be a very painful sensation.
Violent resentment which cannot be gratified is a great tormentor of the human breast.
An innocent man brought to the scaffold by false imputation suffers the most cruel misfortune possible for innocence.
The agony of mind of an innocent man punished for a crime he did not commit may be greater than that of a guilty person punished for the same crime.
Profligate criminals like common thieves and highwaymen often have little sense of the baseness of their conduct and no remorse.
Such criminals are accustomed to expect the gibbet as a likely fate.
When executed, these criminals consider themselves less lucky than some companions and submit to their fate with uneasiness only from fear of death.
The fear of death can be easily and completely conquered even by worthless criminals.
An innocent man suffers uneasiness from fear of death and is also tormented by indignation at the injustice done to him.
An innocent man is horrified by the thought of the infamy the punishment may bring upon his memory.
An innocent man foresees with anguish that he will be remembered with shame and horror by his dearest friends and relations for supposed disgraceful conduct.
The shades of death appear darker and more melancholy to an innocent man condemned unjustly.
Fatal accidents of innocent men being unjustly punished happen rarely but sometimes in all countries, even those with generally well-administered justice.
The unfortunate Calas was broken upon the wheel and burnt at Toulouse for the supposed murder of his son, of which he was perfectly innocent.
Calas, with his last breath, deprecated the disgrace the imputation might bring upon his memory more than the cruelty of the punishment.
At his execution, Calas refused to confess the crime, asking if the monk could believe he was guilty.
Humble philosophy confined to this life can afford little consolation to persons unjustly condemned.
Those unjustly condemned are deprived of everything that could render life or death respectable.
Religion alone can afford effectual comfort to those unjustly condemned.
Religion teaches that it is of little importance what man thinks of their conduct if the all-seeing Judge of the world approves.
Religion presents the view of another world where innocence is declared and virtue finally rewarded.
The principle that strikes terror into triumphant vice also affords consolation to disgraced and insulted innocence.
In smaller offences as well as greater crimes, a person of sensibility is often more hurt by unjust imputation than the real criminal is by actual guilt.
A woman of gallantry laughs at well-founded surmises about her conduct.
The worst-founded surmise about conduct is a mortal stab to an innocent virgin.
A person deliberately guilty of a disgraceful action seldom has much sense of disgrace.
A person habitually guilty of disgraceful actions can scarcely ever have any sense of disgrace.
Men of middling understanding readily despise unmerited applause.
Unmerited reproach often mortifies men of sound and best judgment severely.
Pain is, in almost all cases, a more pungent sensation than the opposite and correspondent pleasure.
Pain almost always depresses us much more below the ordinary or natural state of our happiness than pleasure ever raises us above it.
A man of sensibility is apt to be more humiliated by just censure than he is elevated by just applause.
A wise man rejects unmerited applause with contempt on all occasions.
A wise man often feels very severely the injustice of unmerited censure.
A wise man who suffers himself to be applauded for what he has not performed feels guilty of a mean falsehood.
A wise man who assumes merit that does not belong to him deserves the contempt of those who admired him by mistake.
A wise man may feel some pleasure to find that many people thought him capable of performing what he did not perform.
A wise man would think himself guilty of the greatest baseness if he did not immediately undeceive friends who mistakenly admired him.
A wise man gains little pleasure from viewing himself as others actually look upon him when he knows they would view him differently if they knew the truth.
A weak man is often much delighted with viewing himself in a false and delusive light.
A weak man assumes the merit of every laudable action ascribed to him and pretends to many which nobody thought of ascribing to him.
A weak man pretends to have done what he never did, written what another wrote, and invented what another discovered.
A weak man is led into the vices of plagiarism and common lying.
No man of middling good sense can derive much pleasure from the imputation of a laudable action which he never performed.
A wise man may suffer great pain from the serious imputation of a crime which he never committed.
Nature has rendered the pain of being falsely accused of a crime more pungent than the opposite pleasure, and in a much greater than ordinary degree.
A denial rids a man at once of the foolish and ridiculous pleasure of false praise but will not always rid him of the pain of false accusation.
When a man refuses the merit ascribed to him, nobody doubts his veracity.
When a man denies the crime he is accused of, his veracity may be doubted.
A man falsely accused of a crime is enraged at the falsehood of the imputation and mortified to find any credit given to it.
A man falsely accused feels that his character is not sufficient to protect him.
A man falsely accused knows perfectly that he has not been guilty.
A man may not know perfectly what he himself is capable of doing.
The trust and good opinion of friends and neighbours tends to relieve a man from the disagreeable doubt about his own character.
Distrust and unfavourable opinion from others tends to increase a man's doubt about his own character.
A man may be confident that unfavourable judgment is wrong but that confidence seldom prevents the judgment from making some impression.
The greater a man's sensibility, delicacy, and worth, the greater the impression made by unfavourable judgment.
The agreement or disagreement of other people's sentiments and judgments with our own is important in proportion to our uncertainty about our own sentiments and judgments.
A man of sensibility may feel great uneasiness lest he has yielded too much to an honourable passion such as just indignation.
A man of sensibility may fear that he has done real injury to another person by the vehemence of his emotion.
The opinion of other people is of utmost importance to a man of sensibility in cases of doubt about his conduct.
The approbation of others is the most healing balsam to a man of sensibility.
The disapprobation of others is the bitterest and most tormenting poison to a man of sensibility.
When a man is perfectly satisfied with every part of his own conduct, the judgment of other people is often of less importance to him.
Some noble and beautiful arts have a degree of excellence that can be determined only by a certain nicety of taste, and their decisions appear always somewhat uncertain.
Other arts admit of clear demonstration or very satisfactory proof of success.
Anxiety about public opinion is always much greater in arts where excellence is determined by nicety of taste than in those where success admits clear demonstration.
The beauty of poetry is a matter of such nicety that a young beginner can scarce ever be certain that he has attained it.
A young poet delights most in favourable judgments of friends and the public and is mortified most by contrary judgments.
Mathematicians and natural philosophers have little temptation to form factions or cabals for supporting their own reputation or depressing that of rivals.
Mathematicians and natural philosophers are almost always men of amiable simplicity of manners who live in good harmony with one another.
Mathematicians and natural philosophers are friends of one another's reputation and enter into no intrigue to secure public applause.
Mathematicians and natural philosophers are pleased when their works are approved but are not much vexed or angry when neglected.
Poets and those who value themselves on fine writing are apt to divide into literary factions.
Literary cabals are often avowedly or secretly mortal enemies of the reputation of every other faction.
Literary cabals employ mean arts of intrigue and solicitation to preoccupy public opinion in favor of their own members and against rivals.
In France, Despreaux and Racine led a literary cabal to depress the reputation of Quinault, Perreault, Fontenelle, La Motte, and treated La Fontaine with disrespectful kindness.
In England, Mr. Addison led a cabal to keep down the rising reputation of Mr. Pope.
Mr. Fontenelle, writing about the academy of sciences, frequently celebrated the amiable simplicity of mathematicians and natural philosophers.
The amiable simplicity of manners was so universal among mathematicians and natural philosophers as to be characteristic of that class.
Mr. D'Alembert, writing about the French academy of poets and fine writers, did not represent amiable simplicity as characteristic of that class.
Uncertainty about our own merit and anxiety to think favorably of it naturally make us desirous to know others' opinions about it.
We are more elevated when others' opinions are favorable and more mortified when they are unfavorable.
Desire to obtain favorable opinion or avoid unfavorable opinion by intrigue and cabal is improper.
Bribing judges to win a law suit does not assure a man that he was in the right.
If a man carried on a law suit merely to satisfy himself that he was right, he would not bribe the judges.
Praise is of principal consequence as proof of our own praise-worthiness and also of some consequence on its own account.
Men very much above the common level have sometimes attempted to obtain praise and avoid blame by unfair means.
Praise and blame express what actually are; praise-worthiness and blame-worthiness express what ought to be the sentiments of others regarding our character and conduct.
The love of praise is the desire to obtain favorable sentiments of our brethren.
The love of praise-worthiness is the desire to render ourselves proper objects of favorable sentiments.
The love of praise and the love of praise-worthiness resemble and are akin to one another.
The dread of blame and the dread of blame-worthiness have a similar affinity and resemblance.
A man who desires or does a praiseworthy action may also desire the praise due to it, sometimes more than is due.
How far a man's conduct is influenced by love of praise or love of praise-worthiness may be unknown to himself and almost always unknown to others.
Those disposed to lessen the merit of a man's conduct impute it chiefly or entirely to mere love of praise or vanity.
Those disposed to think more favorably impute a man's conduct chiefly or entirely to love of praise-worthiness and desire to deserve approbation.
The imagination of the spectator colors the interpretation of a man's conduct according to his habits of thinking or favor or dislike of the person.
Some splenetic philosophers have imputed every action to love of praise or vanity rather than to praise-worthiness.
Very few men can be satisfied with their private consciousness of having attained praise-worthy qualities unless it is generally acknowledged.
Some men seem indifferent about praise when satisfied of praise-worthiness; others are more anxious about praise than praise-worthiness.
No man can be completely satisfied with having avoided blame-worthiness unless he has also avoided blame or reproach.
A wise man may neglect praise even when deserved but will carefully avoid blame and probable imputation of blame.
A wise man will not avoid blame by doing anything he judges blame-worthy or by neglecting duties or opportunities for praise-worthy actions.
Anxiety about praise for praise-worthy actions is seldom a mark of great wisdom but often a sign of weakness.
Anxiety to avoid blame or reproach may be praise-worthy prudence rather than weakness.
Cicero said many people despise glory but are severely mortified by unjust reproach, which is inconsistent.
The inconsistency of despising glory but being mortified by unjust reproach is founded in unalterable principles of human nature.
The Author of Nature has taught man to respect the sentiments and judgments of his brethren, to be pleased by approval and hurt by disapproval.
Man is made the immediate judge of mankind and appointed as vicegerent on earth to superintend the behavior of his brethren.
Men are taught by nature to acknowledge the power conferred on them to judge others and to be humbled by censure and elated by applause.
Man has been rendered the immediate judge of mankind only in the first instance.
An appeal lies from man's sentence to a higher tribunal, which is the tribunal of their own consciences.
The higher tribunal includes the supposed impartial and well-informed spectator.
The higher tribunal also includes the man within the breast, the great judge and arbiter of conduct.
The jurisdictions of the man without and the man within are founded on principles that are different and distinct.
The jurisdiction of the man without is founded on the desire of actual praise and aversion to actual blame.
The jurisdiction of the man within is founded on the desire of praise-worthiness and aversion to blame-worthiness.
The man within desires to possess qualities and perform actions admired in other people.
The man within dreads possessing qualities and performing actions hated and despised in other people.
If the man without applauds us for actions not performed or for motives that had no influence, the man within humbles that pride by reminding us we do not deserve it.
If the man without reproaches us for actions not performed or for irrelevant motives, the man within corrects this false judgment and assures us we are not the proper objects of censure.
Sometimes the man within is astonished and confounded by the vehemence and clamor of the man without.
The violence and loudness of blame can stupify and benumb the natural sense of praise-worthiness and blame-worthiness.
The judgments of the man within can be shaken in steadiness and firmness by the judgments of the man without.
The natural effect of the man within's judgments in securing tranquility of mind is frequently destroyed by the judgments of the man without.
We scarcely dare to absolve ourselves when all our brethren loudly condemn us.
The supposed impartial spectator gives his opinion in our favor with fear and hesitation when all real spectators are unanimously and violently against us.
The man within the breast appears partly immortal and partly mortal.
When the man within's judgments are firmly directed by praise-worthiness and blame-worthiness, he acts suitably to his divine extraction.
When the man within is confounded by judgments of ignorant and weak man, he acts suitably to the human part of his origin.
The only effectual consolation in such cases lies in an appeal to a still higher tribunal, the all-seeing Judge of the world.
The all-seeing Judge's eye can never be deceived and his judgments can never be perverted.
A firm confidence in the unerring rectitude of the great tribunal can support a man under weakness and despondency.
Our happiness in this life is dependent on the humble hope and expectation of a life to come.
The hope of a life to come is deeply rooted in human nature.
This hope can support human dignity and illumine the prospect of mortality.
There is a world to come where exact justice will be done to every man.
In that world, every man will be ranked with those who are really his equals in moral and intellectual qualities.
Humble talents and virtues unknown or unrecognized in this life will be placed on a level or above those with high reputation.
The doctrine of a world to come where justice is done is venerable, comfortable to weakness, and flattering to human grandeur.
