A virtuous man who doubts of the doctrine of a world to come cannot avoid wishing earnestly to believe it.
The doctrine would not be exposed to derision if the distribution of rewards and punishments in that world were not often opposed to moral sentiments.
The assiduous courtier is often more favored than the faithful and active servant.
Attendance and adulation are often shorter and surer roads to preferment than merit or service.
A campaign at Versailles or St. James's is often worth two in Germany or Flanders.
This complaint has been heard from many venerable but discontented old officers.
What is considered the greatest reproach to earthly sovereigns has been ascribed as an act of justice to divine perfection.
Duties of devotion and worship of the Deity have been represented as the sole virtues entitling to reward or exemption from punishment in the life to come.
These virtues were perhaps most suitable to the station of those who represented them.
People are naturally disposed to overrate the excellencies of their own characters.
The text compares the mortifications of a monastery to the hardships and hazards of war.
The text states that it is contrary to moral sentiments to suppose that one hour in a monastery has more merit than a whole life spent honorably in war.
The text claims that nature has taught us principles to regulate our contempt or admiration.
The text says that the spirit which reserves celestial regions for monks and friars condemns heroes, statesmen, lawgivers, poets, and philosophers to the infernal.
The text states that those who have invented, improved, or excelled in arts contributing to human life are condemned to the infernal by this spirit.
The text says that great protectors, instructors, and benefactors of mankind are condemned to the infernal by this spirit.
The text states that those to whom natural sense of praise-worthiness ascribes the highest merit and most exalted virtue are condemned to the infernal by this spirit.
The text suggests that this strange application of the doctrine has sometimes exposed it to contempt and derision.
The text implies that those who have no great taste or turn for devout and contemplative virtues may have derided this doctrine.
The approbation of one's own conscience can scarcely content the weakness of man on some extraordinary occasions.
The testimony of the supposed impartial spectator, the great inmate of the breast, cannot always alone support a person.
The influence and authority of conscience is very great on all occasions.
Consulting the judge within is the only way to see what relates to ourselves in its proper shape and dimensions.
Only by consulting the judge within can we make any proper comparison between our own interests and those of other people.
Objects appear great or small to the eye of the body not so much according to their real dimensions as according to their nearness or distance.
Objects appear great or small to the natural eye of the mind in a similar way as to the eye of the body.
We remedy the defects of both the eye of the body and the natural eye of the mind in pretty much the same manner.
The author forms a just comparison between great distant objects and little objects around him by transporting himself in fancy to a different station.
Habit and experience have taught the author to easily and readily form judgments of real proportions of objects by imagining different stations.
A man must be somewhat acquainted with the philosophy of vision to be convinced how little distant objects would appear to the eye without imagination swelling them.

To the selfish and original passions of human nature, the loss or gain of a very small interest of our own appears vastly more important than the greatest concern of another with whom we have no particular connection.
The interests of another person with whom we have no particular connection can never be put into the balance with our own when surveyed from our own station.
Before making any proper comparison of opposite interests, we must change our position and view them from the place and eyes of a third person who judges impartially.
Habit and experience have taught us to view interests from the impartial third person's perspective so easily and readily that we are scarcely aware of doing it.
It requires some degree of reflection and philosophy to be convinced how little interest we would take in the greatest concerns of our neighbor without the sense of propriety and justice.

If the great empire of China with all its inhabitants was suddenly swallowed by an earthquake, a man of humanity in Europe with no connection to that part of the world would first express strong sorrow for the misfortune.
Such a man would make melancholy reflections on the precariousness of human life and the vanity of all the labors of man.
A man of speculation might reason about the effects of the disaster on commerce and trade of the world.
After expressing humane sentiments and philosophy, the man would pursue his business or pleasure with ease and tranquility as if no such accident had happened.
A frivolous disaster to himself would cause a more real disturbance to the man than the destruction of millions of others he never saw.
If the man was to lose his little finger tomorrow, he would not sleep tonight.
The man will snore with profound security over the ruin of a hundred millions of his brethren if he never saw them.
The destruction of an immense multitude seems less interesting to the man than the paltry misfortune of his own.
Human nature would be horrified at the thought of sacrificing the lives of a hundred millions of brethren to prevent a paltry misfortune to oneself.
The world in its greatest depravity and corruption never produced a villain capable of entertaining the thought of sacrificing millions to prevent a small personal misfortune.
Our passive feelings are almost always sordid and selfish.
Our active principles are often generous and noble.
We are more deeply affected by whatever concerns ourselves than by whatever concerns other men.
The generous are prompted on all occasions, and the mean on many, to sacrifice their own interests to the greater interests of others.
It is not the soft power of humanity or the feeble spark of benevolence that counteracts the strongest impulses of self-love.
It is reason, principle, conscience, the inhabitant of the breast, the man within, the great judge and arbiter of our conduct that exerts a stronger power.
This inner judge calls to us with a voice capable of astonishing the most presumptuous of our passions when we are about to act so as to affect the happiness of others.
The inner judge reminds us that we are but one of the multitude, in no respect better than any other in it.
When we prefer ourselves shamefully and blindly to others, we become the proper objects of resentment, abhorrence, and execration.
Only from the inner judge do we learn the real littleness of ourselves and of whatever relates to ourselves.
The natural misrepresentations of self-love can be corrected only by the eye of this impartial spectator.
The inner judge shows us the propriety of generosity and the deformity of injustice.
The inner judge shows us the propriety of resigning the greatest interests of our own for the yet greater interests of others.
The inner judge shows us the deformity of doing the smallest injury to another to obtain the greatest benefit to ourselves.
In misfortunes of the first kind, our emotions may exceed what exact propriety admits.
Emotions in misfortunes of the first kind may also fall short of what exact propriety admits.
A man who feels no more for the death or distress of his own father or son than for those of any other man's father or son would appear neither a good son nor a good father.
Unnatural indifference to the death or distress of one's own family would incur the highest disapprobation.
Some domestic affections are most apt to offend by their excess, and others by their defect.
Parental tenderness is a much stronger affection than filial piety in most men.
The continuance and propagation of the species depend on parental tenderness, not on filial piety.
The existence and preservation of the child depend on the care of the parents.
The existence and preservation of the parents seldom depend on the care of the child.
Parental affection generally requires moderation rather than excitation.
Moralists generally teach how to restrain excessive attachment to one's own children.
Moralists exhort affectionate attention to parents and proper return for their kindness in old age.
The Decalogue commands to honour fathers and mothers but makes no mention of love of children.
Nature has sufficiently prepared us to love our children.
Men are seldom accused of pretending to be fonder of their children than they really are.
Men have sometimes been suspected of displaying piety to their parents with too much ostentation.
The ostentatious sorrow of widows has been suspected of insincerity.
Excess of kind affections, if sincere, should be respected even if not perfectly approved.
The affectation of kind affections is proof that it appears praise-worthy to those who affect it.
Excess of kind affections never appears odious.
Excessive fondness and anxiety of a parent may be hurtful to the child and inconvenient to the parent.
Excessive parental fondness is easily pardoned and never regarded with hatred and detestation.
Defect of usually excessive parental affection appears peculiarly odious.
A man who feels nothing for his own children and treats them with unmerited severity and harshness seems most detestable.
The sense of propriety is more offended by defect than by excess of sensibility to misfortunes of nearest connections.
Stoical apathy in such cases is never agreeable.
Metaphysical sophisms supporting stoical apathy often increase insensibility and impertinence.
Poets and romance writers are better instructors on love and friendship than ancient stoics.
Moderated sensibility to misfortunes of others that does not disqualify duty is not unpleasant.
Melancholy and affectionate remembrance of departed friends are not undelicious sensations.
Though outwardly appearing as pain and grief, such sensations are inwardly stamped with virtue and self-approbation.
In misfortunes affecting ourselves directly, the sense of propriety is more offended by excess than defect of sensibility.
There are few cases where stoical apathy and indifference to our own misfortunes is excessive.
We have very little fellow-feeling with passions originating from the body.
Pain caused by evident bodily injury is the bodily affection with which a spectator feels the most lively sympathy.
The approaching death of a neighbour seldom fails to affect a spectator considerably.
The spectator feels much less pain than the person principally concerned, so the latter rarely offends by appearing to suffer with too much ease.
Mere poverty excites little compassion.
Complaints of poverty are often objects of contempt rather than fellow-feeling.
We despise beggars and rarely seriously commiserate them.
A very young child has no self-command.
Whatever emotions a very young child has, whether fear, grief, or anger, it endeavors to alarm the attention of its nurse or parents by the violence of its outcries.
While under the custody of partial protectors, a child's anger is the first and perhaps the only passion it is taught to moderate.
Parents or nurses often frighten a child into good temper by noise and threatening for their own ease.
The passion which incites a child to attack is restrained by the passion which teaches it to attend to its own safety.
When a child is old enough to go to school or mix with equals, it finds that its equals have no indulgent partiality.
A child naturally wishes to gain the favor of its play-fellows and avoid their hatred or contempt.
Regard to its own safety teaches a child to moderate its anger and other passions to please its companions.
A child enters the school of self-command by studying to be master of itself and exercising discipline over its feelings.
The practice of the longest life is seldom sufficient to bring self-command to complete perfection.
In private misfortunes, pain, sickness, or sorrow, a weak man is immediately impressed with how visitors are likely to view his situation.
The presence of visitors calls off a weak man's attention from his own view and somewhat calms him momentarily.
The calming effect on a weak man by visitors is instantaneous and mechanical but not long-lasting.
A weak man soon returns to his own view of his situation and abandons himself to sighs, tears, and lamentations.
A weak man tries to harmonize his grief with the compassion of the spectator by importunately calling upon the latter.
A man of more firmness tries to fix his attention on how company are likely to view his situation.
A man of more firmness feels esteem and approbation from company when he preserves his tranquility under calamity.
A man of more firmness approves and applauds himself by sympathy with the approbation of others.
The pleasure derived from others' approbation supports a man of firmness in continuing his effort of self-command.
A man of firmness often avoids mentioning his misfortune and company usually avoid mentioning it if well bred.
A man of firmness tries to entertain company on indifferent subjects or talks of his misfortune as he thinks they can handle it.
If not well inured to self-command, a man of firmness soon grows weary of restraint and abandons himself to sorrow after a visit.
Modern good manners forbid visits of strangers to persons under great family distress for some time.
Only nearest relations and most intimate friends are permitted visits during great family distress.
The presence of intimate friends imposes less restraint than that of strangers on sufferers.
Sufferers can more easily accommodate themselves to feelings of intimate friends due to expected indulgent sympathy.
Secret enemies often make charitable visits as early as intimate friends.
The weakest man tries to support a manly countenance and behave with gaiety and ease from indignation and contempt of malice during such visits.
A man of real constancy and firmness maintains control of his passive feelings on all occasions.
A wise and just man thoroughly bred in self-command wears nearly the same countenance and is affected nearly the same in solitude or society.
A man of firmness supports his manhood in success, disappointment, prosperity, adversity, before friends and enemies.
A man of firmness never forgets the judgment the impartial spectator would pass upon his sentiments and conduct.
A man of firmness never allows the man within the breast to be absent from his attention.
A man of firmness regards whatever relates to himself with the eyes of the impartial spectator.
A man of firmness is in constant practice and necessity of modeling his outward conduct and inward feelings according to the impartial spectator.
A man of firmness does not merely affect the sentiments of the impartial spectator but really adopts them.
A man of firmness almost identifies himself with the impartial spectator and feels as that arbiter directs him to feel.
The degree of self-approbation a man has upon surveying his conduct is proportional to the degree of self-command necessary to obtain that self-approbation.
Where little self-command is necessary, little self-approbation is due.
A man who has only scratched his finger cannot much applaud himself even if he immediately forgets the misfortune.
In paroxysms of distress, even the wisest and firmest man must make a considerable and painful exertion to preserve his equanimity.
A man in distress experiences his own natural feeling of distress and his natural view of his situation pressing hard upon him.
Without a very great effort, a man in distress cannot fix his attention upon that of the impartial spectator.
Both the man's own view and the view of the impartial spectator present themselves to him at the same time.
A man's sense of honour and regard to his own dignity directs him to fix his whole attention upon the view of the impartial spectator.
A man's natural, untaught, and undisciplined feelings continually call his attention away from the impartial spectator's view.
In distress, a man does not perfectly identify himself with the ideal man within the breast or become the impartial spectator of his own conduct.
The different views of the man's own feelings and the impartial spectator exist in his mind separate and distinct from one another.
Each view directs the man to a behavior different from that to which the other directs him.
When a man follows the view which honour and dignity point out, he enjoys his own complete self-approbation and the applause of every candid and impartial spectator.
Nature's unalterable laws cause the man to still suffer despite the recompense of self-approbation and applause.
The recompense bestowed by Nature is not sufficient to completely compensate the sufferings inflicted by her laws.
It is not fit that the recompense should completely compensate the sufferings because then the man would have no motive to avoid accidents that diminish his utility.
Nature intends that man should anxiously avoid accidents that diminish his utility to himself and society.
The man suffers and must exert his utmost and most fatiguing efforts to maintain manhood of countenance and sobriety of judgment during the paroxysm.
Agony can never be permanent by the constitution of human nature.
If a man survives the paroxysm, he soon comes without any effort to enjoy his ordinary tranquillity.
A man with a wooden leg suffers a considerable inconvenience but soon views it as an inconvenience under which he can enjoy ordinary pleasures.
The man with a wooden leg soon identifies himself with the ideal man within the breast and becomes the impartial spectator of his own situation.
The man with a wooden leg no longer weeps, laments, or grieves over his misfortune as a weak man may do in the beginning.
The view of the impartial spectator becomes so habitual to the man with a wooden leg that he never thinks of surveying his misfortune in any other view.
All men sooner or later accommodate themselves to whatever becomes their permanent situation.
The Stoics were nearly right in thinking that between one permanent situation and another there is no essential difference regarding real happiness.
Happiness consists in tranquillity and enjoyment.
Without tranquillity there can be no enjoyment.
Where there is perfect tranquillity, there is scarcely anything which is not capable of amusing.
In every permanent situation with no expectation of change, the mind returns to its natural and usual state of tranquillity after a longer or shorter time.
In prosperity, after a certain time, the mind falls back to tranquillity.
In adversity, after a certain time, the mind rises up to tranquillity.
In the confinement and solitude of the Bastile, the Count de Lauzun recovered enough tranquillity to amuse himself with feeding a spider.
A better furnished mind would have recovered tranquillity sooner and found better amusement in its own thoughts.
The great source of misery and disorders in human life arises from over-rating the difference between one permanent situation and another.
Avarice over-rates the difference between poverty and riches.
Ambition over-rates the difference between a private and a public station.
Vain-glory over-rates the difference between obscurity and extensive reputation.
A person under the influence of extravagant passions is miserable in his actual situation and often disposed to disturb the peace of society to achieve what he admires.
In ordinary situations of human life, a well-disposed mind may be equally calm, cheerful, and contented.
Some situations may deserve preference over others but none deserve to be pursued with passionate ardour that violates prudence or justice.
Attempting to change one's situation without prudence or justice is playing an unequal game of hazard, risking everything against little.
The favourite of the king of Epirus asked why the king did not enjoy himself now instead of after conquests, implying that happiness can be found in the present situation.
In misfortunes that admit no remedy, the difference between the wise and the weak man is mainly observable during the initial paroxysm or first attack.
Time gradually restores tranquillity to the weak man in irreparable misfortunes, bringing him to the same degree of calm as the wise man who assumes it from the beginning.
A man with a wooden leg exemplifies how time composes a person to tranquillity after an irreparable misfortune.
Even a wise man may indulge in moderated sorrow for some time after the death of children or close relations.
An affectionate but weak woman may become almost perfectly distracted upon the death of loved ones.
Time eventually composes even the weakest woman to the same degree of tranquillity as the strongest man after irreparable calamities.
A wise man tries from the beginning to anticipate and enjoy the tranquillity he expects time will restore after irreparable calamities.
In misfortunes that admit a remedy but where the means are not accessible, vain attempts and anxiety hinder the sufferer from regaining natural tranquillity.
Repeated disappointments in remedying a misfortune can render a person miserable for life, even if a greater misfortune with no remedy would cause only a short disturbance.
A person who struggles least and readily accepts a misfortune recovers natural tranquillity more quickly.
The most indifferent spectator often views disagreeable circumstances less favorably than a person who has accepted their misfortune.
Faction, intrigue, and cabal disturb the peace of an unfortunate statesman.
Extravagant projects and visions of gold mines interrupt the repose of a ruined bankrupt.
A prisoner who continually plots escape cannot enjoy the security that even a prison can afford.
The medicines of a physician can be the greatest torment to an incurable patient.
A monk comforted Joanna of Castile by telling her a legend of a king restored to life by prayers fourteen years after death.
Joanna of Castile resisted burying her husband Philip and watched his body in hopes of his revival.
Our sensibility to others' feelings is the principle upon which self-command is founded.
The instinct that prompts compassion for others' sorrow also prompts restraint of one's own lamentations.
The instinct that prompts congratulating others' joy also prompts restraint of one's own excessive joy.
The propriety of our own feelings is proportional to the force with which we conceive others' feelings.
The man of perfect virtue combines perfect command of his own selfish feelings with exquisite sensibility to others' feelings.
A man who combines soft, amiable virtues with great, awful, and respectable virtues is the natural object of highest love and admiration.
The person best fitted by nature to acquire command of his own feelings is also best fitted to acquire sensibility to others' feelings.
The man who feels most for others' joys and sorrows is best fitted to acquire the highest degree of self-command.
A man of exquisite humanity may not always have acquired perfect self-command.
A man may have lived too much in ease and tranquillity to acquire perfect self-command.
A man who has never experienced faction, war, insolence, envy, or injustice may lack the opportunity to acquire self-command.
Exercise and practice are necessary to establish the habit of self-command.
Hardships, dangers, injuries, and misfortunes are the only masters under whom self-command can be learned.
Nobody willingly subjects themselves to the hardships necessary to learn self-command.
The situations best for cultivating humanity differ from those best for forming self-command.
A man at ease can best attend to the distress of others.
A man exposed to hardships is most called upon to attend to and control his own feelings.
Humanity flourishes most in undisturbed tranquillity and philosophical leisure.
Self-command prospers most under the boisterous and stormy conditions of war, faction, public tumult, and confusion.
In situations requiring self-command, the strongest suggestions of humanity must often be stifled or neglected.
Neglecting humanity tends to weaken the principle of humanity.
A soldier may sometimes have the duty not to give quarter.
A soldier who must sometimes deny quarter may suffer a considerable diminution of humanity.
In solitude, people tend to feel their personal experiences too strongly.
In solitude, people tend to overrate the good they have done.
In solitude, people tend to overrate the injuries they have suffered.
In solitude, people tend to be too elated by their own good fortune.
In solitude, people tend to be too dejected by their own bad fortune.
The conversation of a friend brings a person to a better temper.
The conversation of a stranger brings a person to an even better temper.
The man within the breast, the abstract and ideal spectator of our sentiments and conduct, often needs to be awakened by the presence of the real spectator.
The real spectator is the one from whom we can expect the least sympathy and indulgence.
We are likely to learn the most complete lesson of self-command from the real spectator.
In adversity, one should not mourn in the darkness of solitude.
In adversity, one should not regulate sorrow according to the indulgent sympathy of intimate friends.
In adversity, one should return as soon as possible to the daylight of the world and society.
In adversity, one should live with strangers who know nothing or care nothing about one's misfortune.
In adversity, one should not shun the company of enemies.
In adversity, one can mortify enemies' malignant joy by showing how little one is affected by calamity.
In prosperity, one should not confine enjoyment of good fortune to one's own house or company of friends.
In prosperity, one should frequent those who are independent and value one only for character and conduct.
In prosperity, one should neither seek nor shun the society of those who were once superiors.
The impertinence of pride may make the company of former superiors disagreeable.
If one gains favor and kindness from former superiors by simplicity and unassuming demeanor, one may be satisfied that one is modest enough.
The propriety of moral sentiments is most apt to be corrupted when the indulgent and partial spectator is near and the indifferent and impartial one is distant.
Neutral nations are the only indifferent and impartial spectators of the conduct of one independent nation towards another.
Neutral nations are placed at such a great distance that they are almost out of sight.
When two nations are at variance, citizens pay little regard to the sentiments of foreign nations.
A citizen's ambition is to obtain the approbation of his own fellow-citizens.
Fellow-citizens are animated by the same hostile passions as the citizen himself.
A citizen can never please his fellow-citizens more than by enraging and offending their enemies.
In war and negotiation, the laws of justice are very seldom observed.
Truth and fair dealing are almost totally disregarded in war and negotiation.
Treaties are violated and such violation, if advantageous, brings little dishonor to the violator.
An ambassador who deceives a foreign minister is admired and applauded.
A just man who refuses to take or give advantage in public transactions is regarded as a fool and an idiot.
The just man incurs contempt and sometimes detestation from his fellow-citizens in public transactions.
In war, the laws of nations are frequently violated without bringing considerable dishonor among one's own fellow-citizens.
Most laws of nations are laid down with little regard to the plainest and most obvious rules of justice.
One plain rule of justice is that the innocent should not suffer or be punished for the guilty.
In the most unjust war, usually only the sovereign or rulers are guilty.
Subjects are almost always perfectly innocent in wars.
Goods of peaceable citizens are seized, lands laid waste, houses burnt, and citizens killed or captured in conformity with the laws of nations.
It is not always necessary for the real and impartial spectator to be at a great distance to pervert the rectitude of our own judgments concerning the propriety of our own conduct.

When the real and impartial spectator is present, the violence and injustice of our own selfish passions can induce the man within the breast to make a report very different from what the real circumstances authorize.
There are two occasions upon which we examine our own conduct and try to view it as the impartial spectator would: first, when we are about to act; second, after we have acted.
Our views are apt to be very partial both when we are about to act and after we have acted.
Our views are most partial when it is most important that they should be otherwise.
When we are about to act, the eagerness of passion seldom allows us to consider what we are doing with the candour of an indifferent person.
The violent emotions that agitate us when about to act discolour our views of things, even when we try to place ourselves in the situation of another.
The fury of our own passions constantly calls us back to our own place, where everything appears magnified and misrepresented by self-love.
We can obtain only instantaneous glimpses of how objects would appear to another, and these glimpses vanish quickly and are not altogether just.
We cannot divest ourselves entirely of the heat and keenness inspired by our peculiar situation, nor consider what we are about to do with complete impartiality.
According to father Malebranche, passions justify themselves and seem reasonable and proportioned to their objects as long as we continue to feel them.
After the action is over and the passions have subsided, we can enter more coolly into the sentiments of the indifferent spectator.
What before interested us becomes almost as indifferent to us as it always was to the impartial spectator after the passions subside.
When the paroxysm of emotion is over, we can identify ourselves with the ideal man within the breast and view our own conduct with the severe eyes of the most impartial spectator.
Our judgments after the passions subside are often of little importance compared to what they were before.
Judgments after the passions subside can frequently produce nothing but vain regret and unavailing repentance.
Judgments after the passions subside do not always secure us from like errors in the future.
It is seldom that our judgments are quite candid even after the passions have subsided.
The opinion we entertain of our own character depends entirely on our judgment concerning our past conduct.
It is disagreeable to think ill of ourselves, so we often purposely turn away from circumstances that might render our judgment unfavorable.
People often endeavor to exasperate anew the unjust passions that formerly misled them rather than see their own behavior under an unpleasant aspect.
People may awaken old hatreds and irritate almost forgotten resentments to avoid acknowledging past injustice.
People sometimes persevere in injustice merely because they once were unjust and are ashamed and afraid to see that they were so.
Views of mankind regarding the propriety of their own conduct are so partial at the time of action and after it that it is difficult for them to view it as an indifferent spectator would.

If people judged their own conduct by a particular power of perception that distinguished the beauty or deformity of passions, it would judge more accurately concerning their own passions than those of others.
Self-deceit is a fatal weakness of mankind and is the source of half the disorders of human life.
If people saw themselves as others see them or as others would see them if they knew all, a reformation would generally be unavoidable.
Nature has not left the weakness of self-deceit altogether without a remedy.
Continual observations upon the conduct of others lead people to form certain general rules about what is fit and proper to be done or avoided.
Some actions shock all natural sentiments and are universally detested by people around us.
Universal detestation of certain actions confirms and exasperates our natural sense of their deformity.
Seeing others view certain actions with detestation satisfies us that we view them in the proper light.
We resolve never to be guilty of actions that render us objects of universal disapprobation.
We naturally lay down general rules that actions which make us odious, contemptible, or punishable are to be avoided.
Other actions call forth approbation and are universally viewed favorably.
Actions that excite love, gratitude, and admiration of mankind are eagerly honored and rewarded.
We become ambitious to perform actions that excite love, gratitude, and admiration.
We naturally lay down rules that opportunities to act in a manner that excites approbation are to be sought after.
General rules of morality are formed from experience of what particular instances our moral faculties approve or disapprove.
We do not originally approve or condemn particular actions because they appear agreeable or inconsistent with a general rule.
General rules are formed by finding from experience that all actions of a certain kind are approved or disapproved.
A man who first saw an inhuman murder committed from avarice, envy, or unjust resentment would feel detestation instantaneously and antecedent to forming any general rule.
The general rule prohibiting the taking away of the life of an innocent person is formed after the detestation felt at particular actions of that kind.
Admiration for generosity and contempt for baseness do not arise from general rules declaring all actions of one kind admirable and all of the other contemptible.
General rules about actions are formed from experience of the effects those actions naturally produce upon us.
An amiable action naturally excites love for the person who performs it.
A respectable action naturally excites respect for the person who performs it.
A horrid action naturally excites horror for the person who performs it.
General rules determining which actions are objects of love, respect, or horror can only be formed by observing what actions actually excite those sentiments.
Once general rules are universally acknowledged and established by the sentiments of mankind, they are appealed to as standards of judgment.
General rules are cited as the ultimate foundations of what is just and unjust in human conduct.
Some authors have mistakenly supposed that original judgments of right and wrong are formed by first considering general rules and then applying them to particular actions.
General rules of conduct fixed in the mind by habitual reflection help correct misrepresentations of self-love about what is fit and proper to do.
A man of furious resentment might regard the death of his enemy as a small compensation for a perceived wrong.
Observations of others' conduct teach that sanguinary revenges appear horrible.
A man educated normally lays down an inviolable rule to abstain from sanguinary revenges on all occasions.
The rule against sanguinary revenge preserves its authority and prevents the man from committing such violence.
If the man considered such an action for the first time, he might determine it just and proper.
Reverence for the rule, impressed by past experience, checks the impetuosity of passion.
Reverence for the rule helps correct partial views suggested by self-love about what is proper to do.
If the man violates the rule under passion, he cannot completely throw off the awe and respect for it.
At the moment of acting under passion, the man hesitates and trembles at the thought of violating the rule.
He is secretly conscious that he is breaking measures of conduct he had resolved never to infringe.
He has never seen others infringe the rule without the highest disapprobation.
He forebodes that infringing the rule will render him the object of disagreeable sentiments.
Before taking the final resolution, he is tormented with agonies of doubt and uncertainty.
He is terrified at the thought of violating the sacred rule.
He is simultaneously urged by the fury of his desires to violate the rule.
He changes his purpose every moment between adhering to the rule and indulging passion.
Sometimes he resolves to adhere to his principle and not indulge a passion that may corrupt his life with shame and repentance.
A momentary calm takes possession of him from the prospect of security and tranquility if he adheres to the rule.
Immediately the passion rouses anew and drives him to commit what he had resolved to abstain from.
Wearied and distracted with continual irresolutions, he at length makes the last fatal and irrecoverable step.
He makes this step with terror and amazement, like one fleeing an enemy who throws himself over a precipice.
He is sure of meeting with more certain destruction by violating the rule than from what pursues him.
His sentiments at the time of acting include less sense of impropriety than afterwards.
After passion is gratified and palled, he views his action as others do.
He actually feels the stings of remorse and repentance after the action.
Remorse and repentance begin to agitate and torment him after the passion subsides.
The regard to general rules of conduct is properly called a sense of duty.
A sense of duty is the only principle by which the bulk of mankind are capable of directing their actions.
Many men behave decently and avoid considerable blame throughout their lives by acting from regard to established rules of behaviour.
A man who has received great benefits may feel little gratitude due to natural coldness of temper.
A man who has been virtuously educated will strive to act as if he feels gratitude, even if he does not.
Such a man will visit his benefactor regularly and behave respectfully.
He will never speak of his benefactor except with expressions of esteem and acknowledgment of obligations.
He will embrace every opportunity to make a proper return for past services.
He may act from reverence for the established rule of duty without hypocrisy, selfish intention, or design to impose.
A wife may not feel tender regard for her husband but will act as if she does if virtuously educated.
Such a wife will be careful, officious, faithful, and sincere in her attentions.
Such a friend or wife may not be the very best of their kinds but may be the second best.
Those strongly impressed with regard to general rules will not fail in any very essential part of their duty.
Only those of the happiest mould can suit their sentiments and behaviour with exact justness to every situation.
The bulk of mankind cannot be wrought up to such perfection.
Almost every man can be impressed by discipline, education, and example to act with tolerable decency and avoid considerable blame.
Without sacred regard to general rules, no man's conduct can be much depended upon.
The essential difference between a man of principle and honour and a worthless fellow is the regard to general rules.
A man of principle adheres steadily and resolutely to his maxims and preserves an even tenour of conduct.
A worthless fellow acts variously and accidentally according to humour, inclination, or interest.
Inequalities of humour can lead a man with delicate sensibility to act absurdly on frivolous occasions without the principle of regard to general rules.
A friend visiting when one is in a disagreeable humour may be seen as an impertinent intrusion.
Regard to general rules of civility and hospitality prevents one from behaving with coldness and contempt in such situations.
Habitual reverence for general rules enables acting with nearly equal propriety despite inequalities of temper.
Without regard to general rules, even duties of politeness would be frequently violated.
Duties of justice, truth, chastity, and fidelity are often difficult to observe and have strong motives to violate.
The tolerable observance of duties of justice, truth, chastity, and fidelity is essential to the existence of human society.
Human society would crumble if mankind were not generally impressed with reverence for important rules of conduct.
Reverence for important rules of morality is enhanced by the opinion that they are commands and laws of the Deity.
This opinion is first impressed by nature and afterwards confirmed by reasoning and philosophy.
Men naturally ascribe to religious beings their own sentiments and passions.
Men conceive unknown intelligences with some resemblance to intelligences they have experience of.
During pagan superstition, mankind ascribed to their divinities all human passions, including lust, hunger, avarice, envy, and revenge.
Mankind also ascribed to their gods sentiments and qualities like love of virtue, beneficence, and abhorrence of vice and injustice.
A man injured called upon Jupiter to witness the wrong and believed the god would feel indignation.
The man who did injury felt himself the object of detestation and resentment of mankind and imputed the same to the gods.
Natural hopes, fears, and suspicions were propagated by sympathy and confirmed by education.
Gods were universally represented as rewarders of humanity and mercy and avengers of perfidy and injustice.
Religion in its rudest form gave a sanction to the rules of morality before philosophical reasoning.
The terrors of religion enforced the natural sense of duty, which was important for the happiness of mankind.
Moral faculties were given to humans for the direction of conduct in this life.
Moral faculties carry evident badges of authority indicating they are supreme arbiters of all actions.
Moral faculties superintend all senses, passions, and appetites, judging how far each should be indulged or restrained.
Moral faculties are not on the same level as other faculties and appetites, having more right to restrain them.
No other faculty or principle of action judges any other faculty or principle.
Love does not judge resentment, nor resentment judge love.
Moral faculties have the peculiar office to judge and bestow censure or applause upon all other principles of our nature.
Moral faculties can be considered as senses whose objects are other principles of our nature.
Every sense is supreme over its own objects, with no appeal from it regarding its judgments.
The eye judges the beauty of colors, the ear judges the harmony of sounds, and the taste judges the agreeableness of flavors.
The essence of qualities like sweetness, beauty, and harmony consists in their ability to please the respective senses.
Moral faculties determine when and how far every principle of our nature ought to be indulged or restrained.
What is agreeable to moral faculties is fit, right, and proper to be done.
What is contrary to moral faculties is wrong, unfit, and improper.
Sentiments approved by moral faculties are graceful and becoming.
Sentiments disapproved by moral faculties are ungraceful and unbecoming.
Words like right, wrong, fit, improper, graceful, and unbecoming mean what pleases or displeases moral faculties.
Moral faculties were plainly intended to be the governing principles of human nature.
The rules prescribed by moral faculties are to be regarded as commands and laws of the Deity.
General rules are commonly denominated laws.
General rules which moral faculties observe in approving or condemning sentiments or actions may be denominated laws.
Moral laws resemble laws laid down by a sovereign to direct the conduct of subjects.
Moral laws are rules to direct the free actions of men.
Moral laws are prescribed by a lawful superior and attended with sanctions of rewards and punishments.
Vicegerents of God within us punish violation of moral laws by inward shame and self-condemnation.
Vicegerents of God within us reward obedience with tranquility of mind, contentment, and self-satisfaction.
The happiness of mankind and all rational creatures seems to have been the original purpose intended by the Author of nature.
No other end seems worthy of the supreme wisdom and divine benignity ascribed to the Author of nature.
The works of nature seem intended to promote happiness and guard against misery.
By acting according to the dictates of moral faculties, humans pursue the most effectual means for promoting the happiness of mankind.
By acting according to moral faculties, humans may be said to cooperate with the Deity and advance the plan of Providence.
By acting otherwise than moral faculties dictate, humans seem to obstruct the scheme established by the Author of nature for happiness and perfection.
Acting contrary to moral faculties declares humans, in some measure, enemies of God.
Humans are naturally encouraged to hope for extraordinary favor and reward from God when obeying moral faculties.
Humans are naturally encouraged to dread God's vengeance and punishment when disobeying moral faculties.
General rules by which external prosperity and adversity are distributed show that every virtue naturally meets with its proper reward.
Every virtue meets with the recompense most fit to encourage and promote it.
It requires an extraordinary concurrence of circumstances to entirely disappoint the natural reward of virtue.
The proper reward for industry, prudence, and circumspection is success in every sort of business.
Wealth and external honors are the recompense which industry, prudence, and circumspection can seldom fail to acquire.
Religion enforces the natural sense of duty.
Mankind generally places great confidence in the probity of those who seem deeply impressed with religious sentiments.
People imagine that religious persons act under an additional tie besides those which regulate the conduct of other men.
The regard to the propriety of action and to reputation are motives that influence both religious men and men of the world.
Religious men lie under another restraint and never act deliberately except as if in the presence of a Great Superior.
The Great Superior is finally to recompense men according to their deeds.
Greater trust is reposed in the regularity and exactness of the conduct of religious men.
Wherever the natural principles of religion are not corrupted by factious and party zeal, the first duty required is to fulfill all the obligations of morality.
Wherever men are not taught to regard frivolous observances as more immediate duties of religion than acts of justice and beneficence, the world judges rightly.

Wherever men are not taught to imagine that sacrifices, ceremonies, and vain supplications can bargain with the Deity for fraud, perfidy, and violence, the world places double confidence in the rectitude of the religious man's behavior.
Religion provides strong motives to practice virtue and powerful restraints against the temptations of vice.
Some have supposed that religious principles are the sole laudable motives of action.
It has been argued that we ought not to reward from gratitude nor punish from resentment.
It has been argued that we ought not to protect children or support infirm parents from natural affection.
All affections for particular objects ought to be extinguished and replaced by the love of the Deity.
The sole principle and motive of conduct in performing duties ought to be a sense that God has commanded them.
The author does not examine the opinion that religious principles should be the sole motive of action in this text.
Christianity's first precept is to love God with all heart, soul, and strength.
Christianity's second precept is to love our neighbour as ourselves.
We love ourselves for our own sakes, not merely because we are commanded to do so.
The sense of duty should be the ruling and governing principle of conduct according to philosophy and common sense.
It is a question in which cases actions should arise chiefly or entirely from a sense of duty or from other sentiments or affections.
The decision depends on the natural agreeableness or deformity of the sentiment or affection prompting the action.
The decision also depends on the precision and exactness or looseness and inaccuracy of the general rules themselves.
Benevolent affections should prompt graceful and admired actions as much as regard to general rules.
A benefactor feels ill requited if good offices are repaid merely from a cold sense of duty without affection.
A husband is dissatisfied with an obedient wife if her conduct is motivated only by regard to her relational duties.
A parent may justly complain of a son's indifference if he lacks affectionate reverence despite fulfilling filial duties.
A son would not be satisfied with a parent who performs duties without fatherly fondness.
For benevolent and social affections, the sense of duty is agreeable when it restrains rather than enlivens them.
It is pleasing to see a father check his fondness, a friend set bounds to generosity, and a beneficiary restrain excessive gratitude.
The opposite maxim applies to malevolent and unsocial passions.
We ought to reward from gratitude and generosity without reluctance or reflection on propriety.
We ought to punish with reluctance and more from a sense of propriety than from a savage disposition to revenge.
A graceful person resents injuries more from a sense of deservedness than from personal fury.
Such a person acts like a judge considering general rules on vengeance for each offence.
In executing punishment, this person feels more for the offender's suffering than for their own.
Even in wrath, this person remembers mercy and interprets rules in the gentlest manner consistent with good sense.
Selfish passions hold a middle place between social and unsocial affections.
In ordinary cases, pursuit of private interest should flow from regard to general rules rather than passion for the objects.
In important or extraordinary cases, passion for the objects should animate us considerably.
Being anxious or plotting to gain or save a small amount degrades a tradesman in the opinion of neighbors.
No attention to small matters for their own sake should appear in conduct, regardless of circumstances.
Severe economy and exact assiduity may be required by one's situation.
Each act of economy and assiduity should proceed from regard to the general rule prescribing such conduct.
Parsimony should not arise from desire for the particular small saving.
Attendance in a shop should not arise from passion for the particular small gain.
The difference between a miser and a person of exact economy is that the miser is anxious about small matters for their own sake.
A person of exact economy attends to small matters only as part of a broader scheme of life.
A person appears mean-spirited if they do not pursue extraordinary and important objects of self-interest with some degree of earnestness for their own sake.
We should despise a prince who is not anxious about conquering or defending a province.
We should have little respect for a private gentleman who does not exert himself to gain an estate or a considerable office when he can acquire them without meanness or injustice.
A member of parliament who shows no keenness about his own election is abandoned by his friends as unworthy of their attachment.
A tradesman is thought a poor-spirited fellow among his neighbors if he does not bestir himself to get an extraordinary job or some uncommon advantage.
The spirit and keenness to pursue great objects of self-interest constitute the difference between a man of enterprise and a man of dull regularity.
The great objects of self-interest, whose loss or acquisition changes a person's rank, are the objects of the passion called ambition.
Ambition is a passion that, when kept within prudence and justice, is always admired in the world.
Ambition can have a certain irregular greatness that dazzles the imagination when it passes the limits of prudence and justice and becomes unjust and extravagant.
There is general admiration for heroes and conquerors and statesmen whose projects have been daring and extensive, even if devoid of justice.
The objects of avarice and ambition differ only in their greatness.
A miser is as furious about a halfpenny as a man of ambition is about the conquest of a kingdom.
The precision and exactness or looseness and inaccuracy of general rules affect how far our conduct should proceed entirely from regard to them.
The general rules of most virtues such as prudence, charity, generosity, gratitude, and friendship are loose and inaccurate and admit many exceptions.
It is scarcely possible to regulate our conduct entirely by regard to the general rules of most virtues.
Common proverbial maxims of prudence are founded in universal experience and are perhaps the best general rules about prudence.
Strict and literal adherence to the common maxims of prudence would be absurd and ridiculous pedantry.
Gratitude is perhaps the virtue whose rules are the most precise and admit the fewest exceptions.
The rule that we should make a return of equal or superior value to services received seems plain and admits of few exceptions.
Upon examination, the rule of returning equal or superior value for services received appears loose and inaccurate and admits many exceptions.
Questions about how to repay a benefactor, such as attending them in sickness or lending money, cannot be precisely answered by any general rule.
Differences in character and circumstances between persons may justify refusing to lend money to a benefactor while still being perfectly grateful.
One may lend or give a benefactor much more than was lent and still be accused of ingratitude and not fulfilling the obligation.
The duties of gratitude are perhaps the most sacred of those prescribed by beneficent virtues.
The general rules determining the duties of gratitude are the most accurate among the beneficent virtues.
The general rules determining actions required by friendship, humanity, hospitality, and generosity are more vague and indeterminate than those of gratitude.
Justice is a virtue whose general rules determine with the greatest exactness every external action it requires.
The rules of justice are highly accurate and admit no exceptions or modifications except those ascertainable as accurately as the rules themselves.
If a person owes ten pounds, justice requires that they pay precisely ten pounds at the agreed time or when demanded.
What, how much, when, and where a person ought to perform an action required by justice are all precisely fixed and determined.
Strict adherence to the rules of justice is not pedantry but is due the most sacred regard.
Actions required by justice are best performed when motivated by reverential and religious regard to the general rules.
In practicing other virtues, conduct should be directed by a sense of propriety and taste rather than strict adherence to precise maxims.
In justice, the man who adheres most obstinately to the general rules is the most commendable and dependable.
The end of the rules of justice is to prevent hurting our neighbor.
Violating the rules of justice can be a crime even if one pretends the violation causes no harm.
A man becomes a villain the moment he begins to chicane or refine in his own heart about adhering to justice.
Departing from strict adherence to the inviolable precepts of justice makes a person untrustworthy and potentially guilty of greater crimes.
A thief may imagine he does no evil when stealing from the rich what they may easily spare or never notice missing.
An adulterer may imagine he does no evil when corrupting a friend's wife if he covers the intrigue and does not disturb family peace.
Giving way to refinements in justice can lead to committing gross enormities.
The rules of justice may be compared to the rules of grammar as precise, accurate, and indispensable.
The rules of other virtues are like critics' rules for sublime and elegant composition: loose, vague, and indeterminate.
The rules of other virtues present a general idea of the perfection to aim at rather than certain and infallible directions.
A man may learn to write grammatically by rule with absolute infallibility and similarly may be taught to act justly.
There are no rules whose observance will infallibly lead to acting with prudence, magnanimity, or beneficence on all occasions.
Some rules may help correct and ascertain imperfect ideas about virtues like prudence, magnanimity, and beneficence.
It may happen that with the most serious desire to deserve approbation, we may mistake the proper rules of conduct.
We can be misled by the very principle which ought to direct us.
Mankind cannot enter into the absurd idea of duty which influenced a person misled by it.
People cannot approve of actions that follow from a wrong sense of duty.
There is something respectable in the character and behaviour of one betrayed into vice by a wrong sense of duty or erroneous conscience.
A person misled by a wrong sense of duty is more the object of commiseration than hatred or resentment among the generous and humane.
The generous and humane lament the weakness of human nature that exposes us to unhappy delusions even when sincerely labouring after perfection.
False notions of religion are almost the only causes that can cause gross perversion of natural sentiments in this way.
The principle that gives the greatest authority to the rules of duty is alone capable of distorting ideas of them in any considerable degree.
In all other cases, common sense is sufficient to direct us to something not very far from the most exquisite propriety of conduct.
If we are earnestly desirous to do well, our behaviour will generally be praise-worthy.
All men agree that to obey the will of the Deity is the first rule of duty.
People differ widely concerning the particular commandments which the will of the Deity may impose.
Great mutual forbearance and toleration is due because of differences in religious commandments.
The defence of society requires that crimes should be punished regardless of the motives behind them.
A good man will punish crimes with reluctance when they evidently proceed from false notions of religious duty.
A good man will not feel the same indignation against those who commit crimes from false religious duty as he does against other criminals.
A good man will regret and sometimes admire the unfortunate firmness and magnanimity of those who commit crimes from false religious duty.
In Voltaire's tragedy of Mahomet, two innocent and virtuous young people are instigated by false religion to commit a horrid murder.
The two young people are commanded to kill a venerable old man who is actually their father, though they do not know it.
The young people experience agonies from the struggle between religious duty and compassion, gratitude, reverence, and love.
The tragedy represents an instructive spectacle of the conflict between religious duty and human feelings.
The sense of duty prevails and the young people execute the crime.
After executing the crime, the young people discover their error and are distracted with horror, remorse, and resentment.
We ought to feel for every person misled by religion the same sentiments as for Seid and Palmira in the tragedy.
We should be sure that it is really religion that misleads a person, not a pretence used to cover bad passions.
A person may act wrong by following a wrong sense of duty.
Nature may sometimes prevail and lead a person to act right in opposition to a wrong sense of duty.
We cannot be displeased to see a motive we think ought to prevail prevail, even if the person thinks otherwise.
Conduct that results from weakness, not principle, does not deserve complete approbation.
A bigoted Roman Catholic who saves Protestants during the massacre of St. Bartholomew out of compassion would not deserve high applause.
We might be pleased with the humanity of such a person's temper but regard him with pity inconsistent with admiration due to perfect virtue.
We do not dislike to see passions exerted properly even when a false notion of duty would direct restraint.
A devout Quaker who retaliates when struck on one cheek would not be disagreeable to us.
We would laugh and be diverted by the Quaker's spirit and like him better for it.
We would not regard the Quaker with the respect and esteem due to one who acted properly from a just sense of what was proper.
No action can properly be called virtuous if it is not accompanied by the sentiment of self-approbation.
Part IV is titled 'Of the Effect of Utility upon the Sentiment of Approbation.'
Part IV consists of one section.
Utility is one of the principal sources of beauty.
The conveniency of a house gives pleasure to the spectator as well as its regularity.
A defect in conveniency or regularity in a house causes displeasure to the observer.
The fitness of any system or machine to produce its intended end bestows propriety and beauty upon the whole.
The thought and contemplation of a well-fitted system or machine is agreeable.
The utility of any object pleases the master by suggesting the pleasure or conveniency it is fitted to promote.
Every time the master looks at a useful object, he is reminded of the pleasure it provides.
The object becomes a source of perpetual satisfaction and enjoyment to the master.
The spectator sympathizes with the master and views the object under the same agreeable aspect.
When visiting the palaces of the great, spectators conceive the satisfaction they would enjoy if they were the masters.
The appearance of inconveniency renders any object disagreeable to both the owner and the spectator.
The fitness or contrivance of a production of art is often more valued than the end for which it was intended.
The exact adjustment of means for attaining conveniency or pleasure is frequently more regarded than the conveniency or pleasure itself.
A person may be angry with a servant for leaving chairs in disorder and may arrange them himself to restore order.
The propriety of the new chair arrangement arises from its superior conveniency in leaving the floor free.
The person voluntarily puts himself to more trouble to arrange the chairs than he would have suffered from the lack of conveniency.
What the person wants is not so much the conveniency itself as the arrangement that promotes it.
The conveniency ultimately recommends the arrangement and bestows its propriety and beauty.
A watch that falls behind more than two minutes a day is despised by a person curious about watches.
Such a person may sell a less accurate watch and buy a more accurate one at a higher price.
The sole use of watches is to tell the time and prevent inconveniency from ignorance of time.
A person who is particular about watch accuracy is not always more punctual or anxious about knowing the exact time.
What interests the person is the perfection of the machine that tells the time, not the knowledge of the time itself.
Many people ruin themselves by spending money on trinkets of frivolous utility.
Lovers of toys are pleased not so much by utility as by the aptness of the machines fitted to promote it.
People carry many little conveniencies and baubles, some of which may be of some use but all could be spared.
The utility of all these baubles is not worth the fatigue of bearing their burden.
This principle influences conduct not only regarding frivolous objects but also serious and important pursuits.
The poor man's son, visited by ambition, admires the condition of the rich when he looks around him.
He finds his father's cottage too small for his accommodation.
He fancies he would be more at ease living in a palace.
He is displeased with having to walk on foot or endure the fatigue of riding horseback.
He sees his superiors carried about in machines and imagines he could travel with less inconvenience in one.
He feels naturally indolent and willing to serve himself as little as possible.
He judges that a numerous retinue of servants would save him from a great deal of trouble.
He thinks that if he attained wealth and greatness, he would sit contentedly and enjoy the happiness and tranquility of his situation.
He is enchanted with the distant idea of felicity associated with wealth and greatness.
He devotes himself forever to the pursuit of wealth and greatness to arrive at this felicity.
To obtain the conveniences of wealth and greatness, he submits in the first year or month to more fatigue and uneasiness than he could have suffered through his whole life from the want of them.
He studies to distinguish himself in some laborious profession.
He labors night and day with unrelenting industry to acquire talents superior to all his competitors.
He endeavors to bring his talents into public view and solicits every opportunity of employment with equal assiduity.
He makes his court to all mankind, serves those he hates, and is obsequious to those he despises.
Throughout his life, he pursues the idea of an artificial and elegant repose which he may never arrive at.
He sacrifices a real tranquility that is always in his power for this artificial repose.
If he attains this repose in old age, he will find it no better than the humble security and contentment he abandoned.

In the last stage of life, his body wasted with toil and diseases, and his mind troubled by memories of injuries and disappointments, he begins to find wealth and greatness to be mere trinkets of frivolous utility.
Wealth and greatness are no more adapted for procuring ease of body or tranquility of mind than the tweezer-cases of a lover of toys.
The conveniences of wealth and greatness are more observable than those of small trinkets.
Palaces, gardens, equipage, and retinues of the great are objects whose obvious convenience strikes everybody.
People readily enter into the utility of the great's possessions and applaud the satisfaction they afford.
The curiosity of small trinkets like tooth-picks or ear-pickers is not so obvious.
The conveniences of small trinkets may be equally great but are less striking and less reasonable subjects of vanity than the magnificence of wealth and greatness.
The sole advantage of wealth and greatness is that they more effectively gratify the love of distinction natural to man.
For a person living alone in a desolate island, it might be doubtful whether a palace or a collection of small conveniences would contribute most to happiness.
In society, people pay more regard to the sentiments of the spectator than to those of the person principally concerned.
People consider how a person's situation will appear to others rather than how it appears to himself.
The spectator admires the condition of the rich and great not so much for their superior ease or pleasure but for the numberless artificial and elegant contrivances promoting this ease or pleasure.
The spectator does not imagine the rich and great are really happier than others but imagines they possess more means of happiness.
The ingenious and artful adjustment of means to ends is the principal source of the spectator's admiration.
In disease and old age, the pleasures of vain and empty distinctions of greatness disappear.
In such a situation, the person curses ambition and regrets the ease and indolence of youth.
He regrets having foolishly sacrificed youth's pleasures for what can afford no real satisfaction.
Greatness appears as enormous and operose machines producing a few trifling conveniences to the body.
These machines consist of delicate springs that must be kept in order with anxious attention and are ready to burst and crush their possessor.
They are immense fabrics requiring a lifetime's labor to raise and threatening to overwhelm their inhabitant.
While standing, these machines may save from smaller inconveniences but cannot protect from severe inclemencies of the season.
They keep off summer showers but not winter storms and leave the person exposed to anxiety, fear, sorrow, diseases, danger, and death.
The same principle, love of system, and regard to the beauty of order, art, and contrivance often recommend institutions that promote public welfare.
A patriot's effort to improve public police does not always arise from pure sympathy with those who benefit.
Public-spirited men do not commonly encourage mending high roads out of fellow-feeling with carriers and waggoners.
Legislatures establish premiums and encouragements to advance linen or woollen manufactures seldom from pure sympathy with the wearer of cloth.
Legislatures' conduct in promoting manufactures seldom proceeds from sympathy with manufacturers or merchants.
The perfection of police, and the extension of trade and manufactures, are considered noble and magnificent objects.
Contemplation of the perfection of police and trade pleases us and interests us in their advancement.
These objects form part of the great system of government.
The wheels of the political machine seem to move with more harmony and ease by means of these objects.
We take pleasure in beholding the perfection of a beautiful and grand system.
We feel uneasy until we remove any obstruction that disturbs or encumbers the regularity of the system's motions.
All constitutions of government are valued only in proportion as they promote the happiness of those who live under them.
The sole use and end of constitutions of government is to promote the happiness of their subjects.
From a spirit of system and love of art and contrivance, people sometimes value means more than the end.
People may promote the happiness of others more to perfect a beautiful and orderly system than from immediate sense of others' suffering or enjoyment.
Some men of great public spirit have shown little sensitivity to feelings of humanity.
Some men of great humanity seem entirely devoid of public spirit.
Examples of men with great public spirit but little humanity, and vice versa, can be found in one's acquaintances.
The celebrated legislator of Muscovy had less humanity but more public spirit.
James the First of Great Britain had little passion for the glory or interest of his country.
Describing the happiness of the rich and great often fails to awaken industry in a man dead to ambition.
Eloquent exhortations about the comforts of the rich have little effect on such a man.
Describing the convenience and arrangement of palaces, equipages, and attendants can make an impression on a man dead to ambition.
These comforts tend only to keep off sun and rain, save from hunger, cold, want, and weariness.
Telling a man heedless of his country's interest about superior advantages of a well-governed state usually makes little impression.
Describing the great system of public police and its parts is more likely to persuade such a man.
Explaining the connections, dependencies, subordination, and subserviency of parts of government to society's happiness can animate public spirit.
Showing how a system might be introduced, what hinders it, and how to remove obstructions can motivate desire to improve government.
It is scarcely possible for a man to listen to such discourse without feeling some degree of public spirit.
At least momentarily, a man will desire to remove obstructions and put into motion a beautiful and orderly machine.
Nothing tends more to promote public spirit than the study of politics and systems of civil government.
Studying the constitution of one's country, its situation, interests, commerce, defense, disadvantages, dangers, and remedies animates public passions.
Political disquisitions, if just, reasonable, and practicable, are the most useful works of speculation.
Even the weakest and worst political disquisitions are not altogether without utility.
Weak political disquisitions serve to animate public passions and rouse men to seek means of promoting society's happiness.
The characters of men, as well as the contrivances of art or institutions of civil government, may promote or disturb the happiness of the individual and society.
The prudent, equitable, active, resolute, and sober character promises prosperity and satisfaction to the person and those connected with him.
The rash, insolent, slothful, effeminate, and voluptuous character forebodes ruin to the individual and misfortune to those connected with him.
The prudent and virtuous character has all the beauty of the most perfect machine invented for promoting agreeable purposes.
The rash and vicious character has all the deformity of the most awkward and clumsy contrivance.
No institution of government could promote the happiness of mankind as much as the general prevalence of wisdom and virtue.
All government is an imperfect remedy for the deficiency of wisdom and virtue.
Any beauty that civil government has on account of its utility must belong in a far superior degree to wisdom and virtue.
The fatal effects of bad government arise from its failure to guard against the mischiefs caused by human wickedness.
Characters appear beautiful or deformed based on their usefulness or inconvenience.
This beauty or deformity strikes those who consider human actions in an abstract and philosophical light.
Philosophers often do not form clear conceptions of particular actions of cruelty or humanity but rely on vague ideas suggested by general names.
The propriety or impropriety, merit or demerit of actions is most obvious and discernible in particular instances.
Particular examples allow us to perceive concord or disagreement between our affections and those of the agent.
In abstract consideration, the qualities that excite sentiments of virtue and vice seem to disappear and the sentiments become less obvious.
The happy effects of virtue and the fatal consequences of vice stand out distinctly when considered abstractly.
An author explained that utility pleases because it produces a species of beauty.
No qualities of the mind are approved as virtuous except those useful or agreeable to oneself or others.
No qualities are disapproved as vicious except those with a contrary tendency to usefulness or agreeableness.
Nature has adjusted our sentiments of approbation and disapprobation to the convenience of the individual and society.
The perception of utility or hurtfulness is not the first or principal source of our approbation and disapprobation.
Sentiments of approbation and disapprobation are enhanced by the perception of beauty or deformity resulting from utility or hurtfulness.
The approbation of virtue is not the same kind of sentiment as the approval of a convenient and well-contrived building.
We have other reasons for praising a man than those for commending a chest of drawers.
The usefulness of any disposition of mind is seldom the first ground of our approbation.
The sentiment of approbation always involves a sense of propriety distinct from the perception of utility.
Qualities approved as virtuous include those useful to ourselves and those useful to others.
The qualities most useful to ourselves are superior reason and understanding, and self-command.
Superior reason and understanding enable us to discern remote consequences of actions and foresee advantages or detriments.
Self-command enables us to abstain from present pleasure or endure present pain to obtain greater future pleasure or avoid greater future pain.
The union of superior reason and self-command constitutes the virtue of prudence.
Prudence is the virtue most useful to the individual.
Superior reason and understanding are originally approved as just, right, and accurate, not merely as useful or advantageous.
The greatest exertions of human reason are displayed in abstruse sciences, especially higher mathematics.
The utility of abstruse sciences to the individual or public is not very obvious and requires complex discussion to prove.
The utility of abstruse sciences was little insisted upon until it was necessary to respond to reproaches that they were useless.
Self-command by restraining present appetites to gratify them more fully later is approved under propriety and utility.
When we act by restraining present appetites for future pleasure, our sentiments coincide with those of the spectator.
The spectator does not feel the solicitations of our present appetites.
The spectator finds future pleasure as interesting as present pleasure.
Sacrificing future pleasure for present pleasure appears absurd and extravagant to the spectator.
The spectator cannot understand the principles influencing conduct that sacrifices future pleasure for present pleasure.
Abstaining from present pleasure to secure greater future pleasure aligns our affections with the spectator's.
The spectator approves of conduct that sacrifices present pleasure for greater future pleasure.
Few people are capable of self-command to sacrifice present pleasure for future gain.
The spectator regards self-command with wonder and admiration.
Steady perseverance in frugality, industry, and application commands eminent esteem.
The firmness to give up present pleasures and endure labor for remote advantage commands approbation.
The agent's view of interest and happiness corresponds with the spectator's idea.
There is perfect correspondence between the agent's sentiments and the spectator's.
The correspondence between agent and spectator sentiments is unexpected due to common human weakness.
We not only approve but admire conduct that sacrifices present pleasure for future gain.
Consciousness of merited approbation supports the agent in self-command conduct.
Pleasure to be enjoyed ten years hence interests us less than pleasure today.
The passion excited by future pleasure is weaker than that excited by present pleasure.
Future pleasure could not balance present pleasure without the sense of propriety and consciousness of esteem.
Acting to merit esteem and approbation supports self-command.
Humanity, justice, generosity, and public spirit are qualities most useful to others.
The propriety of humanity and justice depends on concord between agent's and spectator's affections.
The propriety of generosity and public spirit is founded on the same principle as justice.
Generosity is different from humanity.
Humanity and generosity do not always belong to the same person.
Humanity is the virtue of a woman, generosity of a man.
Women commonly have more tenderness but less generosity than men.
Women rarely make considerable donations, as observed in civil law.
Humanity consists in the spectator's fellow-feeling with the sentiments of those principally concerned.
Humanity causes grief for sufferings, resentment of injuries, and joy at good fortune.
The most humane actions require no self-denial, self-command, or great exertion of propriety.
Humane actions consist of doing what sympathy naturally prompts.
Generosity requires preferring another person to oneself and sacrificing important self-interest.
A man giving up an office ambition to another he judges more entitled acts from generosity.
A man exposing his life to defend a friend judges the friend's life more important than his own.
Acts of generosity are not from humanity or feeling more concern for others than self.
Generous persons consider opposite interests as they appear to others, not as they appear to themselves.
Sacrificing self-interest for another's interest accommodates the sentiments of the spectator.
By an effort of magnanimity, generous persons act according to views natural to any impartial bystander.
A soldier who sacrifices his life to defend his officer acts properly according to the impartial spectator's view.
The soldier might feel less sorrow for the officer's death than for a small disaster to himself.
