The soldier acts to deserve applause and to make the impartial spectator understand his conduct.
To everyone but himself, the soldier's life is a trifle compared to the officer's life.
A young officer exposes his life to acquire some addition to the dominions of his sovereign.
The young officer values his own life more than the conquest of a whole kingdom for the state he serves.
The officer compares the value of his life and the conquest not from his own perspective but from that of the nation he fights for.
To the nation, the success of the war is of the highest importance.
To the nation, the life of a private person is of scarce any consequence.
When the officer puts himself in the nation's situation, he feels he cannot be too prodigal of his blood if it promotes a valuable purpose.
The heroism of the officer's conduct consists in thwarting his strongest natural propensities from a sense of duty and propriety.
Many honest Englishmen would be more disturbed by the loss of a guinea than by the national loss of Minorca.
Those same Englishmen would sacrifice their lives many times rather than let Minorca fall into enemy hands through their fault.
The first Brutus led his own sons to capital punishment because they conspired against the rising liberty of Rome.
Brutus sacrificed what would appear to be the stronger affection (for his sons) to the weaker affection (for Rome's liberty) if he had consulted only his own breast.
Brutus viewed his sons not as a father but as a Roman citizen.
Brutus paid no regard to the tie connecting him with his sons when acting as a Roman citizen.
To a Roman citizen, even the sons of Brutus seemed contemptible compared to the smallest interest of Rome.
Admiration for such actions is founded more on their unexpectedness and noble propriety than on their utility.
Utility bestows a new beauty on such actions and further recommends them to approbation.
The beauty of utility is chiefly perceived by men of reflection and speculation.
The beauty of utility is not the quality that first recommends such actions to the natural sentiments of most people.
Sentiment of approbation arising from perception of utility has no reference to the sentiments of others.
A person growing up without communication with society might find his own actions agreeable or disagreeable based on their tendency to his happiness or disadvantage.
Such a person might perceive beauty in prudence, temperance, and good conduct, and deformity in the opposite behavior.
He might view his own temper and character with satisfaction like a well-contrived machine or with distaste like an awkward contrivance.
These perceptions are a matter of taste and have feebleness and delicacy.
These perceptions probably would not be much attended to by one in a solitary and miserable condition.
Even if such perceptions occur to a solitary person, they would not have the same effect as they would after connection with society.
A solitary person would not be cast down with inward shame at the thought of deformity in his conduct.
A solitary person would not be elevated with secret triumph from the consciousness of beauty in his conduct.
A solitary person would not exult from the notion of deserving reward nor tremble from suspicion of meriting punishment.
Such sentiments suppose the idea of some other being who is the natural judge of the person who feels them.
Only by sympathy with the decisions of this arbiter of conduct can a person conceive triumph of self-applause or shame of self-condemnation.
Part V is titled 'Of the Influence of Custom and Fashion upon the Sentiments of Moral Approbation and Disapprobation.'
Part V consists of one section.
Custom and fashion have a considerable influence upon the moral sentiments of mankind.
Custom and fashion are chief causes of irregular and discordant opinions about what is blameable or praise-worthy in different ages and nations.
Custom and fashion extend their dominion over judgments concerning beauty of every kind.
When two objects have frequently been seen together, the imagination acquires a habit of passing easily from one to the other.
If the first object appears, we expect the second to follow.
Custom connects objects together in our imagination, causing us to feel an impropriety when they are separated.
A suit of clothes seems to want something if it lacks even the most insignificant ornament which usually accompanies it.
Custom increases our sense of natural propriety in the union of objects.
Those accustomed to good taste are more disgusted by clumsy or awkward things.
Where the conjunction of objects is improper, custom diminishes or removes our sense of impropriety.
People accustomed to slovenly disorder lose all sense of neatness or elegance.
Modes of furniture or dress that seem ridiculous to strangers give no offence to those used to them.
Fashion is a particular species of custom.
Fashion is not what everybody wears, but what is worn by those of high rank or character.
The graceful, easy, and commanding manners of the great, combined with richness and magnificence of their dress, give grace to the form they bestow upon it.
As long as the great continue to use a particular form, it is connected in our imaginations with something genteel and magnificent.
When the great drop a form, it loses its grace and seems mean and awkward when used by inferior ranks.
Dress and furniture are entirely under the dominion of custom and fashion.
The influence of custom and fashion extends to all objects of taste, including music, poetry, and architecture.
Modes of dress and furniture are continually changing.
Fashion that is admired five years ago may appear ridiculous today.
Clothes are not made of very durable materials and a well-fancied coat lasts about twelve months.
Furniture changes less rapidly than dress because it is more durable.
In five or six years, furniture generally undergoes an entire revolution in fashion.
Productions of other arts like architecture, music, and poetry are more lasting than dress and furniture.
A well-contrived building may endure many centuries.
A beautiful air may be transmitted by tradition through many successive generations.
A well-written poem may last as long as the world.
These lasting works continue for ages to give vogue to the particular style or taste according to which they were composed.
Few men have the opportunity to see fashion change considerably in the arts during their own times.
Few men have enough experience with different modes from remote ages and nations to judge impartially between them and current fashions.
Few men are willing to admit that custom or fashion influence their judgments about beauty in the arts.
Many imagine that the rules they think should be observed in arts are founded on reason and nature, not habit or prejudice.
A little attention can convince people that custom and fashion influence judgments in architecture, poetry, and music as much as in dress and furniture.
The Doric capital is appropriated to a pillar whose height is equal to eight diameters.
The Ionic volute is appropriated to a pillar whose height is equal to nine diameters.
The Corinthian foliage is appropriated to a pillar whose height is equal to ten diameters.
The propriety of these appropriations is founded on habit and custom.
The eye is offended if particular proportions are not joined with their customary ornaments.
Each of the five orders of architecture has peculiar ornaments that cannot be changed without offending those knowledgeable in architectural rules.
An eminent artist will bring about a considerable change in the established modes of each of those arts.
An eminent artist introduces a new fashion of writing, music, or architecture.
The dress of an agreeable man of high rank, though peculiar and fantastical, soon comes to be admired and imitated.
The excellencies of an eminent master recommend his peculiarities, and his manner becomes the fashionable style in the art he practises.
The taste of the Italians in music and architecture has undergone a considerable change within fifty years from imitating the peculiarities of some eminent masters.
Seneca is accused by Quintilian of having corrupted the taste of the Romans.
Seneca introduced a frivolous prettiness in place of majestic reason and masculine eloquence.
Sallust and Tacitus have been charged with corrupting taste by giving reputation to a style that was concise, elegant, expressive, and poetical but lacked ease, simplicity, and nature.
The style of Sallust and Tacitus was evidently the production of the most laboured and studied affectation.
An author who can render his faults agreeable must possess many great qualities.
The highest eulogy for an author may be to say that he corrupted the taste of a nation.
Mr. Pope and Dr. Swift each introduced a manner different from what was practised before into all works written in rhyme.
Mr. Pope introduced a manner in long verses.
Dr. Swift introduced a manner in short verses.
The quaintness of Butler has given place to the plainness of Swift.
The rambling freedom of Dryden and the correct but often tedious and prosaic languor of Addison are no longer objects of imitation.
All long verses are now written after the manner of the nervous precision of Mr. Pope.
Custom and fashion influence judgments regarding the beauty of natural objects.
Various and opposite forms are deemed beautiful in different species of things.
The proportions admired in one animal are altogether different from those esteemed in another.
Every class of things has its own peculiar conformation which is approved of and has a beauty distinct from every other species.
Father Buffier determined that the beauty of every object consists in the form and colour most usual among things of that particular sort.
In the human form, the beauty of each feature lies in a certain middle equally removed from various other forms that are ugly.
A beautiful nose is neither very long nor very short, neither very straight nor very crooked, but a middle among these extremes.
Nature seems to have aimed at a certain form in features, but deviates in many ways and seldom hits exactly.
Drawings made after one pattern will all resemble the pattern more than they resemble one another.
In each species of creatures, what is most beautiful bears the strongest characters of the general fabric of the species.
Monsters or what is perfectly deformed are always most singular and odd and have the least resemblance to the generality of their species.
The beauty of each species is the rarest of all things because few individuals hit the middle form exactly.
The beauty of each species is also the most common because all deviations from the middle form resemble it more than they resemble one another.
The most customary form in each species of things is the most beautiful according to Father Buffier.
Practice and experience in contemplating each species of objects is requisite before judging its beauty or knowing its middle and most usual form.
The nicest judgment concerning the beauty of the human species will not help judge the beauty of flowers, horses, or other species.
In different climates and customs, the generality of any species receives a different conformation and different ideas of its beauty prevail.
The beauty of a Moorish horse is not exactly the same as that of an English horse.
Different nations form different ideas concerning the beauty of the human shape and countenance.
A fair complexion is considered a shocking deformity on the coast of Guinea.
Thick lips and a flat nose are considered beautiful on the coast of Guinea.
In some nations, long ears that hang down upon the shoulders are objects of universal admiration.
In China, if a lady's foot is large enough to walk upon, she is regarded as a monster of ugliness.
Sentiments concerning beauty of every kind are much influenced by custom and fashion.
Sentiments concerning the beauty of conduct are not entirely exempted from the influence of custom and fashion.
The influence of custom and fashion on moral sentiments is much less than it is on other kinds of beauty.
No form of external objects, however absurd or fantastical, is beyond reconciliation by custom or rendered agreeable by fashion.
The characters and conduct of a Nero or a Claudius are not reconciled or rendered agreeable by custom or fashion.
Nero's character and conduct are objects of dread and hatred.
Claudius's character and conduct are objects of scorn and derision.
The principles of the imagination, upon which our sense of beauty depends, are of a very nice and delicate nature.
The principles of the imagination may easily be altered by habit and education.
Sentiments of moral approbation and disapprobation are founded on the strongest and most vigorous passions of human nature.
Sentiments of moral approbation and disapprobation may be somewhat warped but cannot be entirely perverted.
When custom and fashion coincide with natural principles of right and wrong, they heighten the delicacy of our sentiments.
When custom and fashion coincide with natural principles of right and wrong, they increase our abhorrence for everything which approaches to evil.
People educated in truly good company are more shocked by conduct inconsistent with justice, modesty, humanity, and good order.
People brought up amidst violence, licentiousness, falsehood, and injustice lose all sense of the dreadful enormity of such conduct.
Custom renders habitual the conduct of violence, licentiousness, falsehood, and injustice for those brought up amidst them.
Those accustomed to violence and injustice often regard such conduct as the way of the world.
Fashion sometimes gives reputation to a certain degree of disorder.
Fashion sometimes discounts qualities which deserve esteem.
In the reign of Charles II, a degree of licentiousness was deemed the characteristic of a liberal education.
In the reign of Charles II, licentiousness was connected with generosity, sincerity, magnanimity, loyalty, and proved that the person was a gentleman.
Severity of manners and regularity of conduct were unfashionable in the reign of Charles II.
Severity of manners and regularity of conduct were connected with cant, cunning, hypocrisy, and low manners in the imagination of that age.
To superficial minds, the vices of the great seem agreeable.
Superficial minds connect the vices of the great with the splendour of fortune and many superior virtues.
Superficial minds associate the vices of the great with the spirit of freedom, independency, frankness, generosity, humanity, and politeness.
The virtues of the inferior ranks, such as parsimonious frugality, painful industry, and rigid adherence to rules, seem mean and disagreeable to superficial minds.
Superficial minds connect the virtues of the inferior ranks with the meanness of their station.
Superficial minds associate the virtues of the inferior ranks with many great vices such as abject, cowardly, ill-natured, lying, pilfering disposition.
Different professions and states of life habituate men to very different passions and form very different characters and manners.
We expect in each rank and profession a degree of manners which experience has taught us belonged to it.
We are particularly pleased with the middle conformation in each species of men, which agrees most exactly with the general standard nature seems to have established.
A man should look like his trade and profession.
The pedantry of every profession is disagreeable.
Different periods of life have different manners assigned to them.
In old age, we expect gravity and sedateness.
In youth, we expect sensibility, gaiety, and sprightly vivacity.
The flirting levity of youth and the immoveable insensibility of old age are equally disagreeable.
The young are most agreeable when their behaviour has something of the manners of the old.
The old are most agreeable when they retain something of the gaiety of the young.
The customary character of some professions is founded entirely in habit without being confirmed or enlivened by reflections.
Custom leads us to associate gaiety, levity, sprightly freedom, and some degree of dissipation with the military profession.
A serious and thoughtful turn of mind might be more suitable for those whose lives are continually exposed to uncommon danger.
Men in the military profession are more constantly occupied with thoughts of death and its consequences than other men.
The prevalence of a contrary turn of mind among military men may be due to the effort required to conquer the fear of death.
Those constantly exposed to death find it easier to turn away their thoughts from it and immerse themselves in amusement and dissipation.
A camp is not the natural environment for a thoughtful or melancholy man.
Thoughtful or melancholy men can, by great effort, proceed with inflexible resolution to unavoidable death.
Continual exposure to less imminent danger exhausts and depresses the mind, making it incapable of happiness and enjoyment.
Gay and careless men who avoid effort and anxiety support dangerous circumstances more easily.
Officers not exposed to uncommon danger tend to lose the gaiety and dissipated thoughtlessness typical of their profession.
A captain of a city-guard is commonly as sober, careful, and penurious as other citizens.
A long peace tends to diminish the difference between civil and military character.
The usual situation of military men renders gaiety and some dissipation their usual character.
Custom strongly connects gaiety and dissipation with the military profession in our imagination.
We tend to despise men whose humor or situation makes them incapable of acquiring the customary military character.
We laugh at the grave and careful faces of city-guards because they do not resemble the expected military character.
City-guards often seem ashamed of their regular manners and affect levity to conform to their trade's fashion.
We associate the usual deportment of a respectable order of men so strongly with that order that we expect to find both together.
When we see a character that affects to be different from the usual, we are embarrassed and unsure how to address it.
Different ages and countries give different characters to the generality of those who live in them.
Sentiments about the degree of each quality that is blameworthy or praiseworthy vary according to what is usual in a country and time.
A degree of politeness esteemed in one country may be thought effeminate adulation or rudeness in another.
A degree of order and frugality considered excessive parsimony in one culture may be regarded as extravagance in another.
Every age and country regard the common degree of each quality among their esteemed people as the golden mean of that virtue.
Sentiments about the exact propriety of character and behavior vary according to the habitual qualities of a society.
Among civilized nations, virtues founded on humanity are more cultivated than those founded on self-denial and command of passions.
Among rude and barbarous nations, virtues of self-denial are more cultivated than those of humanity.
General security and happiness in civilized ages afford little exercise to contempt of danger and patience in enduring hardship.
Poverty may be easily avoided in civilized ages, so contempt of poverty almost ceases to be a virtue.
Abstinence from pleasure becomes less necessary in civilized ages.
The mind is more at liberty to unbend and indulge natural inclinations in civilized ages.
Every savage undergoes a sort of Spartan discipline.
Savages are inured to every sort of hardship by the necessity of their situation.
Savages are in continual danger.
Savages are often exposed to the greatest extremities of hunger.
Savages frequently die of pure want.
Savages' circumstances habituate them to every sort of distress.
Savages are taught to give way to none of the passions which distress is apt to excite.
Savages can expect no sympathy or indulgence for weakness from their countrymen.
Before feeling much for others, one must be at ease oneself.
If one's own misery pinches severely, one has no leisure to attend to the misery of others.
All savages are too much occupied with their own wants and necessities to give much attention to those of another person.
A savage expects no sympathy from those about him regardless of the nature of his distress.
A savage disdains to expose himself by allowing the least weakness to escape him.
Savages' passions, however furious and violent, are never permitted to disturb the serenity of their countenance or composure of their conduct and behaviour.
Savages in North America assume the greatest indifference on all occasions.
North American savages would think themselves degraded if they appeared overcome by love, grief, or resentment.
The magnanimity and self-command of North American savages in this respect are almost beyond the conception of Europeans.
In a country where all men are upon a level regarding rank and fortune, all marriages are made up by the parents without exception.

A young man in such a country would think himself disgraced forever if he showed preference for one woman over another or did not express complete indifference about the time and person of his marriage.
The weakness of love is regarded among savages as the most unpardonable effeminacy.
After marriage, the two parties seem ashamed of a connection founded upon necessity.
Married savages do not live together.
Married savages see one another only by stealth.
Married savages continue to dwell in the houses of their respective fathers.
Open cohabitation of the two sexes is considered the most indecent and unmanly sensuality among savages.
Savages exert absolute self-command over passions beyond love, including injuries, reproach, and gross insults.
Savages often bear injuries, reproach, and insults with the appearance of greatest insensibility and without expressing resentment.
When a savage is made prisoner of war and sentenced to death, he hears it without expressing any emotion.
A condemned savage submits to dreadful torments without bemoaning himself or showing any passion except contempt of his enemies.
While hung by the shoulders over a slow fire, a savage derides his tormentors and tells them how he had tortured their countrymen.
After being scorched, burnt, and lacerated for several hours, a savage is often allowed a short respite to prolong his misery.
During the respite, the savage talks on indifferent subjects, inquires after news, and seems indifferent about everything except his own situation.
Spectators of such torture express the same insensibility and make little impression from the sight.
Spectators scarcely look at the prisoner except when helping to torment him.
At other times, spectators smoke tobacco and amuse themselves as if no torture is occurring.
Every savage prepares from earliest youth for the dreadful end of torture and death.
Savages compose a 'song of death' to sing when expiring under tortures inflicted by enemies.
The song of death consists of insults upon tormentors and expresses the highest contempt of death and pain.
Savages sing the song of death on extraordinary occasions, when going to war, meeting enemies, or to show familiarization with dreadful misfortunes.
The same contempt of death and torture prevails among all other savage nations.
No negro from the coast of Africa lacks a degree of magnanimity regarding contempt of death and torture.
Fortune subjected nations of heroes to the refuse of European jails.
The refuse of European jails are wretches who possess neither the virtues of their countries of origin nor those of the countries they go to.
These wretches' levity, brutality, and baseness expose them to the contempt of the vanquished.
Savages are required by the custom and education of their country to have heroic and unconquerable firmness.
People brought up in civilized societies are not required to have the same heroic firmness as savages.
In civilized societies, people who complain when in pain or grieve when in distress are easily pardoned.
Allowing oneself to be overcome by love or discomposed by anger is not seen as affecting the essential character in civilized societies.
In civilized societies, people lose little reputation if their countenance or behavior is somewhat disturbed, as long as they do not act against justice or humanity.
Humane and polished people have more sensibility to the passions of others and can more readily enter into animated and passionate behavior.
People in civilized societies can more easily pardon some little excess in emotional expression.
People are more likely to express stronger emotions in the presence of friends than strangers because they expect more indulgence from friends.
Rules of decorum among civilized nations admit of more animated behavior than is approved among barbarians.
Civilized people converse with the openness of friends, while barbarians converse with the reserve of strangers.
The French and Italians express themselves with more emotion on interesting occasions than people from nations with duller sensibility.
A young French nobleman may weep in the presence of the whole court upon being refused a regiment.
An Italian expresses more emotion on being fined twenty shillings than an Englishman does on receiving a death sentence.
Cicero could weep with bitterness of sorrow in the sight of the whole senate and people without degrading himself.
Orators of earlier and ruder ages of Rome probably could not express themselves with as much emotion as Cicero.
Ancient Roman warriors like the Scipios, Leliuses, and elder Cato would have regarded public displays of tenderness as violations of nature and propriety.
Ancient Roman warriors expressed themselves with order, gravity, and good judgment but were strangers to passionate eloquence.
Sublime and passionate eloquence was introduced into Rome shortly before Cicero's birth by the Gracchi, Crassus, and Sulpitius.
Animated eloquence has long been practiced in France and Italy and is only beginning to be introduced into England.
There is a wide difference between the degrees of self-command required in civilized and barbarous nations.
Polished people, accustomed to give way to natural movements, become frank, open, and sincere.
Barbarians, obliged to smother and conceal every passion, acquire habits of falsehood and dissimulation.
Savage nations in Asia, Africa, and America are equally impenetrable when they want to conceal the truth.
Savages cannot be made to confess what they do not want to tell, even under torture.
The passions of a savage lie concealed but are mounted to the highest pitch of fury.
Savages seldom show symptoms of anger outwardly, but their vengeance is always sanguinary and dreadful.
The least affront can drive a savage to despair.
A savage's countenance and discourse are sober and composed, expressing perfect tranquility of mind.
A savage's actions can be furious and violent despite a calm outward appearance.
Among North Americans, it is not uncommon for young or fearful persons to drown themselves after a slight reprimand from their mothers without expressing passion or speaking.
In civilized nations, men's passions are often clamorous and noisy but seldom very hurtful.
In civilized nations, passions often aim to convince spectators of the rightness of the emotion and to procure sympathy and approval.
Custom and fashion have greater effects on the propriety or impropriety of particular usages than on the general style of character and behavior.
Different manners taught by custom in different professions and states of life concern things of small moment.
Truth and justice are expected equally from old and young, clergymen and officers.
There is often some unobserved circumstance showing propriety in the character custom assigns to each profession.
The perversion of natural sentiment in manners of different nations is not very great.
Different nations require different degrees of the same quality in characters they esteem.
The duties of one virtue are sometimes extended to encroach upon another due to custom.
Rustic hospitality among Poles may encroach upon economy and good order.
Hurting an infant is considered a greater barbarity.
An infant's helplessness, innocence, and amiableness call forth compassion even from an enemy.
Not sparing an infant is regarded as the most furious effort of an enraged and cruel conqueror.
The murder of new-born infants was a practice allowed in almost all the states of Greece.
The practice of abandoning infants to hunger or wild beasts was regarded without blame or censure in ancient Greece.
The practice of infanticide probably began in times of the most savage barbarity.
The uniform continuance of the custom of infanticide hindered people from perceiving its enormity.
The practice of infanticide prevails among all savage nations at the present day.
Infanticide is more pardonable in the rudest and lowest state of society than in any other.
Extreme indigence in savages often exposes them to the greatest extremity of hunger.
Savages often die of pure want.
It is frequently impossible for a savage to support both himself and his child.
A savage parent abandoning a child due to inability to support it is not surprising.
A person fleeing from an enemy who throws down his infant because it retards his flight would be excusable.
In the state of society of savages, a parent is allowed to judge whether he can bring up his child.
In the latter ages of Greece, infanticide was permitted from views of remote interest or convenience.
Uninterrupted custom thoroughly authorized the practice of infanticide in later Greece.
The loose maxims of the world tolerated the practice of infanticide.
The doctrine of philosophers supported the practice of infanticide by far-fetched considerations of public utility.
Aristotle talked of infanticide as something the magistrate ought to encourage on many occasions.
Plato, despite his love of mankind, did not mark the practice of infanticide with disapprobation.
Custom can give sanction to dreadful violations of humanity.
People often excuse unjust and unreasonable conduct by saying it is commonly done.
Custom should never pervert our sentiments regarding the general style and character of conduct and behaviour as much as it does with particular usages.
No society could subsist if the usual strain of men's conduct and behaviour was like the practice of infanticide.
The character of virtue is discussed in Part VI.
Part VI consists of three sections.
When considering the character of any individual, it is naturally viewed under two different aspects.
The first aspect is how the character may affect the individual's own happiness.
The second aspect is how the character may affect the happiness of other people.
The preservation and healthful state of the body are the objects which Nature first recommends to the care of every individual.
The appetites of hunger and thirst, and sensations of pleasure and pain, heat and cold, are lessons delivered by Nature directing what to choose and avoid.
The first lessons taught in childhood mostly aim to teach how to keep out of harm's way.
As a person grows up, he learns that care and foresight are necessary to provide means to gratify natural appetites and avoid pain.
The art of preserving and increasing external fortune consists in the proper direction of care and foresight.
Advantages of external fortune are originally recommended to supply necessities and conveniences of the body.
Respect of equals, credit, and rank in society depend much on the degree to which one possesses or is supposed to possess advantages of fortune.
The desire to become objects of respect and to obtain credit and rank is perhaps the strongest of all desires.
Anxiety to obtain advantages of fortune is more excited by the desire for respect and rank than by the desire to supply bodily necessities.
Rank and credit among equals depend very much on character and conduct, or on the confidence, esteem, and goodwill they excite.
The care of health, fortune, rank, and reputation, which are supposed to be principal objects of comfort and happiness, is the business of the virtue called Prudence.
We suffer more when falling from a better to a worse situation than we enjoy when rising from a worse to a better.
Security is the first and principal object of prudence.
Prudence is averse to exposing health, fortune, rank, or reputation to any hazard.
Prudence is rather cautious than enterprising and more anxious to preserve existing advantages than to acquire greater ones.
Methods of improving fortune recommended by prudence are those exposing to no loss or hazard.
Real knowledge and skill in trade or profession, assiduity, industry, frugality, and some degree of parsimony in expenses are methods prudence recommends.
The prudent man studies seriously and earnestly to understand what he professes to understand.
The prudent man's talents may not be brilliant but are always genuine.
The prudent man does not try to impose by cunning, arrogance, or confident superficial assertions.
The prudent man is not ostentatious of his real abilities.
The prudent man's conversation is simple and modest.
The prudent man is averse to quackish arts used to gain public notice and reputation.
The prudent man relies on the solidity of his knowledge and abilities for reputation in his profession.
The prudent man does not always seek favor from exclusive societies that judge merit in superior arts and sciences.
If the prudent man joins such societies, it is for self-defense to prevent being imposed upon.
The prudent man is always sincere and feels horror at the thought of disgrace from falsehood detection.
Though always sincere, the prudent man is not always frank and open.
The prudent man does not always think himself bound to tell the whole truth when not properly called upon.
The prudent man is cautious in actions and reserved in speech.
The prudent man never rashly or unnecessarily obtrudes his opinion about things or persons.
The prudent man is capable of friendship but not of ardent, passionate, and often transitory affection.
The prudent man's friendship is sedate, steady, and faithful attachment to a few well-tried and well-chosen companions.
In choosing friends, the prudent man is guided by sober esteem of modesty, discretion, and good conduct, not by admiration of shining accomplishments.
The prudent man is not much disposed to general sociality.
The prudent man rarely frequents convivial societies known for jollity and gaiety of conversation.
Such convivial societies might interfere with the prudent man's temperance, industry, or frugality.
The prudent man's conversation may not be sprightly or diverting but is always perfectly inoffensive.
The prudent man hates the thought of being guilty of petulance or rudeness.
The prudent man never assumes impertinently over anybody and is willing to place himself below his equals on common occasions.
In conduct and conversation, the prudent man is an exact observer of decency and respects established decorums and ceremonials of society with almost religious scrupulosity.
The prudent man sets a better example in respect to decorum than men of more splendid talents and virtues who have shown contempt for ordinary decorums.
Men like Socrates, Aristippus, Dr. Swift, Voltaire, Philip, Alexander the Great, and Czar Peter of Moscovy have often shown improper and insolent contempt of ordinary decorums.
Such contemptuous behavior has set pernicious examples to those who wish to resemble these men.
The prudent man steadily sacrifices present ease and enjoyment for the probable expectation of greater ease and enjoyment in a more distant but lasting future.
The prudent man is supported and rewarded by the entire approbation of the impartial spectator and the man within the breast.
The impartial spectator does not feel worn out by the present labor of those whose conduct he surveys.
The impartial spectator is not solicited by the importunate calls of the present appetites of those he surveys.
The impartial spectator sees the present and likely future situation of persons nearly the same and is affected by them nearly the same.
The persons principally concerned see their present and future situations as very different and are affected differently.
The impartial spectator approves and applauds the exertion of self-command that enables persons to act as if their present and future situations affect them as the spectator is affected.
A man who lives within his income is naturally contented with his situation.
By continual, though small accumulations, a man's situation living within his income grows better every day.
A man living within his income gradually relaxes in the rigour of his parsimony and severity of his application.
A man living within his income feels double satisfaction from gradual increase of ease and enjoyment after having felt hardship.
A man living within his income has no anxiety to change his comfortable situation.
A man living within his income does not seek new enterprises and adventures that might endanger his secure tranquillity.
If a man living within his income enters new projects, they are likely to be well concerted and well prepared.
A man living within his income is never hurried or driven into new projects by necessity.
A man living within his income has time and leisure to deliberate soberly and coolly about consequences of new projects.
A prudent man is not willing to take responsibility beyond what his duty imposes.
A prudent man is not a bustler in business where he has no concern.
A prudent man is not a meddler in other people's affairs.
A prudent man is not a professed counsellor or adviser who obtrudes advice where it is not asked.
A prudent man confines himself to his own affairs as much as his duty permits.
A prudent man has no taste for foolish importance derived from influence in others' affairs.
A prudent man is averse to party disputes and hates faction.
A prudent man is not always forward to listen to the voice of noble and great ambition.
A prudent man will not decline service to his country when distinctly called upon.
A prudent man will not cabal to force himself into public service.
A prudent man would prefer public business to be well managed by another rather than bear the trouble and responsibility himself.
A prudent man prefers undisturbed enjoyment of secure tranquillity to vain splendour of ambition or solid glory of great actions.
Prudence directed to care of health, fortune, rank, and reputation is regarded as respectable and somewhat amiable.
Prudence directed to individual care is not considered among the most endearing or ennobling virtues.
Prudence directed to individual care commands cold esteem but not ardent love or admiration.
Wise and judicious conduct directed to greater purposes than individual care is frequently called prudence.
The prudence of great generals, statesmen, and legislators is combined with valour, benevolence, justice, and self-command.
Superior prudence supposes the art, talent, and habit of acting with perfect propriety in every circumstance.
Superior prudence supposes the utmost perfection of all intellectual and moral virtues.
Superior prudence is the best head joined to the best heart.
Superior prudence is the most perfect wisdom combined with the most perfect virtue.
Superior prudence constitutes nearly the character of the Academical or Peripatetic sage.
Inferior prudence constitutes the character of the Epicurean.
Mere imprudence or lack of capacity to take care of oneself is an object of compassion for the generous and humane.
Mere imprudence is an object of neglect or contempt for those with less delicate sentiments.
Mere imprudence is never an object of hatred or indignation.
Imprudence combined with other vices greatly aggravates infamy and disgrace.
An artful knave with dexterity and address often escapes punishment or detection.
An artful knave is often received with undue indulgence.
An awkward and foolish person lacking dexterity is convicted and punished and is universally hated, contemned, and derided.
In countries where great crimes frequently go unpunished, atrocious actions become familiar and cease to impress horror.
The character of every individual, so far as it can affect the happiness of other people, must do so by its disposition either to hurt or to benefit them.
Proper resentment for injustice attempted or actually committed is the only motive which can justify hurting or disturbing the happiness of a neighbour.
Hurting or disturbing the happiness of a neighbour from any other motive is a violation of the laws of justice.
The laws of justice require that force be employed either to restrain or to punish those who hurt or disturb others.
Every state or commonwealth endeavors to employ the force of society to restrain those subject to its authority from hurting or disturbing the happiness of one another.
The rules established by a state to restrain hurting or disturbing others constitute the civil and criminal law of that state or country.
The principles upon which civil and criminal laws are or ought to be founded are the subject of natural jurisprudence.
Natural jurisprudence is a particular science that is very important but perhaps the least cultivated.
A sacred and religious regard not to hurt or disturb the happiness of a neighbour, even when no law can protect him, constitutes the character of the perfectly innocent and just man.
The character of the perfectly innocent and just man, when carried to a certain delicacy of attention, is highly respectable and venerable.
The character of the perfectly innocent and just man is usually accompanied by many other virtues, including great feeling for other people, great humanity, and great benevolence.
The character of the perfectly innocent and just man is sufficiently understood and requires no further explanation.
The present section endeavors to explain the foundation of the order which nature has traced for the distribution of good offices or beneficence.
The order of beneficence is directed first towards individuals and secondly towards societies.
Nature's wisdom regulates the order of recommendations for beneficence.
Nature's recommendations for beneficence are stronger or weaker in proportion as beneficence is more or less necessary or useful.
Every man is first and principally recommended to his own care.
Every man is fitter and abler to take care of himself than of any other person.
Every man feels his own pleasures and pains more sensibly than those of other people.
Original sensations are the substance, while reflected or sympathetic images of those sensations are the shadow.
After himself, a man naturally directs his warmest affections to members of his own family who usually live in the same house with him.
Members of a man's family include his parents, children, brothers, and sisters.
A man is more habituated to sympathize with his family members than with most other people.
A man's sympathy with his family members is more precise and determinate than with most other people.
Sympathy and affections are by nature more strongly directed towards a man's children than towards his parents.
A parent's tenderness for their children is generally a more active principle than their reverence and gratitude towards their parents.
In the natural state, a child's existence depends on the care of the parent, but a parent's existence does not depend on the care of the child.
Nature considers a child a more important object than an old man.
A child excites a more lively and universal sympathy than an old man.
Very little can be expected or hoped from an old man in ordinary cases.
The weakness of childhood interests the affections of even the most brutal and hard-hearted.
Only the virtuous and humane do not view the infirmities of old age with contempt and aversion.
In ordinary cases, an old man dies without being much regretted by anybody.
Scarce a child can die without deeply affecting somebody.
The earliest friendships are naturally contracted among brothers and sisters.
Good agreement among brothers and sisters is necessary for family tranquillity and happiness.
Brothers and sisters can give more pleasure or pain to one another than to most other people.
The situation of brothers and sisters makes their mutual sympathy of utmost importance to their common happiness.
Living together obliges brothers and sisters to accommodate to one another, making their sympathy more habitual, lively, distinct, and determinate.
The children of brothers and sisters are connected by the friendship continuing between their parents.
Good agreement between parents improves the enjoyment of friendship between their children.
Discord between parents would disturb the friendship between their children.
Children of brothers and sisters seldom live in the same family.
Children of brothers and sisters are of more importance to one another than most other people but less than brothers and sisters.
Mutual sympathy among children of brothers and sisters is less necessary and less habitual than among brothers and sisters.
Children of cousins are less connected and of less importance to one another than children of brothers and sisters.
Affection gradually diminishes as the relation grows more remote.
Affection is in reality nothing but habitual sympathy.
Concern in the happiness or misery of those we affectionately regard is either the actual feeling of habitual sympathy or its necessary consequence.
Relations are usually placed in situations that naturally create habitual sympathy.
It is expected that a suitable degree of affection should take place among relations.
People are shocked when relations do not show the expected degree of affection.
There is a general rule that persons related in a certain degree ought to be affected towards one another in a certain manner.
It is highly improper and sometimes impious for relations to be affected differently than expected.
A parent without parental tenderness and a child without filial reverence appear as monsters and objects of horror.
In some instances, circumstances may prevent natural affections from taking place.
Respect for the general rule of affection can sometimes supply the place of natural affections.
A father is apt to be less attached to a child separated from him in infancy who returns only in adulthood.
The father feels less paternal tenderness and the child less filial reverence in such cases.
Brothers and sisters educated in distant countries tend to feel diminished affection.
Dutiful and virtuous people may have affection resembling natural affections despite separation.
During separation, family members are not indifferent to one another.
Family members consider one another as persons to and from whom certain affections are due.
Family members live in hopes of enjoying friendship naturally expected among close relations.
Absent sons and brothers are often considered favorite and all-perfect by their family.
Offenses by absent family members are often forgotten as childish tricks.
Accounts heard about absent family members are usually flattering and favorable if conveyed by people of good nature.
Family members often have romantic hopes about happiness to be enjoyed in friendship and conversation upon reunion.
Upon meeting, family members often imagine they have conceived habitual sympathy and behave accordingly.
Time and experience frequently undeceive family members about the presence of habitual sympathy.
Upon familiar acquaintance, family members often discover habits, humors, and inclinations different from expectations.
Lack of habitual sympathy makes it difficult for family members to accommodate to each other.
Family members who have not lived together may be sincerely desirous but incapable of assuming habitual sympathy.
Familiar conversation and intercourse among such family members soon become less pleasing and less frequent.
Family members may continue to live with mutual exchange of essential good offices and external appearances of regard.
They seldom completely enjoy the cordial satisfaction, delicious sympathy, and confidential openness typical of long familiar family relations.
The general rule has slender authority only with the dutiful and the virtuous.
The dissipated, the profligate, and the vain entirely disregard the general rule.
The dissipated, the profligate, and the vain seldom talk of the general rule except with indecent derision.
An early and long separation of the dissipated, profligate, and vain from others estranges them completely.
Respect for the general rule among the dissipated, profligate, and vain produces only cold and affected civility.
The slightest offence or opposition of interest commonly ends the cold civility among the dissipated, profligate, and vain.
Education of boys at distant great schools, young men at distant colleges, and young ladies in distant nunneries and boarding-schools has hurt domestic morals and happiness in France and England.
To educate children to be dutiful and affectionate, they should be educated in their own house.
Children may attend public schools daily but their dwelling should always be at home.
Respect for parents imposes a useful restraint on children's conduct.
Respect for children may impose a useful restraint on parents' conduct.
No acquisition from public education can compensate for what is lost by it compared to domestic education.
Domestic education is the institution of nature.
Public education is a contrivance of man.
The force of blood or natural affection between near relations is found only in tragedies and romances.
The force of blood is supposed to exist only between relations bred up in the same house, such as parents and children or brothers and sisters.
It is ridiculous to imagine mysterious affection between cousins or between aunts or uncles and nephews or nieces.
In pastoral countries where law authority is insufficient, branches of the same family commonly choose to live near one another.
Family association in such countries is frequently necessary for common defense.
All members of the same family are of more or less importance to one another.
Concord strengthens family association; discord weakens or might destroy it.
Family members have more intercourse with one another than with members of any other tribe.
The remotest members of the same tribe claim some connection and expect more distinguished attention than those with no such pretensions.
In the Scottish Highlands, the Chieftain used to consider the poorest man of his clan as his cousin and relation.
Similar extensive regard to kindred exists among the Tartars, Arabs, Turkomans, and other nations in similar societal states.
In commercial countries where law authority is sufficient, descendants of the same family naturally separate and disperse.
Separated family members soon cease to be important to one another.
In a few generations, separated family members lose care and remembrance of their common origin and ancestral connection.
Regard for remote relations decreases as the state of civilization is longer and more completely established.
The state of civilization has been longer and more completely established in England than in Scotland.
Remote relations are more considered in Scotland than in England.
The difference in regard for remote relations between England and Scotland is decreasing.
Great lords in every country are proud to remember and acknowledge their connection with one another, however remote.
Remembering illustrious relations flatters family pride.
This remembrance is maintained not from affection but from vanity.
Humble nearer kinsmen reminding great men of their relation are often told that the great men are bad genealogists and ill-informed about their family history.
Natural affection is more the effect of moral than physical connection between parent and child.
A jealous husband may regard a child he supposes to be from his wife's infidelity with hatred and aversion despite moral connection and education in his house.
Such a child is a lasting monument of a disagreeable adventure, the husband's dishonor, and family disgrace.
Among well-disposed people, mutual accommodation often produces friendship similar to that among family members.
The most respectable attachment to an individual is founded altogether upon esteem and approbation of his good conduct and behaviour, confirmed by much experience and long acquaintance.
Friendships arising from natural sympathy and involuntary feeling of esteem and approbation can exist only among men of virtue.
Men of virtue can feel entire confidence in the conduct and behaviour of one another, assuring them they can never offend or be offended by one another.
Vice is always capricious, whereas virtue is regular and orderly.
Attachment founded upon the love of virtue is the most virtuous, happiest, most permanent, and secure of all attachments.
Such friendships may safely embrace all the wise and virtuous with whom we have been long and intimately acquainted and upon whose wisdom and virtue we can entirely depend.
Confined friendship to two persons confounds the wise security of friendship with the jealousy and folly of love.
Hasty, fond, and foolish intimacies of young people are commonly founded upon slight similarity of character, unrelated to good conduct.
Such youthful intimacies often arise from shared tastes for the same studies, amusements, diversions, or agreement in some singular principle or opinion.
Intimacies that begin and end by a freak, however agreeable while they last, do not deserve the name of friendship.
Nature points out those to whom our peculiar beneficence is most properly directed as those whose beneficence we have already experienced.
Nature renders every man the peculiar object of kindness to the persons to whom he himself has been kind.
Though gratitude may not always correspond to beneficence, the sense of merit and sympathetic gratitude of the impartial spectator will always correspond to it.
General indignation against ingratitude can increase the general sense of a benefactor's merit.
No benevolent man ever loses altogether the fruits of his benevolence.
If a benevolent man does not gather fruits of benevolence from those he helped, he seldom fails to gather them with a tenfold increase from other people.
Kindness is the parent of kindness.
The surest way to be beloved by our brethren is to show by our conduct that we really love them.
After persons recommended to our beneficence by connection, qualities, or past services, come those pointed out for benevolent attention and good offices by their extraordinary situation.
Those distinguished by extraordinary situation include the greatly fortunate and the greatly unfortunate, the rich and the powerful, the poor and the wretched.
The distinction of ranks, peace, and order of society are founded in great measure upon the respect naturally conceived for the great.
The relief and consolation of human misery depend altogether upon our compassion for the miserable.
The peace and order of society is of more importance than even the relief of the miserable.
Respect for the great is most apt to offend by its excess.
Fellow-feeling for the miserable is most apt to offend by its defect.
Moralists exhort charity and compassion and warn against the fascination of greatness.
The rich and the great are too often preferred to the wise and the virtuous due to the fascination of greatness.

Nature has judged that distinction of ranks, peace, and order of society rest more securely upon the plain and palpable difference of birth and fortune than upon the invisible and uncertain difference of wisdom and virtue.
The undistinguishing eyes of the great mob of mankind can perceive differences of birth and fortune well enough.
The nice discernment of the wise and virtuous can sometimes distinguish the difference of wisdom and virtue.
The benevolent wisdom of nature is evident in the order of all those recommendations.
Combination of two or more exciting causes of kindness increases the kindness.
Favour and partiality naturally borne to greatness increase when joined with wisdom and virtue, provided there is no envy.

If a great man with wisdom and virtue falls into misfortunes, dangers, and distresses, people are more deeply interested in his fortune than in that of an equally virtuous person in a more humble situation.
The most interesting subjects of tragedies and romances are the misfortunes of virtuous and magnanimous kings and princes.
If virtuous and magnanimous kings and princes extricate themselves from misfortunes and recover their former superiority and security, they are viewed with enthusiastic and extravagant admiration.
The grief felt for the distress of great and virtuous persons and the joy for their prosperity combine to enhance partial admiration for their station and character.
When different beneficent affections draw different ways, it is perhaps impossible to determine by precise rules in what cases to comply with one or the other.

Decisions about when friendship ought to yield to gratitude, or vice versa, and when natural affection may prevail over regard for safety of superiors, must be left to the impartial spectator within the breast.
If we place ourselves in the situation of the impartial spectator and listen attentively to his suggestions, his voice will never deceive us.
The same principles that direct the order in which individuals are recommended to our beneficence also direct the order in which societies are recommended to it.
Societies to which beneficence is or may be of most importance are first and principally recommended to it.
The state or sovereignty in which we have been born and educated is the greatest society upon whose happiness or misery our conduct can have much influence.
The state or sovereignty under whose protection we live is by nature most strongly recommended to us.
Our children, parents, relations, friends, and benefactors are commonly comprehended within the state or sovereignty.
The prosperity and safety of those we love depend in some measure upon the prosperity and safety of the state.
The state is endeared to us by both selfish and private benevolent affections.
The prosperity and glory of the state seem to reflect some sort of honour upon ourselves.
We feel pride when comparing our state with other societies of the same kind if it appears superior.
We feel mortification if our state appears in any respect below other societies of the same kind.
We view illustrious characters produced by our state in former times with partial admiration.
We sometimes rank illustrious characters of our state above those of all other nations, sometimes unjustly.
A patriot who lays down his life for the safety or glory of his society appears to act with exact propriety.
The patriot views himself as one of the multitude, bound to sacrifice himself to the safety, service, and glory of the greater number.
Making the sacrifice of life for the society is difficult and few people are capable of making it.
The conduct of the patriot excites entire approbation, highest wonder, and admiration.
The patriot's conduct seems to merit all the applause due to the most heroic virtue.
A traitor who betrays his native country to a public enemy is the most detestable of villains.
The love of our own nation often disposes us to view the prosperity and aggrandisement of neighbouring nations with malignant jealousy and envy.
Independent and neighbouring nations, having no common superior, live in continual dread and suspicion of one another.
Each sovereign expects little justice from neighbours and treats them with as little as he expects.
The regard for the laws of nations or rules among independent states is often mere pretence and profession.
Rules of nations are often evaded or directly violated without shame or remorse upon slight provocation.
Each nation foresees or imagines its own subjugation in the increasing power and aggrandisement of neighbours.
The principle of national prejudice is often founded upon the love of our own country.
Elder Cato concluded every speech in the senate with the opinion that Carthage ought to be destroyed.
Cato's sentence was the natural expression of savage patriotism of a strong but coarse mind enraged against a foreign nation.
Scipio Nasica concluded all his speeches with the opinion that Carthage ought not to be destroyed.
Scipio Nasica's sentence was the liberal expression of a more enlarged and enlightened mind.
Scipio Nasica felt no aversion to the prosperity of an old enemy when reduced to a state no longer formidable to Rome.
France and England may each have some reason to dread the increase of the naval and military power of the other.
It is beneath the dignity of France and England to envy the internal happiness and prosperity of the other.

The cultivation of lands, advancement of manufactures, increase of commerce, security and number of ports and harbours, and proficiency in liberal arts and sciences are real improvements of the world.
Mankind are benefited and human nature is ennobled by such improvements.
Each nation ought to endeavour to excel in such improvements and to promote the excellence of its neighbours.
Such improvements are proper objects of national emulation, not of national prejudice or envy.
The love of our own country is not derived from the love of mankind.
The love of our own country is independent of the love of mankind and sometimes disposes us to act inconsistently with it.
France may contain near three times the number of inhabitants which Great Britain contains.
In the great society of mankind, the prosperity of France should appear to be an object of much greater importance than that of Great Britain.
Every independent state is divided into many different orders and societies.
Each order or society has its own particular powers, privileges, and immunities.
Every individual is naturally more attached to his own particular order or society than to any other.
An individual's interest and vanity, as well as those of his friends and companions, are commonly connected with his own order or society.
Individuals are ambitious to extend the privileges and immunities of their own order or society.
Individuals are zealous to defend the privileges and immunities of their own order or society against encroachments by other orders or societies.
The constitution of a particular state depends on how the state is divided into different orders and societies and the distribution of their powers, privileges, and immunities.
The stability of a particular constitution depends on the ability of each order or society to maintain its powers, privileges, and immunities against encroachments by others.
A constitution is altered whenever any subordinate part is raised above or depressed below its former rank and condition.
All different orders and societies are dependent upon the state for their security and protection.
All orders and societies are subordinate to the state and established only to serve its prosperity and preservation.
Even the most partial member of any order or society acknowledges that the state is superior to that order or society.
It may be hard to convince a member of an order or society that the state's prosperity and preservation require diminishing the powers, privileges, and immunities of that order or society.
Partiality to one's own order or society checks the spirit of innovation.
Partiality tends to preserve the established balance among the different orders and societies in a state.
Partiality sometimes obstructs alterations of government that are fashionable and popular at the time.
Partiality contributes to the stability and permanency of the whole system of government.
Love of country generally involves respect and reverence for the established constitution or form of government.
Love of country also involves an earnest desire to make the condition of fellow-citizens safe, respectable, and happy.
A person who does not respect laws and obey civil magistrates is not a citizen.
A good citizen wishes to promote the welfare of the whole society of fellow-citizens by every means in his power.
In peaceable and quiet times, respect for government and desire for fellow-citizens' welfare generally coincide and lead to the same conduct.
Supporting the established government is the best way to maintain the safe, respectable, and happy situation of fellow-citizens when the government actually maintains that situation.
In times of public discontent, faction, and disorder, respect for the constitution and desire for fellow-citizens' welfare may conflict.
A wise person may think some alteration necessary in a constitution that appears unable to maintain public tranquillity.
It often requires the highest political wisdom to decide when a patriot should support the old system or give way to innovation.
Foreign war and civil faction provide the most splendid opportunities for displaying public spirit.
A hero who serves his country successfully in foreign war gratifies the whole nation and is universally admired.
Leaders of contending parties in civil discord are admired by one half of their fellow-citizens but execrated by the other half.
The characters and merits of leaders in civil faction are commonly more doubtful than those of heroes in foreign war.
Glory acquired by foreign war is almost always more pure and splendid than that acquired in civil faction.
A leader of a successful party who can temper his friends' actions may render a service more essential than victories and conquests.
Such a leader may re-establish and improve the constitution and secure internal tranquillity and happiness for many generations.
Amidst faction turbulence, a spirit of system often mixes with public spirit founded on love of humanity and fellow-feeling.
This spirit of system animates and often inflames public spirit to fanaticism.
Leaders of discontented parties often propose plausible plans of reformation to remove inconveniences and prevent their return.
These leaders often propose to remodel the constitution and alter essential parts of the government system.
The great body of the party is commonly intoxicated with the imaginary beauty of the ideal system painted by their leaders.
Leaders may originally seek only their own aggrandisement but become dupes of their own sophistry and eager for reformation.
Even if leaders avoid fanaticism, they often act as if under delusion to meet followers' expectations.
The violence of the party, refusing all palliatives and reasonable accommodations, often obtains nothing.
Inconveniences and distresses that might be relieved with moderation are left without hope of remedy due to party violence.
A man whose public spirit is prompted by humanity and benevolence respects established powers and privileges of individuals and orders.
Such a man, even if he considers some powers abusive, will moderate rather than annihilate them to avoid great violence.
When he cannot conquer rooted prejudices by reason and persuasion, he will not attempt to subdue them by force.
He will observe the maxim never to use violence to his country any more than to his parents.
He will accommodate public arrangements to the confirmed habits and prejudices of the people as well as he can.
He will remedy inconveniences flowing from lack of regulations that people are averse to submitting to.
When he cannot establish the right, he will not disdain to ameliorate the wrong.
Like Solon, when he cannot establish the best system of laws, he will endeavor to establish the best that the people can bear.
The man of system is often very wise in his own conceit.
The man of system is often enamoured with the supposed beauty of his own ideal plan of government.
The man of system cannot suffer the smallest deviation from any part of his ideal plan of government.
The man of system goes on to establish his plan completely and in all its parts.
The man of system does not regard the great interests or strong prejudices which may oppose his plan.
The man of system imagines he can arrange the different members of a great society with as much ease as the hand arranges pieces on a chess-board.
The pieces on a chess-board have no other principle of motion besides that which the hand impresses upon them.
In human society, every single piece has a principle of motion of its own, different from that which the legislature might choose to impress upon it.
If the principle of motion of society's members and the legislature's principle coincide and act in the same direction, society will go on easily and harmoniously.
If the principles of motion are opposite or different, society will go on miserably and be in a high degree of disorder.
Some general and systematical idea of the perfection of policy and law may be necessary for directing the views of the statesman.
To insist on establishing all at once everything which the idea of perfection may require, in spite of all opposition, is often the highest degree of arrogance.
This insistence is to erect one's own judgment into the supreme standard of right and wrong.
This insistence is to fancy oneself the only wise and worthy man in the commonwealth.
This insistence is to expect fellow-citizens to accommodate themselves to oneself and not vice versa.
Of all political speculators, sovereign princes are by far the most dangerous.
Sovereign princes are perfectly familiar with this arrogance.
Sovereign princes entertain no doubt of the immense superiority of their own judgment.
Imperial and royal reformers seldom see anything so wrong in the constitution as the obstructions it may oppose to the execution of their own will.
Such reformers hold in contempt the divine maxim of Plato.
Such reformers consider the state as made for themselves, not themselves for the state.
The great object of their reformation is to remove obstructions to their will.
Their reformation aims to reduce the authority of the nobility.
Their reformation aims to take away the privileges of cities and provinces.
Their reformation aims to render the greatest individuals and orders of the state as incapable of opposing their commands as the weakest and most insignificant.
Our effectual good offices can very seldom be extended to any wider society than that of our own country.
Our good-will is circumscribed by no boundary and may embrace the immensity of the universe.
We cannot form the idea of any innocent and sensible being whose happiness we should not desire.
We cannot form the idea of any innocent and sensible being to whose misery, when distinctly brought home to the imagination, we should not have some degree of aversion.
The idea of a mischievous, though sensible, being naturally provokes our hatred.
The ill-will we bear to a mischievous being is the effect of our universal benevolence.
The ill-will towards a mischievous being is the effect of the sympathy we feel with the misery and resentment of other innocent and sensible beings whose happiness is disturbed by its malice.

Universal benevolence can be the source of no solid happiness to any man who is not thoroughly convinced that all inhabitants of the universe are under the immediate care and protection of a great, benevolent, and all-wise Being.
This great Being directs all the movements of nature.
This great Being is determined by his own unalterable perfections to maintain at all times the greatest possible quantity of happiness.
The suspicion of a fatherless world is the most melancholy of all reflections to universal benevolence.
The thought that all unknown regions of infinite and incomprehensible space may be filled with endless misery and wretchedness overshadows the imagination with gloom.
All the splendour of the highest prosperity can never enlighten the gloom caused by the idea of a fatherless world.
In a wise and virtuous man, all the sorrow of the most afflicting adversity cannot dry up the joy which springs from the habitual and thorough conviction of the truth of the contrary system.
A wise and virtuous man is at all times willing that his own private interest should be sacrificed to the public interest of his own particular order or society.
A wise and virtuous man is at all times willing that the interest of his order or society should be sacrificed to the greater interest of the state or sovereignty of which it is a subordinate part.
A wise and virtuous man should be equally willing that all inferior interests be sacrificed to the greater interest of the universe.
The greater interest of the universe is the interest of the great society of all sensible and intelligent beings, of which God is the immediate administrator and director.

If a man is deeply impressed with the conviction that the benevolent and all-wise Being admits no partial evil not necessary for universal good, he must consider all misfortunes that befall himself, his friends, his society, or his country as necessary for the prosperity of the universe.
Such a man ought to submit to these misfortunes with resignation.
Such a man ought to sincerely and devoutly wish for these misfortunes if he had known all the connexions and dependencies of things.
Magnanimous resignation to the will of the great Director of the universe seems within the reach of human nature.

Good soldiers who love and trust their general frequently march with more gaiety and alacrity to the forlorn station from which they never expect to return than to one where there is neither difficulty nor danger.
In marching to a safe station, soldiers feel only the dulness of ordinary duty.
In marching to a forlorn station, soldiers feel they are making the noblest exertion possible for man.
Soldiers know their general would not have ordered them to a forlorn station if it were not necessary for the safety of the army and the success of the war.
Soldiers cheerfully sacrifice their own little systems to the prosperity of a greater system.
Soldiers take an affectionate leave of their comrades, wishing them happiness and success.
Soldiers march out to a fatal but splendid and honourable station with submissive obedience and often with shouts of joyful exultation.
No conductor of an army can deserve more unlimited trust and more ardent and zealous affection than the great Conductor of the universe.
In the greatest public and private disasters, a wise man ought to consider that he, his friends, and countrymen have only been ordered upon the forlorn station of the universe.
A wise man ought to consider that if it had not been necessary for the good of the whole, they would not have been so ordered.
It is the duty of a wise man to submit with humble resignation to this allotment.
A wise man should endeavour to embrace this allotment with alacrity and joy.
A wise man should be capable of doing what a good soldier holds himself in readiness to do at all times.

The idea of the divine Being whose benevolence and wisdom have contrived and conducted the immense machine of the universe to produce the greatest possible quantity of happiness is the most sublime object of human contemplation.
Every other thought appears mean in comparison to the contemplation of this divine Being.
A man principally occupied in this sublime contemplation seldom fails to be the object of highest veneration.
Though such a man's life may be altogether contemplative, he is often regarded with religious respect superior to that given to the most active and useful servant of the commonwealth.

The Meditations of Marcus Antoninus, which turn principally upon this subject, have contributed more to the general admiration of his character than all the transactions of his just, merciful, and beneficent reign.
The administration of the great system of the universe, the care of universal happiness of all rational and sensible beings, is the business of God and not of man.
Man is allotted a much humbler department, suitable to the weakness of his powers and narrowness of his comprehension.
Man's department is the care of his own happiness, that of his family, friends, and country.
Contemplating the more sublime cannot excuse man from neglecting his more humble department.
Man must not expose himself to the charge of neglecting active duties by employing himself in philosophical speculations and contemplating the prosperity of the universe.
Avidius Cassius is said to have charged Marcus Antoninus with neglecting the Roman empire while engaged in philosophical speculations and contemplating the prosperity of the universe.
The most sublime speculation of the contemplative philosopher can scarce compensate the neglect of the smallest active duty.
A man who acts according to the rules of perfect prudence, strict justice, and proper benevolence may be said to be perfectly virtuous.
Perfect knowledge of the rules of prudence, justice, and benevolence alone does not always enable a man to act virtuously.
A man's own passions can mislead him and cause him to violate rules he approves of in sober and cool hours.
Perfect knowledge unsupported by perfect self-command will not always enable a man to do his duty.

Some ancient moralists divided passions into two classes: those requiring considerable self-command to restrain even for a moment, and those easy to restrain for a moment but dangerous over a lifetime.
Fear and anger, along with related passions, constitute the first class of passions that are difficult to restrain even momentarily.
The love of ease, pleasure, applause, and other selfish gratifications constitute the second class of passions that are easy to restrain momentarily but persistently solicit.
Extravagant fear and furious anger are often difficult to restrain even for a single moment.
The love of ease, pleasure, applause, and other selfish gratifications is always easy to restrain for a short period but can mislead over time.
The first set of passions often drives a person from duty, while the second set seduces a person from duty.
The command of fear and anger was called fortitude, manhood, and strength of mind by ancient moralists.
The command of love of ease, pleasure, applause, and other selfish gratifications was called temperance, decency, modesty, and moderation by ancient moralists.
The command of both sets of passions has a beauty of its own beyond its utility.
The strength and greatness of exertion in restraining fear and anger excites esteem and admiration.
The uniformity, equality, and steadiness of exertion in restraining selfish gratifications deserve esteem and admiration.
A man who preserves his tranquility unaltered in danger, torture, or approaching death commands a very high degree of admiration.
If a man suffers for liberty, justice, humanity, and love of country with dignity, he inspires compassion, indignation against persecutors, gratitude, and admiration.
Many heroes remembered with favor and affection died on the scaffold in the cause of truth, liberty, and justice.
The dignity and interest of characters who were beheaded in English history is enhanced by the emblem of the axe engraved under their portraits.
Magnanimity gives some degree of favorable regard even to the greatest criminals who behave decently and firmly at the scaffold.
War is a great school for acquiring and exercising magnanimity.
Men who have conquered the fear of death are unlikely to lose their presence of mind at the approach of other natural evils.
In war, men become familiar with death and are cured of the superstitious horror with which it is viewed by the weak and inexperienced.
