Soldiers consider death merely as the loss of life and no further object of aversion than life may be desired.
Experience teaches soldiers that many seemingly great dangers are not as great as they appear.
With courage, activity, and presence of mind, soldiers often have a good probability of extricating themselves with honor from hopeless situations.
The dread of death is greatly diminished and the hope of escaping it is increased by experience in war.
Soldiers learn to expose themselves to danger with less reluctance and are less anxious to escape it.
Habitual contempt of danger and death ennobles the profession of a soldier and gives it a rank and dignity superior to other professions.
The skilful and successful exercise of the soldier's profession in service of their country is a distinguishing feature of favorite heroes of all ages.
Great warlike exploits, even if unjust and inhumane, sometimes interest us and command some esteem for the worthless characters who conduct them.
The exploits of Buccaneers and other worthless men enduring hardships and dangers are read with some esteem and admiration.
The command of anger can be as generous and noble as the command of fear.
Proper expression of just indignation composes many splendid and admired passages of ancient and modern eloquence.
The Philippics of Demosthenes and the Catilinarians of Cicero derive their beauty from the noble propriety of expressed anger.
Just indignation is anger restrained and properly tempered to what the impartial spectator can understand.
Blustering and noisy passion that exceeds just indignation is odious and offensive.
Nobleness of pardoning can be superior to the propriety of resenting.
When public interest requires enemies to unite, a man who casts away animosity and acts with confidence and cordiality merits highest admiration.
Fear is contrary to anger and often restrains it.
When anger is restrained by fear, the motive is mean and takes away the nobleness of the restraint.
Anger prompts to attack.
The indulgence of anger sometimes shows a sort of courage and superiority to fear.
The indulgence of anger is sometimes an object of vanity.
The indulgence of fear is never an object of vanity.
Vain and weak men often affect to be ostentatiously passionate among their inferiors or those who dare not resist them.
Such men fancy that they show spirit by being ostentatiously passionate.
A bully tells many stories of his own insolence which are not true.
A bully imagines that telling such stories renders himself more formidable to his audience.
Modern manners, by favoring duelling, may encourage private revenge.
Modern manners contribute to making the restraint of anger by fear more contemptible.
There is always something dignified in the command of fear regardless of its motive.
The command of anger is not perfectly agreeable unless founded on decency, dignity, and propriety.
Acting according to prudence, justice, and proper beneficence has no great merit where there is no temptation to do otherwise.
Acting with cool deliberation in great dangers and difficulties is the character of exalted wisdom and virtue.
Observing sacred rules of justice despite temptations and injuries is a mark of exalted wisdom and virtue.
Never allowing benevolence to be damped by malignity and ingratitude is a mark of exalted wisdom and virtue.
Self-command is a great virtue.
All other virtues seem to derive their principal lustre from self-command.
The command of fear and anger are always great and noble powers.
When directed by justice and benevolence, the command of fear and anger are great virtues and increase the splendour of other virtues.
The command of fear and anger may be directed by different motives and be dangerous though still great and respectable.
The most intrepid valour may be employed in the cause of the greatest injustice.
Apparent tranquillity and good-humour amidst great provocations may conceal determined and cruel resolution to revenge.
The strength of mind required for such dissimulation is contaminated by the baseness of falsehood.
The dissimulation of Catharine of Medicis is celebrated by the historian Davila.
The dissimulation of Lord Digby, later Earl of Bristol, is praised by Lord Clarendon.
The dissimulation of the first Ashley Earl of Shaftesbury is praised by Mr. Locke.
Cicero considers this deceitful character not of highest dignity but suitable to a certain flexibility of manners.
Cicero exemplifies this character by Homer’s Ulysses, Themistocles, Lysander, and Marcus Crassus.
This character of deep dissimulation occurs most commonly in times of great public disorder.
When law is largely impotent and innocence cannot ensure safety, men resort to dexterity, address, and accommodation to prevailing parties.
This false character is frequently accompanied by the coolest and most determined courage.
The proper exercise of this dissimulation requires courage because detection commonly leads to death.
This dissimulation may be used to exasperate or allay animosities of adverse factions.
This dissimulation may sometimes be useful but is equally liable to be excessively pernicious.
The command of less violent passions is less liable to be abused.
Temperance, decency, modesty, and moderation are always amiable and seldom directed to bad ends.
The virtues of chastity, industry, and frugality derive their sober lustre from steady self-command.
The disposition to affections such as anger, hatred, envy, malice, and revenge tends to break the bands of human society.
The excess of these affections renders a man wretched and miserable in his own mind.
The excess of these affections makes a man the object of hatred and sometimes horror to other people.
The defect of these affections is very seldom complained of.
The want of proper indignation is an essential defect in the manly character.
The lack of proper indignation can render a man incapable of protecting himself or his friends from insult and injustice.
Envy is a passion that views with malignant dislike the superiority of those who are really entitled to it.
A man who tamely suffers others who are not entitled to superiority to rise above him is justly condemned as mean-spirited.
This weakness is commonly founded in indolence, good-nature, aversion to opposition, bustle, solicitation, or ill-judged magnanimity.
Such weakness is commonly followed by regret and repentance.
What initially appears as magnanimity often gives place to malignant envy and hatred of superiority.
It is necessary to defend our dignity and rank as much as our life or fortune to live comfortably in the world.
Sensibility to personal danger and distress is more apt to offend by excess than by defect.
No character is more contemptible than that of a coward.
The man who faces death with intrepidity and maintains presence of mind amidst dangers is highly admired.
We esteem men who support pain and torture with manhood and firmness.
We have little regard for those who abandon themselves to outcries and lamentations under pain.
A fretful temper that feels too much sensibility to small accidents renders a man miserable and offensive to others.
A calm temper that is not disturbed by small injuries or disasters is a blessing to the man and his companions.
Sensibility to one's own injuries and misfortunes may be too strong or too weak.
A man who feels little for his own misfortunes will feel less for those of others and be less disposed to relieve them.
A man who has little resentment for injuries done to himself will have less for those done to others and be less disposed to protect or avenge them.
A stupid insensibility to human life events extinguishes attention to the propriety of one's conduct.
We feel little anxiety about the propriety of our actions when indifferent about the events resulting from them.
A man who feels the distress of calamity and baseness of injustice but governs his conduct by restrained emotions is the real man of virtue.
Insensibility and noble firmness founded in dignity and propriety are not the same.
As insensibility increases, the merit of noble firmness is often taken away.
Total lack of sensibility to personal injury, danger, and distress removes the merit of self-command.
Sensibility may be too exquisite and frequently is so.
When the sense of propriety controls extreme sensibility, the authority of the judge within the breast appears noble and great.
The exertion of controlling extreme sensibility may be too fatiguing and have too much to do.
The contest between sensibility and propriety may be too violent to allow internal tranquillity and happiness.
A wise man with too exquisite sensibility and insufficiently hardened by education will avoid situations for which he is not fitted.
A man too sensitive to pain and hardship should not wantonly embrace the profession of a soldier.
A man too sensitive to injury should not rashly engage in contests of faction.
Even if the sense of propriety commands sensibilities, the mind's composure is disturbed in the struggle.
In this disorder, judgment cannot always maintain its acuteness and precision.
A man may mean to act properly but often acts rashly and imprudently and later feels ashamed.
Intrepidity, firmness of nerves, and hardiness of constitution are the best preparatives for self-command.
War and faction are the best schools for forming hardiness and firmness of temper.
The principle of self-estimation may be too high.
The principle of self-estimation may be too low.
It is very agreeable to think highly of ourselves.
It is very disagreeable to think meanly of ourselves.
To the person himself, some degree of excess in self-estimation is much less disagreeable than any degree of defect.
To the impartial spectator, the defect in self-estimation is always less disagreeable than the excess.
We more frequently complain of excess in self-estimation in our companions than of defect.
When companions assume superiority over us, their self-estimation mortifies our own.
Our own pride and vanity prompt us to accuse others of pride and vanity.
We cease to be impartial spectators of the conduct of those who assume superiority over us.
When companions allow others to assume superiority over them without merit, we blame and often despise them as mean-spirited.
When companions push themselves forward beyond their merit, we may not approve but are often diverted by it.
Without envy, we are less displeased by others pushing themselves forward than by them sinking below their proper station.
In estimating our own merit, we naturally compare ourselves to two standards.
The first standard is the idea of exact propriety and perfection as we comprehend it.
The second standard is the degree of approximation to this idea commonly attained in the world.
We seldom or never judge ourselves without giving attention to both standards.
The attention of different men, and of the same man at different times, is unequally divided between the two standards.
Sometimes attention is principally directed towards the first standard, sometimes towards the second.
When attention is directed towards the first standard, even the wisest see only weakness and imperfection in themselves.
When attention is directed towards the first standard, there is no ground for arrogance but much for humility, regret, and repentance.
When attention is directed towards the second standard, we may feel ourselves either above or below that standard.
The wise and virtuous man directs his principal attention to the first standard.
Every man has an idea of exact propriety and perfection formed from observations on himself and others.
This idea is gradually formed and is the work of the great judge and arbiter of conduct within the breast.
The idea of propriety and perfection is more or less accurately drawn according to the delicacy and acuteness of sensibility and care in observation.
In the wise and virtuous man, observations are made with the most acute sensibility and utmost care.
Every day the wise man improves some feature and corrects some blemish in his idea of propriety.
The wise man has studied the idea of propriety more than others and comprehends it more distinctly.
The wise man is deeply enamoured of the exquisite and divine beauty of the idea of propriety.
The wise man endeavors to assimilate his own character to this archetype of perfection.
The wise man feels the imperfect success of his endeavors and sees how the mortal copy falls short of the immortal original.
The wise man remembers with concern and humiliation how often he has violated the exact rules of perfect propriety.
When the wise man directs attention to the second standard, he may be sensible of his own superiority.
The wise man's principal attention is always directed towards the first standard.
The wise man is much more humbled by comparison to the first standard than elevated by comparison to the second.
The wise man is never so elated as to look down with insolence on those below him.
The wise man knows his own imperfection and the difficulty of attaining rectitude.
The wise man cannot regard with contempt the greater imperfection of other people.
The wise man views the inferiority of others with indulgent commiseration and promotes their advancement by advice and example.
If others are superior in any qualification, the wise man esteems and honors their excellence.
The wise man never envies the superiority of others and bestows full applause on their merit.
The wise man's mind and behavior are stamped with real modesty.
The wise man has a very moderate estimation of his own merit.
The wise man has a full sense of the merit of other people.
In all liberal and ingenious arts, the great artist always feels the real imperfection of his own best works.
The great artist is more sensible than any man of how much his works fall short of an ideal perfection.
The great artist forms some conception of ideal perfection which he imitates as well as he can but despairs of ever equalling.
The inferior artist is the only one who is ever perfectly satisfied with his own performances.
The inferior artist has little conception of ideal perfection and has little employed his thoughts about it.
The inferior artist chiefly compares his own works to those of other artists of perhaps a still lower order.
Boileau, the great French poet, said that no great man was ever completely satisfied with his own works.
Santeuil, a writer of Latin verses, assured Boileau that he himself was always completely satisfied with his own works.
Boileau replied that Santeuil was certainly the only great man that ever was completely satisfied with his own works.
Boileau judged his own works by comparing them with the standard of ideal perfection in his branch of poetic art.
Santeuil judged his own works chiefly by comparing them to those of other Latin poets of his own time.
Supporting and finishing the conduct and conversation of a whole life to some resemblance of ideal perfection is more difficult than producing works in the ingenious arts.
The artist works undisturbed, at leisure, in full possession of skill, experience, and knowledge.
The wise man must support the propriety of his conduct in health and sickness, success and disappointment, fatigue and drowsy indolence, and awakened attention.
The wise man must not be surprised by sudden and unexpected assaults of difficulty and distress.
The injustice of other people must never provoke the wise man to injustice.
The violence of faction must never confound the wise man.
All hardships and hazards of war must never dishearten or appal the wise man.
Some persons who judge their own merit by the ordinary degree of excellence commonly attained by others really and justly feel themselves very much above it.
Such persons are acknowledged by every intelligent and impartial spectator to be above the ordinary degree of excellence.
These persons have little sense of their own weaknesses and imperfections.
These persons have little modesty and are often assuming, arrogant, and presumptuous.
These persons are great admirers of themselves and great contemners of other people.
Their characters are generally much less correct and their merit much inferior to that of the man of real and modest virtue.
Their excessive presumption, founded on excessive self-admiration, dazzles the multitude and often imposes even upon those superior to the multitude.
The frequent and often wonderful success of the most ignorant quacks and impostors demonstrates how easily the multitude are imposed upon by extravagant and groundless pretensions.

When pretensions are supported by a very high degree of real and solid merit, displayed with splendour, supported by high rank and great power, and often successfully exerted, they are attended by loud acclamations of the multitude.
Even the man of sober judgment often abandons himself to the general admiration of such great men.
The noise of foolish acclamations often confounds the understanding of the sober man.
The sober man, seeing great men only at a distance, is often disposed to worship them with sincere admiration.
The admiration of the sober man can be superior to that with which the great men appear to worship themselves.
When there is no envy, people take pleasure in admiring and are naturally disposed to render complete and perfect in every respect the characters they admire.
The excessive self-admiration of great men is well understood and sometimes seen through with derision by wise men familiar with them.
Wise men who are familiar with great men secretly smile at their lofty pretensions.
People at a distance often regard the lofty pretensions of great men with reverence and almost with adoration.
In all ages, the greater part of men who have procured noisy fame and extensive reputation have had such characteristics.
The noisy fame and extensive reputation of such men have often descended to the remotest posterity.
Great success in the world and great authority over the sentiments and opinions of mankind have very seldom been acquired without some degree of excessive self-admiration.

The most splendid characters and men who have performed the most illustrious actions have often been distinguished not only for their great merit but also for a degree of presumption and self-admiration disproportionate to that merit.
This presumption was perhaps necessary to prompt great men to undertakings which a more sober mind would never have thought of.
This presumption was also necessary to command the submission and obedience of followers to support great undertakings.
When crowned with success, presumption has often betrayed great men into vanity that approached insanity and folly.
Alexander the Great wished that other people should think him a God and was well disposed to fancy himself such.
Upon his death-bed, Alexander requested that his old mother Olympia be added to the respectable list of Deities.
Socrates did not fancy himself a God but fancied that he had secret and frequent intimations from some invisible and divine Being.
Caesar was pleased with his divine genealogy from the goddess Venus.
Caesar received the Roman Senate without rising from his seat when they came to present him with decrees conferring extravagant honours.
Caesar's insolence and childish vanity seem to have exasperated public jealousy and hastened the execution of his assassins' conspiracy.
The religion and manners of modern times give great men little encouragement to fancy themselves either Gods or Prophets.
Success joined to great popular favour has often made great men ascribe to themselves importance and ability beyond what they really possessed.
The great Duke of Marlborough never committed a single rash action or word despite ten years of uninterrupted and splendid success.
The same temperate coolness and self-command as the Duke of Marlborough cannot be ascribed to Prince Eugene, the late King of Prussia, the great Prince of Conde, or Gustavus Adolphus.
Turrenne approached the temperate coolness and self-command of the Duke of Marlborough but was not as perfect in it.
Great abilities and successful enterprise have frequently encouraged undertakings that led to bankruptcy and ruin in the end.
The esteem and admiration for the real merit of spirited, magnanimous, and high-minded persons is a just, well-founded, steady, and permanent sentiment.
Admiration for excessive self-estimation and presumption depends on success and changes with good or bad fortune.
While successful, people often admire excessive self-estimation and presumption and overlook imprudence and injustice.
When unsuccessful, excessive self-estimation and presumption are seen as extravagant rashness and folly.
If Caesar had lost the battle of Pharsalia, his character would be ranked little above that of Catiline.

Caesar's real merit includes justness of taste, simplicity and elegance of writings, propriety of eloquence, skill in war, resources in distress, cool judgment in danger, faithful attachment to friends, and generosity to enemies.
The insolence and injustice of Caesar's ambition would have darkened and extinguished the glory of his real merit if he had been unsuccessful.
Fortune has great influence over the moral sentiments of mankind and can render the same character the object of love and admiration or hatred and contempt.
The disorder in moral sentiments caused by fortune's influence has utility and reflects the wisdom of God in human weakness and folly.
Admiration of success is founded on the same principle as respect for wealth and greatness and is necessary for establishing social ranks and order.
Admiration of success teaches people to submit more easily to superiors assigned by the course of human affairs.
People regard with reverence and sometimes respectful affection the fortunate violence of mighty conquerors.
The great mob of mankind naturally looks up with weak and foolish admiration to mighty conquerors like Caesar, Alexander, Attila, Gengis, or Tamerlane.
Admiration of success teaches people to acquiesce with less reluctance under governments imposed by irresistible force.
In prosperity, the man of excessive self-estimation may appear to have some advantage over the man of correct and modest virtue.
The applause of the multitude is often louder in favor of the man of excessive self-estimation than the man of modest virtue.
All things fairly computed, the real balance of advantage is greatly in favor of the man of correct and modest virtue over the man of excessive self-estimation.
The man who ascribes to himself only the merit that really belongs to him fears no humiliation and dreads no detection.
The man of genuine truth and solidity in character rests contented and secure upon his own character.
The admirers of the man of modest virtue may neither be very numerous nor very loud in their applause.
The wisest man who knows the man of modest virtue best admires him the most.
The judicious and well-weighed approbation of a single wise man gives more heartfelt satisfaction than the noisy applause of ten thousand ignorant though enthusiastic admirers.
Parmenides, upon reading a philosophical discourse before a public assembly at Athens, continued to read on after all but Plato had left, saying that Plato alone was audience sufficient for him.
The wise men who see the man of excessive self-estimation the nearest admire him the least.
The man of excessive self-estimation regards the sober and just esteem of others as mere malignity and envy.
The man of excessive self-estimation suspects his best friends and finds their company offensive.
The man of excessive self-estimation drives his best friends from his presence.
The man of excessive self-estimation often rewards the services of his friends with ingratitude, cruelty, and injustice.
The man of excessive self-estimation abandons his confidence to flatterers and traitors who pretend to idolize his vanity and presumption.
The character of the man of excessive self-estimation, initially amiable and respectable, becomes contemptible and odious in the end.
Alexander killed Clytus for preferring the exploits of his father Philip to his own.
Alexander put Calisthenes to death by torture for refusing to adore him in the Persian manner.
Alexander murdered Parmenio, the great friend of his father, after sending Parmenio's only remaining son to torture and the scaffold on groundless suspicions.
Philip said that the Athenians were fortunate to find ten generals every year, while he could never find one but Parmenio.
Philip reposed with confidence and security on the vigilance and attention of Parmenio.
Philip used to say in mirth that they could drink with safety because Parmenio never drinks.
Alexander gained all his victories with the presence and counsel of Parmenio.
Alexander never gained a single victory without the presence and counsel of Parmenio.
Alexander's humble, admiring, and flattering friends divided his empire among themselves after his death.
Alexander's friends robbed his family and kindred of their inheritance.
Alexander's friends put every single surviving individual of his family and kindred to death, whether male or female.
People frequently pardon and sympathize with the excessive self-estimation of splendid characters who show great and distinguished superiority above the common level of mankind.
People call splendid characters with great superiority spirited, magnanimous, and high-minded.
People cannot sympathize with the excessive self-estimation of characters without distinguished superiority.
People are disgusted and revolted by the excessive self-estimation of characters without distinguished superiority.
Excessive self-estimation without distinguished superiority is called pride or vanity.
Vanity always involves a considerable degree of blame, and pride for the most part does as well.
Pride and vanity are both modifications of excessive self-estimation but differ in many respects.
The proud man is sincere and convinced of his own superiority.
The proud man wishes others to view him only as he views himself.
The proud man demands no more respect than what he thinks is justice.
If others do not respect the proud man as he respects himself, he feels offended and indignant as if injured.
The proud man does not explain the grounds of his pretensions and disdains to court esteem.
The proud man affects to despise others' esteem and tries to maintain his station by making others feel their own meanness.
The proud man wishes to mortify others' self-esteem rather than excite their esteem for himself.
The vain man is not sincere and is seldom convinced of the superiority he wishes others to ascribe to him.
The vain man wishes others to view him in more splendid colors than he views himself.
The vain man is more mortified than offended when others view him in his proper colors.
The vain man displays the grounds of his claim ostentatiously, sometimes falsely.
The vain man courts others' esteem with anxious assiduity and flatters to be flattered.
The vain man studies to please and bribes others into a good opinion by politeness, complaisance, and sometimes real good offices.
The vain man wishes to usurp respect paid to rank and fortune as well as talents and virtues.
The vain man's dress, equipage, and way of living announce a higher rank and greater fortune than he really has.
The vain man courts the company of his superiors.
The proud man shuns the company of his superiors.
The vain man believes the splendour of his superiors reflects upon him.
The vain man haunts the courts of kings and the levees of ministers.
The vain man acts as if he is a candidate for fortune and preferment.
The vain man actually possesses the happiness of not being a candidate for fortune and preferment.
The vain man is fond of being admitted to the tables of the great.
The vain man magnifies to others the familiarity with which he is honoured by the great.
The vain man associates with fashionable people, those who direct public opinion, the witty, the learned, and the popular.
The vain man shuns the company of his best friends when public favour runs against them.
The vain man is not always delicate about the means he employs to recommend himself.
The vain man uses unnecessary ostentation, groundless pretensions, constant assentation, and frequently flattery.
The vain man's flattery is mostly pleasant and sprightly, and seldom gross and fulsome like a parasite.
The proud man never flatters.
The proud man is frequently scarce civil to anybody.
Vanity is almost always a sprightly, gay, and often good-natured passion.
Pride is always a grave, sullen, and severe passion.
The falsehoods of the vain man are innocent and meant to raise himself.
The proud man seldom stoops to falsehood.
When the proud man lies, his falsehoods are mischievous and meant to lower other people.
The proud man is full of indignation at what he thinks unjust superiority given to others.
The proud man views those he envies with malignity and envy.
The proud man often tries to lessen the grounds of others' supposed superiority.
The proud man often believes and repeats tales circulated to the disadvantage of those he envies.
The worst falsehoods of vanity are white lies.
The falsehoods of pride, when they occur, are of the opposite complexion to white lies.
People generally dislike pride and vanity and rank those accused of these vices below the common level.
Both the proud and the vain man are often above the common level.
The proud and vain men are not as superior as they think or wish others to think.
Pride is frequently attended with virtues such as truth, integrity, high sense of honour, steady friendship, and inflexible firmness.
Vanity is frequently attended with virtues such as humanity, politeness, desire to oblige, and sometimes real generosity.
Vanity often wishes to display generosity in the most splendid colours.
In the last century, the French were accused of vanity by their rivals and enemies.
In the last century, the Spaniards were accused of pride by their rivals and enemies.
Foreign nations considered vanity more amiable and pride more respectable.
The words vain and vanity are never taken in a good sense.
Sometimes vanity is considered a foible and a ridicule in a man's character.
The words proud and pride are sometimes taken in a good sense.
Pride is sometimes confounded with magnanimity.
Aristotle described the magnanimous man as deliberate in resolutions, slow in actions, grave in voice, and determined in great occasions.
Men of merit considerably above the common level sometimes under-rate as well as over-rate themselves.
Men of merit who are modest and unassuming are often far from being disagreeable in private society.
Companions feel much at ease in the society of a man who is perfectly modest and unassuming.
Companions who lack both more discernment and more generosity than ordinary seldom have much respect for a modest man of merit.
The warmth of kindness from companions is very seldom sufficient to compensate for the coldness of their respect.
Men of no more than ordinary discernment never rate any person higher than he appears to rate himself.
Men of ordinary discernment prefer an impudent blockhead who entertains no doubt about his own qualifications over a modest man who seems doubtful of his fitness.
Men who have discernment but lack generosity take advantage of a modest man's simplicity and assume an impertinent superiority.
A modest man may bear impertinent superiority for some time but grows weary and may lose rank irrecoverably.
A modest man often loses rank to more forward but less meritorious companions due to his own backwardness.
A man of modest character must be very fortunate in the early choice of his companions to always meet with fair justice.
A youth who is too unassuming and too unambitious is frequently followed by an insignificant, complaining, and discontented old age.
Persons formed by nature a good deal below the common level sometimes rate themselves even lower than they really are.
This humility in persons below the common level sometimes sinks them into idiotism.
Many idiots have faculties of understanding that are not weaker than those of several other people who are not considered idiots.
Many idiots with ordinary education have been taught to read, write, and account tolerably well.
Many persons not accounted idiots have never been able to acquire reading, writing, or accounting in any tolerable degree despite careful education.
Persons not accounted idiots set themselves upon a level with their equals in age and situation by an instinct of pride.
Idiots feel themselves below every company into which they are introduced.
Ill-usage can throw idiots into violent fits of rage and fury.
No kindness or indulgence can raise an idiot to converse as an equal.
Idiots' answers in conversation can be sufficiently pertinent and sensible but are always stamped with a consciousness of their own inferiority.
Idiots seem to shrink and retire from the look and conversation of others.
Some idiots seem so chiefly from numbness or torpidity in the faculties of understanding.
Other idiots have faculties of understanding not more torpid than many people not accounted idiots.
The instinct of pride necessary to support equality with others seems totally wanting in some idiots and present in others.
The degree of self-estimation that contributes most to happiness and contentment is also most agreeable to the impartial spectator.
A man who esteems himself as he ought and no more seldom fails to obtain from others all the esteem he thinks due.
The proud and the vain man are constantly dissatisfied.
The proud man is tormented with indignation at what he thinks the unjust superiority of others.
The vain man is in continual dread of the shame that would attend detection of his groundless pretensions.
The extravagant pretensions of a man of real magnanimity supported by splendid abilities, virtues, and good fortune impose upon the multitude.
Wise men whose approbation a magnanimous man values see through and despise his excessive presumption.
A magnanimous man often becomes a jealous, secret, and later open and vindictive enemy of those whose friendship he would have been happiest to enjoy.
Dislike to the proud and vain often disposes people to rank them below their proper station.
Unless provoked by personal impertinence, people seldom venture to use the proud and vain ill.
In common cases, people accommodate themselves to the folly of the proud and vain for their own ease.
People without both more discernment and generosity than most men seldom fail to do all the injustice to a man who under-rates himself that he does to himself, and frequently more.
A man who under-rates himself is more unhappy in his own feelings than either the proud or the vain.
A man who under-rates himself is much more liable to every sort of ill-usage from other people.
In almost all cases, it is better to be a little too proud than too humble.
Some degree of excess in self-estimation is less disagreeable than any degree of defect to both the person himself and the impartial spectator.
The degree of emotion, passion, or habit most agreeable to the impartial spectator is also most agreeable to the person himself.
The degree of excess or defect least offensive to the impartial spectator is in proportion least disagreeable to the person himself.
Concern for our own happiness recommends the virtue of prudence.
Concern for the happiness of other people recommends the virtues of justice and beneficence.
Justice restrains us from hurting others.
Beneficence prompts us to promote the happiness of others.
The virtue of prudence is originally recommended by our selfish affections.
The virtues of justice and beneficence are originally recommended by our benevolent affections.
Regard to the sentiments of other people enforces and directs the practice of prudence, justice, and beneficence.
No man who trod steadily and uniformly in the paths of prudence, justice, or beneficence was not principally directed by regard to the sentiments of the supposed impartial spectator.
The supposed impartial spectator is the great inmate of the breast, the great judge and arbiter of conduct.
If during the day we have swerved from the rules prescribed by the impartial spectator, he calls us to account in the evening.
The impartial spectator reproaches us for omissions and violations related to frugality, industry, hurting others, or neglecting to promote others' happiness.
The impartial spectator's reproaches often make us blush inwardly for folly, inattention to our own happiness, and indifference to that of others.
The virtues of prudence, justice, and beneficence may be recommended by two different principles on different occasions.
The virtues of self-command are principally and almost entirely recommended by one principle: the sense of propriety.
The sense of propriety is related to regard for the sentiments of the supposed impartial spectator.
Without the restraint imposed by the sense of propriety, every passion would rush headlong to its own gratification on most occasions.
Anger would follow the suggestions of its own fury without restraint.
Fear would follow the suggestions of its own violent agitations without restraint.
Vanity would not refrain from loud and impertinent ostentation without regard to time or place.
Voluptuousness would indulge in the most open, indecent, and scandalous ways without restraint.
Respect for the sentiments of other people is the sole principle that overawes mutinous and turbulent passions into a tone the impartial spectator can sympathize with.
On some occasions, passions are restrained not by a sense of impropriety but by prudential considerations of bad consequences.
Passions restrained by prudential considerations often remain lurking with their original fury.
A man whose anger is restrained by fear does not always lay aside his anger but reserves its gratification for a safer opportunity.
A man who relates an injury to a companion who sympathizes with moderate sentiments may have his anger cooled and subdued.
Sympathy with a companion's moderate sentiments can cause a man to view an injury in a milder and fairer light.
Passions restrained by the sense of propriety are moderated and subdued to some degree.
Passions restrained only by prudential considerations are frequently inflamed by the restraint.
Passions restrained only by prudential considerations sometimes burst out absurdly and unexpectedly with tenfold fury and violence.
Anger may be properly restrained by prudential considerations on many occasions.
Some exertion of manhood and self-command is necessary for restraint by prudential considerations.
The impartial spectator may view restraint by prudential considerations with cold esteem as a matter of vulgar prudence.
The impartial spectator views restraint by the sense of propriety with affectionate admiration.
Restraint by prudential considerations may show some degree of propriety and virtue but of a much inferior order.
The virtues of prudence, justice, and beneficence have a tendency to produce only agreeable effects.
Regard to the agreeable effects originally recommends the virtues of prudence, justice, and beneficence to the actor.
The impartial spectator also regards the agreeable effects of prudence, justice, and beneficence.
Approving the prudent man, we feel the security he enjoys under the safeguard of sedate and deliberate virtue.
Approving the just man, we feel the security derived by those connected with him from his scrupulous anxiety never to hurt or offend.
Approving the beneficent man, we enter into the gratitude of those within the sphere of his good offices and conceive their high sense of his merit.
Our approbation of prudence, justice, and beneficence joins our sense of their agreeable effects and their propriety.
In approbation of virtues of self-command, complacency with their effects sometimes constitutes no part or only a small part of that approbation.
The effects of virtues of self-command may sometimes be agreeable and sometimes disagreeable.
Our approbation of virtues of self-command is stronger when their effects are agreeable but is not destroyed when effects are disagreeable.
Heroic valour may be employed in the cause of justice or injustice.
Heroic valour is more loved and admired in the cause of justice but still appears great and respectable in the cause of injustice.
In virtues of self-command, the splendid and dazzling quality is the greatness and steadiness of exertion.
A strong sense of propriety is necessary to make and maintain the exertion in virtues of self-command.
The effects of virtues of self-command are too often but too little regarded.
Part VII is titled 'Of Systems of Moral Philosophy.'
Part VII consists of four sections.
Almost all celebrated and remarkable theories concerning the nature and origin of moral sentiments coincide with some part of the account given by the author.
Every system of morality that has had any reputation in the world has perhaps ultimately been derived from some one or other of the principles the author has been endeavouring to unfold.
All systems of morality are founded upon natural principles.
All systems of morality are in some measure in the right.
Many systems of morality are derived from a partial and imperfect view of nature.
Many systems of morality are in some respects in the wrong.
In treating the principles of morals, two questions are to be considered.
The first question is wherein virtue consists, or what tone of temper and tenour of conduct constitutes the excellent and praise-worthy character.
The excellent and praise-worthy character is the natural object of esteem, honour, and approbation.
The second question is by what power or faculty in the mind the virtuous character is recommended to us.
The second question can be restated as how and by what means the mind prefers one tenour of conduct to another.
The second question also asks how the mind denominates one conduct right and another wrong.
The second question also asks how the mind considers one conduct as the object of approbation, honour, and reward, and another as the object of blame, censure, and punishment.
The first question is examined by considering whether virtue consists in benevolence, as Dr. Hutcheson imagines.
The first question is examined by considering whether virtue consists in acting suitably to the different relations we stand in, as Dr. Clarke supposes.
The first question is examined by considering whether virtue consists in the wise and prudent pursuit of our own real and solid happiness, as has been the opinion of others.
The second question is examined by considering whether the virtuous character is recommended to us by self-love.
Self-love makes us perceive that the virtuous character, both in ourselves and others, tends most to promote our own private interest.
The second question is examined by considering whether the virtuous character is recommended to us by reason.
Reason points out to us the difference between one character and another, in the same manner as it does that between truth and falsehood.
The second question is examined by considering whether the virtuous character is recommended to us by a peculiar power of perception called a moral sense.
The moral sense gratifies and pleases with the virtuous character and is disgusted and displeased by the contrary.
The second question is examined by considering whether the virtuous character is recommended to us by some other principle in human nature, such as a modification of sympathy.
The author will begin by considering the systems formed concerning the first question.
The author will afterwards proceed to examine the systems concerning the second question.
According to Plato, Aristotle, and Zeno, virtue consists in the propriety of conduct or in the suitableness of the affection from which we act to the object which excites it.
In Plato's system, the soul is considered as a little state or republic composed of three different faculties or orders.
The first faculty is the judging faculty, which determines the proper means for attaining any end, the ends fit to be pursued, and the relative value to put upon each.
Plato called the judging faculty reason and considered it the governing principle of the whole soul.
Reason includes the faculty by which we judge truth and falsehood and the propriety or impropriety of desires and affections.
The passions and appetites are natural subjects of reason but often rebel against it.
Plato divided the passions into two classes: those founded in pride and resentment (the irascible part) and those founded in the love of pleasure (the concupiscible part).
The irascible passions include ambition, animosity, love of honour, dread of shame, desire of victory, superiority, and revenge.
The concupiscible passions include all appetites of the body, love of ease and security, and all sensual gratifications.
We rarely break from the plan of conduct prescribed by reason except when prompted by either the irascible or concupiscible passions.
The irascible passions are necessary to defend against injuries, assert rank and dignity, aim at what is noble and honourable, and distinguish those who act similarly.
The concupiscible passions are necessary to provide for the support and necessities of the body.
Prudence, the essential virtue according to Plato, consists in just and clear discernment of proper ends and means, founded on general and scientific ideas.
Fortitude and magnanimity arise when the irascible passions have strength and firmness to despise dangers in pursuit of what is honourable and noble under reason's direction.
The irascible passions are considered more generous and noble than the concupiscible passions.
The irascible passions can act as auxiliaries of reason to check and restrain the concupiscible appetites.
We often become angry at ourselves when the love of pleasure prompts us to do what we disapprove of, and the irascible part assists reason against the concupiscible.
Temperance is the perfect harmony of the soul when reason, irascible, and concupiscible passions are in concord, approving and willing to perform each other's commands.
Justice, the greatest of the four cardinal virtues, occurs when each faculty confines itself to its proper office without encroaching on others.
Justice consists in reason directing, passion obeying, and each passion performing its proper duty with suitable force and energy.
The Greek word for justice has several meanings, including abstaining from harming others and showing proper love, respect, and esteem.
One sense of justice is abstaining from doing positive harm to another's person, estate, or reputation.
This sense of justice can be extorted by force and its violation exposes one to punishment.
Another sense of justice involves conceiving love, respect, and esteem for a neighbor and acting accordingly.
Failing to exert oneself to serve a person of merit connected to us, even without harming them, is considered injustice in this second sense.
The first sense of justice coincides with Aristotle's commutative justice and Grotius's justitia expletrix.
The second sense of justice coincides with distributive justice and Grotius's justitia attributrix.
Distributive justice consists in proper beneficence, the becoming use of what is our own, and applying it suitably to charity or generosity.
In this second sense, justice comprehends all the social virtues.
A third, more extensive sense of justice involves valuing objects with the degree of esteem or ardour they deserve.
Doing injustice to a poem or picture means not admiring it enough, and doing more than justice means admiring it too much.
Doing injustice to oneself means not giving sufficient attention to any particular object of self-interest.
In this last sense, justice means exact and perfect propriety of conduct and behavior.
This last sense of justice includes the offices of commutative and distributive justice and every other virtue such as prudence, fortitude, and temperance.
Plato understands justice in this last sense, encompassing the perfection of every sort of virtue.
Plato described virtue as a temper of mind where every faculty confines itself within its proper sphere without encroaching on others.
According to Plato, virtue involves each faculty performing its proper office with the precise degree of strength and vigor it belongs to.
Plato's account of virtue coincides with the concept of propriety of conduct.
Aristotle defined virtue as the habit of mediocrity according to right reason.
Each particular virtue lies in a middle between two opposite vices, one of excess and one of deficiency.
The virtue of fortitude or courage lies between cowardice and presumptuous rashness.
Cowardice is a vice caused by being too little affected by objects of fear.
Presumptuous rashness is a vice caused by being too much affected by objects of fear.
The virtue of frugality lies between avarice and profusion.
Avarice is an excess of attention to objects of self-interest.
Profusion is a defect in attention to objects of self-interest.
Magnanimity lies between arrogance and pusillanimity.
Arrogance is an excess of sentiment of one's own worth and dignity.
Pusillanimity is a defect of sentiment of one's own worth and dignity.
Aristotle considered virtue as the habit of reasonable moderation.
Virtue can be considered as the quality of an action or as the quality of a person.
As a quality of an action, virtue consists in reasonable moderation of the affection from which the action proceeds.
As a quality of a person, virtue consists in the habit of reasonable moderation as a customary disposition of the mind.
A single generous action does not necessarily make a person generous.
The disposition of heart behind a single virtuous action may be accidental rather than steady or permanent.
Calling a character virtuous means the disposition is usual and customary for the person.
Single virtuous actions are of little consequence to prove a person's habitual virtue.
If a single action sufficed to define virtue, even the most worthless could claim all virtues.
Most people have acted with prudence, justice, temperance, and fortitude on some occasions.
A single vicious action by a usually virtuous person greatly diminishes or destroys our opinion of their virtue.
A single vicious action shows that a person's habits are not perfect.
Aristotle opposed Plato's doctrine that just sentiments and reasonable judgments alone constitute perfect virtue.
Plato considered virtue as a species of science where clear knowledge of right and wrong leads to right action.
Plato believed passion might cause acting contrary to doubtful opinions but not to plain and evident judgments.
Aristotle believed no conviction of understanding could overcome inveterate habits.
Aristotle held that good morals arise from action, not from knowledge.
Zeno, founder of Stoical doctrine, taught that every animal is naturally recommended to its own care.
Zeno taught that animals are endowed with self-love to preserve their existence and parts in the best state.
Human self-love embraces body, mind, faculties, and powers, desiring their preservation in best condition.
Things that support the state of existence are naturally pointed out as fit to be chosen.
Things that tend to destroy existence are naturally pointed out as fit to be rejected.
Health, strength, agility, ease of body, and external conveniences promoting these are naturally eligible.
Wealth, power, honors, respect, and esteem of others are naturally pointed out as preferable possessions.
Sickness, infirmity, unwieldiness, pain, poverty, lack of authority, contempt, and hatred are to be shunned.
Among objects of choice, some are more to be chosen than others, e.g., health over strength, reputation over power.
Among objects of rejection, some are more to be avoided than others, e.g., sickness over unwieldiness, ignominy over poverty.
Virtue and propriety of conduct consist in choosing and rejecting objects according to their natural degree of choice or rejection.
Choosing the most to be chosen when not all can be obtained, and rejecting the least to be avoided when not all can be avoided, is virtuous.
The Stoics called living with this discernment 'to live consistently' or 'to live according to nature.'
Living according to nature means obeying the laws and directions prescribed by nature or its Author.
The Stoical idea of propriety and virtue is not very different from that of Aristotle and the ancient Peripatetics.
Nature recommended the prosperity of our family, relations, friends, country, mankind, and the universe in general as primary objects.
Nature taught that the prosperity of two is preferable to that of one.
Nature taught that the prosperity of many or all is infinitely more preferable than that of one or two.
We ourselves are but one, and our prosperity should yield to the prosperity of the whole or any considerable part of the whole.
All events in the world are conducted by the providence of a wise, powerful, and good God.
Whatever happens tends to the prosperity and perfection of the whole.
If we are in poverty, sickness, or any calamity, we ought to use our utmost endeavors to rescue ourselves, as far as justice and duty to others allow.
If after all efforts we cannot escape our disagreeable circumstance, we ought to be satisfied that the order and perfection of the universe require us to continue in this situation.
The prosperity of the whole is preferable even to ourselves.
Our situation, whatever it is, ought to become the object of our liking to maintain propriety and rectitude of sentiment and conduct.
If an opportunity to extricate ourselves arises, it becomes our duty to embrace it.
The order of the universe no longer requires our continuance in a situation if a clear road to leave it is pointed out.
If it is in our power to prevent or end the calamity of our relations, friends, or country without violating more sacred obligations, it is our duty to do so.
If it is out of our power to prevent or end such calamities, we ought to consider the event as the most fortunate possible.
We may be assured that such events tend most to the prosperity and order of the whole.
Our own final interest, as part of the whole, should be the principal and sole object of our desire.
Epictetus says some things are according to our nature and others contrary to it in the sense that we consider ourselves as separated and detached from other things.
Considering the foot as detached, it is agreeable to its nature to be always clean.
Considering the foot as part of the body, it must sometimes trample in dirt, tread on thorns, or be cut off for the sake of the whole body.
If the foot refuses these duties, it ceases to be a foot.
Similarly, if a man considers himself as separated and detached, it is agreeable to his nature to live to old age, be rich, and be in health.
If a man considers himself as part of a whole, he must sometimes be in sickness, exposed to inconveniences, be in want, or die before his time.
Complaining about such conditions is equivalent to ceasing to be a man.
A wise man never complains of the destiny of Providence nor thinks the universe is in confusion when he is out of order.
A wise man does not look upon himself as a whole separated and detached from every other part of nature.
A wise man regards himself as an atom or particle of an immense and infinite system disposed according to the convenience of the whole.
A wise man is assured of the wisdom directing all events of human life.
Whatever lot befalls a wise man, he accepts it with joy.
A wise man is satisfied that if he knew all connections and dependencies of the universe, he would have wished for the lot he received.
If the lot is life, a wise man is contented to live.
If the lot is death, a wise man willingly goes where he is appointed as nature has no further occasion for his presence.
A cynical philosopher accepts with equal joy and satisfaction whatever fortune befalls him.
The cynical philosopher regards riches or poverty, pleasure or pain, health or sickness as all alike.
The cynical philosopher would not desire the Gods to change his destination in any respect.
The cynical philosopher would ask the Gods to inform him beforehand what they please to do with him so he could place himself in that situation cheerfully.
Epictetus says he chooses the best ship and pilot and waits for the fairest weather that circumstances and duty allow before sailing.
Prudence and propriety require Epictetus to prepare well but no more.
If a storm arises that the vessel and pilot cannot withstand, Epictetus gives himself no trouble about the consequence.
Epictetus says all he had to do is done already.
The directors of Epictetus's conduct never command him to be miserable, anxious, desponding, or afraid.
Whether to be drowned or to come to harbor is the business of Jupiter, not Epictetus.

The Stoical wise man considers all events of human life to be largely indifferent.
The happiness of the Stoical wise man consists first in contemplating the happiness and perfection of the universe.
The Stoical wise man finds happiness in the good government of the great republic of Gods and men.
The Stoical wise man finds happiness in discharging his duty in the affairs of the great republic.
The success or disappointment of the Stoical wise man's endeavors excites no passionate joy or sorrow.
The Stoical wise man does not regard some events as better or worse in themselves.
The Stoical wise man chooses and rejects events based on the propriety of action given by the Gods.
All affections of the Stoical wise man are absorbed in the discharge of his own duty and the happiness of all rational beings.
The Stoical wise man rests securely on the wisdom and power of the great Superintendent of the universe for the happiness of all beings.
The Stoical wise man's sole anxiety is about the propriety of his own endeavors, not about their outcomes.
The Stoical wise man trusts a superior power to turn any event to promote the great end he desires.
The propriety of choosing and rejecting was originally recommended by the things chosen and rejected.
The order, grace, and beauty discerned in proper conduct are of greater value than obtaining or avoiding objects of choice.
From observing propriety arises happiness and glory; from neglecting it arises misery and disgrace.
A wise man finds it equally easy to observe propriety in all occasions.
In prosperity, the wise man thanks Jupiter for circumstances easily mastered with little temptation to do wrong.
In adversity, the wise man thanks the director of human life for a vigorous contest that offers glorious and certain victory.

The events of human life never find the wise man unprepared to maintain propriety of sentiment and conduct.
Human life is considered by the Stoics as a game of great skill mixed with chance.

A good player who loses has made no false stroke and has enjoyed the pleasure of the game.
A bad player who wins is mortified by the remembrance of faults committed.
A bad player enjoys no part of the pleasure of the game due to fear, doubt, hesitation, and mortification.
Human life should be regarded as a mere two-penny stake, too insignificant to merit anxious concern.
Our only anxious concern should be about the proper method of playing life.

Placing happiness in playing well, fairly, wisely, and skillfully places it in what is under our own power and direction.

According to the Stoics, it might be the duty of a weak man to remain in life though he was necessarily miserable.
If there are more circumstances which are natural objects of rejection than of choice, the whole situation becomes the object of rejection.

A wise man places his happiness not in obtaining objects of choice or avoiding objects of rejection but in always choosing and rejecting with exact propriety.

If there are more circumstances which are natural objects of choice than of rejection, the whole situation becomes the proper object of choice.

During the age of the founders of the principal sects of ancient philosophy, the Greek republics were almost always distracted by furious factions at home.
During the same age, Greek republics were involved in sanguinary wars abroad.

Philosophers endeavored to show that happiness was either altogether or in great measure independent of fortune.

The Academic and Peripatetic philosophers taught that happiness was independent of fortune in a great measure.
Wise, prudent, and good conduct was most likely to ensure success in every species of undertaking.

The virtuous man might feel calm, peace, and concord within despite external untoward things.
The virtuous man might comfort himself with the love and esteem of every intelligent and impartial spectator.

Diogenes Laertius preferred the story of Zeno's violent death given by Apollonius.
Lucian and Lactantius also gave credit to the story of Zeno's great age and violent death.

The author suspects that some Stoical paradoxes may have been misunderstood or misrepresented.

Nature's plan for human conduct is different from that of Stoical philosophy.
Events that immediately affect ourselves, our friends, and our country interest us the most and excite our passions.
Nature has provided a remedy for passions that are too vehement: the presence of the impartial spectator or the man within the breast.

Mr. Woollaston's system places virtue in acting according to the truth of things and their proper nature and essence.
Lord Shaftesbury's system places virtue in maintaining a proper balance of affections and allowing no passion to exceed its proper sphere.
These modern systems are more or less inaccurate descriptions of the same fundamental idea.
None of the discussed systems provide a precise or distinct measure to ascertain or judge the fitness or propriety of affection.
The precise and distinct measure of the fitness or propriety of affection can only be found in the sympathetic feelings of the impartial and well-informed spectator.
The description of virtue given or intended in each of those systems is just as far as it goes.
There is no virtue without propriety.
Wherever there is propriety, some degree of approbation is due.
The description of virtue in those systems is imperfect.
Propriety is an essential ingredient in every virtuous action.
Propriety is not always the sole ingredient in virtuous actions.
Beneficent actions have another quality that makes them appear to deserve not only approbation but recompense.
None of those systems account easily or sufficiently for the superior degree of esteem due to beneficent actions.
None of those systems account easily or sufficiently for the diversity of sentiment naturally excited by beneficent actions.
The description of vice in those systems is not more complete than the description of virtue.
Impropriety is a necessary ingredient in every vicious action.
Impropriety is not always the sole ingredient in vicious actions.

None of those systems easily and sufficiently account for the superior degree of detestation felt for such pernicious actions.
Epicurus is said to have borrowed the leading principles of his philosophy from predecessors, particularly Aristippus.
Epicurus's manner of applying philosophical principles was probably his own.
According to Epicurus, bodily pleasure and pain were the sole ultimate objects of natural desire and aversion.
Epicurus thought it required no proof that bodily pleasure and pain were always the natural objects of desire and aversion.
Pleasure might sometimes be avoided not because it was pleasure, but to avoid forfeiting a greater pleasure or to avoid a pain more to be avoided than the pleasure was to be desired.
Pain might sometimes be chosen not because it was pain, but to avoid a greater pain or to acquire a more important pleasure.
Epicurus believed that whatever else was desired or avoided was so because of its tendency to produce bodily pleasure or pain.
Power and riches were desirable because they tended to procure pleasure.
Poverty and insignificancy were objects of aversion because they tended to produce pain.
Honour and reputation were valued because the esteem and love of those we live with were important to procure pleasure and defend from pain.
Ignominy and bad fame were to be avoided because hatred, contempt, and resentment from others destroyed security and exposed one to bodily evils.
All pleasures and pains of the mind were ultimately derived from those of the body according to Epicurus.
The mind was happy when it thought of past bodily pleasures and hoped for future ones.
The mind was miserable when it thought of past bodily pains and dreaded the same or greater pains in the future.
The pleasures and pains of the mind were vastly greater than those of the body.
The body felt only the sensation of the present instant.
The mind felt the past by remembrance and the future by anticipation.
When under the greatest bodily pain, the chief torment is the remembrance of past pain or dread of future pain, not the present instant's suffering.
The pain of each instant, considered alone, is a trifle not worth regarding.
When enjoying the greatest pleasure, the bodily sensation of the present instant makes only a small part of happiness.
Enjoyment chiefly arises from cheerful recollection of the past or joyous anticipation of the future.
The mind contributes by much the largest share of the entertainment in pleasure.
Happiness and misery depend chiefly on the mind.
If the mind is well disposed, the manner in which the body is affected is of little importance.
Under great bodily pain, a person might still enjoy considerable happiness if reason and judgment maintain superiority.
One might entertain oneself with remembrance of past and hopes of future pleasure despite bodily pain.
One might soften the rigour of pains by recollecting the necessity of suffering them.
The bodily sensation of the present instant's pain by itself could never be very great.
Agony from dread of pain's continuance is an effect of the mind's opinion, which can be corrected by juster sentiments.
Considering that violent pains are probably short and long pains probably moderate with intervals of ease can correct fear of pain.
Death is always at hand and can deliver us from pain and pleasure sensations.
According to Epicurus, death puts an end to all sensation of pain or pleasure and therefore cannot be regarded as an evil.
When we are, death is not; and when death is, we are not.
The sensation of positive pain is little to be feared.
The sensation of pleasure is naturally much less pungent than that of pain.
If pain takes little from the happiness of a well-disposed mind, pleasure adds scarcely anything to it.
When the body is free from pain and the mind from fear and anxiety, bodily pleasure is of very little importance.
Bodily pleasure might diversify happiness but cannot properly be said to increase it.
According to Epicurus, the most perfect state of human nature and complete happiness consists in ease of body and security or tranquillity of mind.
The sole object of all virtues is to bring about the state of ease of body and tranquillity of mind.
Virtues are not desirable upon their own account but for their tendency to bring about happiness.

Prudence is not desirable upon its own account.
Prudence is a careful, laborious, and circumspect state of mind, watchful and attentive to distant consequences of every action.
Prudence is pleasant or agreeable only because of its tendency to procure the greatest goods and keep off the greatest evils.
Temperance is the virtue of abstaining from pleasure to curb and restrain natural passions for enjoyment.
Temperance is not desirable for its own sake but for its utility in postponing present enjoyment for greater future pleasure or avoiding greater pain.
Temperance is prudence with regard to pleasure.
Fortitude involves supporting labour, enduring pain, and exposure to danger or death.
Labour, pain, danger, and death are not objects of natural desire.
Labour is submitted to in order to avoid greater shame and pain of poverty.
Danger and death are exposed to in defence of liberty and property, which are means and instruments of pleasure and happiness.
Danger and death are also faced in defence of country, whose safety includes one's own.
Fortitude enables cheerful endurance of labour, pain, danger, and death as the best possible actions in the present situation.
Fortitude is prudence, good judgment, and presence of mind in properly appreciating pain, labour, and danger.
Fortitude always chooses the lesser evil to avoid the greater.
To abstain from what is another's was not desirable on its own account.

Epicurus attended only to the species of propriety related to bodily ease and security in virtue.
Epicurus accounted for all appearances from as few principles as possible.
Epicurus referred all primary objects of natural desire and aversion to the pleasures and pains of the body.
Epicurus's system agreed with Plato, Aristotle, and Zeno in making virtue consist in acting suitably to obtain primary objects of natural desire.
Epicurus differed from Plato, Aristotle, and Zeno in the account of primary objects of natural desire.
Epicurus differed from the other three philosophers in the account of the excellence of virtue and why it ought to be esteemed.
According to Epicurus, the primary objects of natural desire consisted only in bodily pleasure and pain.
According to Plato, Aristotle, and Zeno, there were many other primary objects of natural desire such as knowledge and happiness of relations.

According to Epicurus, virtue was eligible only because it tends to prevent pain and procure ease and pleasure.
