The system which makes virtue consist in benevolence is of very great antiquity.
This system was the doctrine of many philosophers around and after the age of Augustus who called themselves Eclectics.
The Eclectics pretended to follow chiefly the opinions of Plato and Pythagoras.
The Eclectics are commonly known by the name of the later Platonists.
According to these authors, benevolence or love was the sole principle of action in the divine nature.
Benevolence directed the exertion of all the other attributes in the divine nature.
The wisdom of the Deity was employed in finding out the means for bringing about those ends which his goodness suggested.
The infinite power of the Deity was exerted to execute the ends suggested by his goodness.
Benevolence was the supreme and governing attribute to which the others were subservient.
The whole excellency or morality of the divine operations was ultimately derived from benevolence.
The whole perfection and virtue of the human mind consisted in some resemblance or participation of the divine perfections.
The perfection and virtue of the human mind consisted in being filled with the same principle of benevolence and love which influenced all the actions of the Deity.
Only actions of men which flowed from benevolence were truly praise-worthy or could claim any merit in the sight of the Deity.
Actions of charity and love alone could imitate the conduct of God.
By fostering benevolence in our own minds, we could bring our affections to a greater resemblance with the holy attributes of God.
The great object of this philosophy was to raise us to immediate converse and communication with the Deity.
This system was much esteemed by many ancient fathers of the Christian church.
After the Reformation, this system was adopted by several divines of eminent piety, learning, and amiable manners.
Dr. Ralph Cudworth, Dr. Henry More, and Mr. John Smith of Cambridge were notable adopters of this system.
Dr. Hutcheson was the most acute, distinct, philosophical, sober, and judicious patron of this system.
Proper benevolence is the most graceful and agreeable of all the affections.
Benevolence is recommended to us by a double sympathy.
Benevolence's tendency is necessarily beneficent.
Benevolence is the proper object of gratitude and reward.
Benevolence appears to our natural sentiments to possess a merit superior to any other.
The weaknesses of benevolence are not very disagreeable to us.
The weaknesses of every other passion are always extremely disgusting.
Excessive malice, excessive selfishness, or excessive resentment are abhorred.
The most excessive indulgence of partial friendship is not so offensive.
Benevolent passions can exert themselves without regard to propriety and yet retain something engaging.
There is something pleasing in mere instinctive good-will that does good offices without reflecting on blame or approbation.
Other passions cease to be agreeable when deserted or unaccompanied by the sense of propriety.
Benevolence bestows upon actions a beauty superior to all others.
The want of benevolence or the contrary inclination communicates a peculiar deformity to actions.
Pernicious actions are often punishable because they show a want of sufficient attention to the happiness of our neighbour.
Whenever an action supposed to proceed from benevolent affections is found to have another motive, the sense of its merit is diminished.
If an action supposed to proceed from gratitude is discovered to arise from expectation of a new favour, its merit is destroyed.
If an action supposed to proceed from public spirit is found to originate from hope of pecuniary reward, it loses all notion of merit or praise-worthiness.
The mixture of any selfish motive diminishes or takes away the merit of an action.
Virtue must consist in pure and disinterested benevolence alone.
Dr. Hutcheson did not allow self-love to be a motive of virtuous actions.
According to Dr. Hutcheson, regard to the pleasure of self-approbation diminishes the merit of a benevolent action.
Dr. Hutcheson thought that self-approbation was a selfish motive.
Dr. Hutcheson believed that any action influenced by self-approbation demonstrated weakness of pure and disinterested benevolence.
In common judgments of mankind, regard to the approbation of our own minds is not considered to diminish the virtue of any action.
Common judgments of mankind consider regard to self-approbation as the sole motive deserving the appellation of virtuous.
The system described nourishes and supports the noblest and most agreeable of all affections in the human heart.
The system described checks the injustice of self-love and discourages the principle altogether.
The system does not sufficiently explain the source of approbation for virtues like prudence, vigilance, circumspection, temperance, constancy, and firmness.
The system attends only to the view and aim of affections and their beneficent or hurtful effects.
The system disregards the propriety, impropriety, suitableness, and unsuitableness of affections to the cause which excites them.
Regard to our own private happiness and interest appears on many occasions as a laudable principle of action.
Habits of economy, industry, discretion, attention, and application of thought are generally supposed to be cultivated from self-interested motives.
Habits cultivated from self-interested motives are apprehended to be praiseworthy qualities deserving esteem and approbation.
The mixture of a selfish motive often sullies the beauty of actions that ought to arise from benevolent affection.
The cause of the sullied beauty of actions is not that self-love can never be the motive of a virtuous action.
The cause is that the benevolent principle appears to lack due strength and to be unsuitable to its object in such cases.
The character of an action mixed with selfish motive and insufficient benevolence seems imperfect and deserves blame rather than praise.
The mixture of a benevolent motive in an action prompted by self-love alone does not diminish the sense of its propriety or the virtue of the person.
People are not ready to suspect anyone of being defective in selfishness.
Selfishness is not the weak side of human nature or a failing people are suspicious of.
If a man would not take proper care of his health, life, or fortune without regard to family and friends, it would be a failing.
Such a failing would be amiable and render a person an object of pity rather than contempt or hatred.
This failing would diminish the dignity and respectableness of a person's character.
Carelessness and want of economy are universally disapproved of.
Carelessness and want of economy are disapproved not as proceeding from lack of benevolence but from lack of proper attention to self-interest.
Casuists frequently determine right or wrong in human conduct by its tendency to the welfare or disorder of society.
A regard to the welfare of society should not be the sole virtuous motive of action.
In any competition of motives, regard to the welfare of society ought to outweigh all other motives.
Benevolence may be the sole principle of action in the Deity.
There are several arguments that tend to persuade us that benevolence is the sole principle of action in the Deity.
It is not easy to conceive what other motive an independent and all-perfect Being can act from.
An independent and all-perfect Being stands in need of nothing external and has complete happiness in himself.
Man, as an imperfect creature, must often act from many other motives besides benevolence.
The condition of human nature is peculiarly hard if affections that ought to influence conduct could never appear virtuous or deserve esteem.
Three principal accounts of the nature of virtue are: virtue in propriety, virtue in prudence, and virtue in benevolence.
All other descriptions of virtue are reducible to one or other of these three principal accounts.
The system that places virtue in obedience to the will of the Deity can be counted among those that make virtue consist in prudence or propriety.
The question why we ought to obey the will of the Deity can admit only two answers.
The first answer is that we ought to obey because the Deity is infinitely powerful and will reward or punish us eternally.
The second answer is that independent of rewards or punishments, there is congruity and fitness that a creature should obey its creator.
If the first answer is proper, virtue consists in prudence or pursuit of our own final interest and happiness.
If the second answer is proper, virtue consists in propriety, grounded on the suitableness of humility and submission to the superior object.
The system that places virtue in utility coincides with that which makes it consist in propriety.
According to the utility system, qualities agreeable or advantageous to oneself or others are approved as virtuous.
According to the utility system, qualities that are not agreeable or advantageous are disapproved as vicious.
The agreeableness or utility of any affection depends on the degree to which it subsists.
Every affection is useful when confined to a certain degree of moderation.
Every affection is disadvantageous when it exceeds proper bounds.
According to the utility system, virtue consists in the proper degree of all affections.
The difference between the utility system and the system being established is that the former makes utility the natural and original measure of the proper degree.
The system being established makes sympathy or the correspondent affection of the spectator the natural and original measure of the proper degree.
All the systems discussed suppose a real and essential distinction between vice and virtue.
There is a real and essential difference between the propriety and impropriety of any affection.
There is a real and essential difference between benevolence and any other principle of action.
There is a real and essential difference between real prudence and short-sighted folly or precipitate rashness.
In the main, all the systems contribute to encourage the praiseworthy disposition and discourage the blamable disposition.
Some systems tend to break the balance of the affections and give the mind a particular bias to some principles of action beyond their due proportion.
Ancient systems that place virtue in propriety chiefly recommend the great, lawful, and respectable virtues.
The ancient systems emphasize virtues of self-government and self-command such as fortitude, magnanimity, and independence upon fortune.
The ancient systems value contempt of outward accidents like pain, poverty, exile, and death.
The noblest propriety of conduct is displayed in great exertions like fortitude and magnanimity.
The soft, amiable, and gentle virtues of indulgent humanity are little insisted upon by the ancient systems.
The Stoics often regarded the gentle virtues as mere weaknesses that a wise man should not harbor.
The benevolent system fosters and encourages the milder virtues in the highest degree.
The benevolent system neglects the more lawful and respectable qualities of the mind.
The benevolent system denies the lawful and respectable qualities the appellation of virtues.
The benevolent system calls lawful and respectable qualities moral abilities and treats them as less esteemed than proper virtues.
Principles of action aiming only at our own interest are treated worse by the benevolent system.
The benevolent system asserts that prudence employed only in promoting private interest can never be imagined a virtue.
The system that makes virtue consist in prudence only encourages habits of caution, vigilance, sobriety, and judicious moderation.
The prudence-only system degrades both the amiable and respectable virtues.
The prudence-only system strips the amiable virtues of their beauty and the respectable virtues of their grandeur.
Despite their defects, the general tendency of the three systems is to encourage the best and most laudable habits of the human mind.
It would be beneficial for society if mankind or those living by philosophical rules regulated their conduct by the precepts of any one of the three systems.
Each of the three systems offers something valuable and peculiar to learn.
The ancient systems of propriety seem sufficient to inspire the mind with fortitude and magnanimity by precept and exhortation.
The benevolent system can soften the mind into humanity and awaken affections of kindness and general love.
The system of Epicurus shows how the practice of both amiable and respectable virtues is conducive to our own interest, ease, safety, and quiet in this life.
Epicurus placed happiness in the attainment of ease and security.
Epicurus exerted himself to show that virtue was the best, surest, and only means of acquiring ease and security.
Other philosophers chiefly celebrated the good effects of virtue on inward tranquility and peace of mind.
Epicurus chiefly insisted upon the influence of virtue on outward prosperity and safety.
Epicurus's writings were much studied in the ancient world by men of different philosophical parties.
Cicero, an enemy of the Epicurean system, borrows his most agreeable proofs that virtue alone is sufficient to secure happiness from Epicurus.
Seneca, a Stoic, quotes Epicurus more frequently than any other philosopher.
There is a system that takes away altogether the distinction between vice and virtue, which is wholly pernicious.
The system of Dr. Mandeville takes away the distinction between vice and virtue.
Dr. Mandeville's notions are in almost every respect erroneous.
Some appearances in human nature seem at first sight to favor Dr. Mandeville's notions.
Dr. Mandeville describes and exaggerates these appearances with lively, humorous, though coarse and rustic eloquence.
Dr. Mandeville considers whatever is done from a sense of propriety as being done from a love of praise and vanity.
Man is naturally more interested in his own happiness than in that of others, according to Dr. Mandeville.
It is impossible that man can really prefer others' prosperity to his own, according to Dr. Mandeville.
When man appears to prefer others' prosperity, he is imposing upon us and acting from selfish motives.
Vanity is one of the strongest selfish passions in man, according to Dr. Mandeville.
Man is easily flattered and greatly delighted with the applause of those about him.
When man sacrifices his own interest to that of companions, he expects extravagant praises in return.
The pleasure expected from praise overbalances the interest abandoned, making the conduct selfish.
Man flatters himself that his conduct is disinterested because otherwise it would not merit commendation.
All public spirit and preference of public to private interest is, according to Dr. Mandeville, a mere cheat and imposition upon mankind.
Human virtue is, according to Dr. Mandeville, the mere offspring of flattery begot upon pride.
The author does not examine whether the most generous and public spirited actions may be regarded as proceeding from self-love.
The decision of whether generous actions proceed from self-love is not important for establishing the reality of virtue.
Self-love may frequently be a virtuous motive of action.
The desire to do what is honourable and noble and to be the proper object of esteem and approbation cannot properly be called vanity.
The love of well-grounded fame and reputation, or the desire to acquire esteem by what is really estimable, does not deserve to be called vanity.
The love of virtue is the noblest and best passion of human nature.
The love of true glory is a passion inferior to the love of virtue but comes immediately after it in dignity.
A person is guilty of vanity if they desire praise for qualities that are not praise-worthy or not to the degree they expect.
A person is guilty of vanity if they base their character on frivolous ornaments of dress and equipage or on frivolous accomplishments of ordinary behaviour.
A person is guilty of vanity if they desire praise for qualities they know do not belong to them.
An empty coxcomb who gives himself airs of importance without title is properly accused of vanity.
A silly liar who assumes merit for adventures that never happened is guilty of vanity.
A foolish plagiary who claims authorship of works they have no right to is guilty of vanity.
A person who is not content with silent sentiments of esteem and approbation but prefers noisy expressions and acclamations is guilty of vanity.
A person who anxiously solicits external marks of respect, titles, compliments, visits, attendance, and public notice with deference is guilty of vanity.
The frivolous passion of vanity is different from the love of virtue and the love of true glory.
The love of virtue and the love of true glory are always approved of, while vanity is always despised.
There is a remote affinity between vanity and the love of true glory because both aim at acquiring esteem and approbation.
The love of true glory is a just, reasonable, and equitable passion.
Vanity is an unjust, absurd, and ridiculous passion.
A man who desires esteem for what is really estimable desires what he is justly entitled to.
A man who desires esteem on other terms demands what he has no just claim to.
A man who desires esteem for what is really estimable is easily satisfied and not apt to be jealous or suspicious.
A vain man is never satisfied, is full of jealousy and suspicion that others do not esteem him enough.
A vain man considers the least neglect of ceremony as a mortal affront and an expression of contempt.
A vain man is restless, impatient, and perpetually afraid that others have lost respect for him.
A vain man is always anxious to obtain new expressions of esteem and cannot be kept in temper without continual attendance and adulation.
There is an affinity between the desire to become honourable and estimable and the desire for honour and esteem.
The love of virtue and the love of true glory resemble each other in aiming to be what is honourable and noble.
The love of virtue and the love of true glory both have some reference to the sentiments of others.
A man of great magnanimity desires virtue for its own sake and is indifferent to actual opinions of mankind about him.
A magnanimous man delights in the thought of what opinions others ought to have of him if they were cool, candid, consistent, and properly informed.
A magnanimous man values the opinions that ought to be entertained of him more than the opinions actually entertained.
A magnanimous man acts from the motive that he might think himself worthy of honourable sentiments regardless of others' actual opinions.
Even in the love of virtue there is some reference to what in reason and propriety ought to be the opinion of others.
There is a great difference between a man who acts solely from regard to what is right and a man who desires to merit approbation and is anxious to obtain it.
A man who acts solely from regard to what is right acts from the most sublime and godlike motive human nature can conceive.
A man who desires to merit approbation and is anxious to obtain it has motives with a greater mixture of human infirmity.
A man anxious to obtain approbation is in danger of being mortified by the ignorance and injustice of mankind.
The happiness of a man who acts solely from regard to what is right is secure and independent of fortune and the caprice of others.
A man who acts solely from regard to what is right is not mortified by contempt and hatred thrown upon him by the ignorance of mankind.
Mankind despise and hate a man who acts rightly from a false notion of his character and conduct.
If mankind knew a man who acts rightly better, they would esteem and love him.
A man of real magnanimity considers that those who hate him from ignorance hate another person whom they mistake him to be.
It seldom happens that human nature arrives at the degree of firmness of a man of real magnanimity.
Only the weakest and most worthless of mankind are much delighted with false glory.
False ignominy is often capable of mortifying those who appear the most resolute and determined.
Dr. Mandeville is not satisfied with representing vanity as the sole source of actions commonly accounted virtuous.
Dr. Mandeville argues that human virtue is imperfect in many respects.
According to Dr. Mandeville, virtue falls short of complete self-denial and is often a concealed indulgence of passions.
Dr. Mandeville treats any reserve regarding pleasure that is less than ascetic abstinence as gross luxury and sensuality.
Dr. Mandeville considers everything exceeding what is necessary for human support as luxury.
Dr. Mandeville claims there is vice even in using a clean shirt or a convenient habitation.
Dr. Mandeville regards the lawful indulgence of sexual inclination as the same sensuality as harmful gratification of that passion.
Dr. Mandeville derides temperance and chastity that can be practiced at a low cost.
Some passions have names only for their disagreeable and offensive degrees.
People tend to notice passions more when they are offensive or cause antipathy.
When passions align with a person's natural state of mind, they are often overlooked or given names that emphasize restraint.
Common names for love of pleasure and love of sex denote vicious and offensive degrees of those passions.
Words like temperance and chastity mark the restraint and subjection of passions rather than their complete absence.
Dr. Mandeville argues that because passions still exist to some degree, virtues like temperance and chastity are mere impositions.
Virtues of temperance and chastity do not require complete insensibility to the objects of the passions they govern.
These virtues aim to restrain the violence of passions to avoid harm to the individual and disturbance to society.
Dr. Mandeville's great fallacy is representing every passion as wholly vicious in any degree or direction.
Dr. Mandeville treats everything related to the sentiments of others as vanity.
Dr. Mandeville uses this sophistry to conclude that private vices are public benefits.
If love of magnificence and taste for elegant arts are regarded as luxury and ostentation, then luxury and ostentation are public benefits.
Without qualities labeled as luxury and ostentation, arts of refinement would lack encouragement and languish.
Some ascetic doctrines before Dr. Mandeville placed virtue in the complete extirpation of all passions.
Dr. Mandeville proved that complete conquest of passions never actually took place among men.
Dr. Mandeville argued that universal conquest of passions would be harmful to society by ending industry and commerce.
Dr. Mandeville's first proposition suggested there was no real virtue and that pretended virtue was a cheat.
His second proposition suggested private vices were public benefits because society could not prosper without them.
Dr. Mandeville's system once made a significant impact in the world.
Dr. Mandeville's system taught vice to appear with more effrontery and to openly avow corrupt motives.
Dr. Mandeville's system would not have imposed on many people or alarmed friends of better principles if it had not bordered on truth.
A natural philosophy system can be plausible and widely accepted yet have no foundation in nature or truth.
Descartes' vortices were regarded as a satisfactory account of heavenly revolutions for nearly a century.
It has been demonstrated that Descartes' vortices do not exist and could not produce the effects ascribed to them.
Systems of moral philosophy cannot deceive as grossly or depart as far from truth as natural philosophy systems.
An author explaining the origin of moral sentiments cannot depart far from truth because the subject concerns familiar matters.
A traveler can impose absurd fictions about distant countries, but an author explaining local moral affairs must have some truth.
Even if we are careless, the greatest falsehoods in moral philosophy must have some resemblance to truth.
An author assigning causes to natural sentiments without connection or resemblance to those sentiments appears absurd.
The next question of importance in Moral Philosophy after the inquiry concerning the nature of virtue is concerning the principle of approbation.
The principle of approbation concerns the power or faculty of the mind which renders certain characters agreeable or disagreeable to us.
The principle of approbation makes us prefer one tenour of conduct to another.
The principle of approbation causes us to denominate one conduct as right and another as wrong.
The principle of approbation causes us to consider one conduct as the object of approbation, honour, and reward.
The principle of approbation causes us to consider another conduct as the object of blame, censure, and punishment.
Three different accounts have been given of the principle of approbation.
According to some, we approve and disapprove both of our own actions and those of others from self-love only.
According to some, we approve and disapprove actions from some view of their tendency to our own happiness or disadvantage.
According to others, reason enables us to distinguish between what is fit and unfit both in actions and affections.
Reason is the same faculty by which we distinguish between truth and falsehood.
According to others, the distinction of approbation is altogether the effect of immediate sentiment and feeling.
The distinction of approbation arises from the satisfaction or disgust with which the view of certain actions or affections inspires us.
Self-love, reason, and sentiment are the three different sources assigned for the principle of approbation.
The determination of the question concerning the principle of approbation is of the greatest importance in speculation.
The determination of the question concerning the principle of approbation is of no importance in practice.
The question concerning the nature of virtue has some influence upon our notions of right and wrong in many particular cases.
The question concerning the principle of approbation can possibly have no effect on our notions of right and wrong in particular cases.
To examine from what contrivance or mechanism within those different notions or sentiments arise is a mere matter of philosophical curiosity.
Those who account for the principle of approbation from self-love do not all account for it in the same manner.
There is a good deal of confusion and inaccuracy in all the different systems that deduce the principle of approbation from self-love.

According to Mr. Hobbes and many of his followers, man is driven to take refuge in society not by any natural love for his own kind but because he is incapable of subsisting with ease or safety without the assistance of others.
Society becomes necessary to man because without it he cannot subsist with ease or safety.
Whatever tends to the support and welfare of society is considered by man as having a remote tendency to his own interest.
Whatever is likely to disturb or destroy society is regarded as in some measure hurtful or pernicious to man himself.
Virtue is the great support of human society.
Vice is the great disturber of human society.
Virtue is agreeable to every man because it supports society.
Vice is offensive to every man because it disturbs society.
The tendency of virtue to promote the order of society reflects a great beauty upon virtue.
The tendency of vice to disturb the order of society reflects a great deformity upon vice.
Human society, when contemplated abstractly and philosophically, appears like a great, immense machine whose regular and harmonious movements produce many agreeable effects.
Virtue is like the fine polish to the wheels of society, making its movements smooth and easy.
Vice is like vile rust that makes the wheels of society jar and grate upon one another.
Virtue necessarily pleases because it smooths the movements of society.
Vice is necessarily offensive because it obstructs the movements of society.
The account of the origin of approbation and disapprobation derived from regard to the order of society runs into the principle which gives beauty to utility.
Authors who describe the advantages of a cultivated and social life above a savage and solitary life expatiate upon the necessity of virtue and good order for the maintenance of society.
These authors demonstrate how the prevalence of vice and disobedience to laws tend to bring back a savage and solitary life.
Readers are often charmed with the novelty and grandeur of the views that virtue has a new beauty and vice a new deformity when seen as supporting or disturbing society.
This political view of virtue and vice cannot be the ground of the approbation and disapprobation with which people have always considered these qualities.

Authors who deduce from self-love the interest taken in the welfare of society do not mean that current applause or detestation of historical figures is influenced by actual benefit or detriment to us.

These philosophers imagined that our sentiments were influenced by benefits or damages that might have redounded to us had we lived in distant ages or might still redound to us if we meet similar characters.
The idea these authors were groping about was the indirect sympathy felt with the gratitude or resentment of those who received benefit or suffered damage from opposite characters.

These authors said it was not the thought of what we had gained or suffered that prompted applause or indignation but the imagination of what we might gain or suffer if we acted in society with such associates.
Sympathy cannot in any sense be regarded as a selfish principle.
When one sympathizes with another's sorrow or indignation, the emotion arises from imagining oneself in the other's situation.
Sympathy arises from an imaginary change of situations with the person principally concerned, not from imagining the event happening to oneself in one's own person and character.
When condoling with someone for the loss of their only son, one considers what one would suffer if one were really that person, not what one would suffer as oneself.
Grief felt by sympathy is entirely on account of the other person and not on one's own account.
Sympathy is not a selfish passion because it does not arise from imagining anything that has befallen oneself in one's own person and character.
A man may sympathize with a woman in child-bed even though it is impossible for him to conceive himself as suffering her pains in his own person and character.
The account of human nature that deduces all sentiments and affections from self-love has never been fully and distinctly explained.
This account of human nature seems to have arisen from some confused misapprehension of the system of sympathy.
Mr. Hobbes taught that a state of nature is a state of war.
According to Mr. Hobbes, antecedent to civil government, there could be no safe or peaceable society among men.
Mr. Hobbes believed that preserving society was equivalent to supporting civil government.
Destroying civil government was, according to Mr. Hobbes, the same as putting an end to society.
The existence of civil government depends on obedience to the supreme magistrate.
When the supreme magistrate loses authority, all government ends.
Self-preservation teaches men to approve whatever promotes the welfare of society and to blame whatever harms it.
According to the text, the ideas of laudable and blamable should be the same as those of obedience and disobedience.
The laws of the civil magistrate ought to be regarded as the sole ultimate standards of justice and injustice.
Mr. Hobbes intended to subject men's consciences to civil powers rather than ecclesiastical powers.
Mr. Hobbes regarded ecclesiastical powers as the principal source of societal disorders.
Theologians were offended by Mr. Hobbes's doctrine and expressed their indignation with asperity and bitterness.
Sound moralists were offended by Mr. Hobbes's doctrine because it denied a natural distinction between right and wrong.
Mr. Hobbes's doctrine claimed that right and wrong were mutable and depended on the arbitrary will of the civil magistrate.
Mr. Hobbes's doctrine was attacked by sober reason and furious declamation.
To refute Mr. Hobbes's doctrine, it was necessary to prove that the mind naturally distinguishes right and wrong before any law.
Dr. Cudworth observed that law could not be the original source of distinctions between right and wrong.
If a law is indifferent to obedience, it cannot be the source of distinctions between right and wrong.
If it is right to obey a law and wrong to disobey it, this supposes antecedent notions of right and wrong.
The mind has notions of right and wrong antecedent to all law.
It was concluded that reason is the faculty from which the mind derives the notion of right and wrong.
This conclusion was more easily accepted when the science of human nature was in its infancy.
At the time of the controversy with Mr. Hobbes, no other faculty besides reason was thought to produce ideas of right and wrong.
The popular doctrine became that virtue and vice consist in conformity or disagreement with reason.
Reason was considered the original source and principle of approbation and disapprobation.
Virtue consists in conformity to reason in some respects.
Reason may be considered as the source and principle of approbation and disapprobation and of solid judgments about right and wrong.
By reason, we discover general rules of justice to regulate our actions.
Reason forms vague and indeterminate ideas of what is prudent, decent, generous, or noble.
General maxims of morality are formed from experience and induction.
Induction is regarded as an operation of reason.
We regulate most moral judgments by maxims and ideas derived from induction and reason.
Moral judgments would be uncertain if they depended solely on immediate sentiment and feeling.
Virtue may properly be said to consist in conformity to reason.
It is absurd to suppose that first perceptions of right and wrong can be derived from reason.
First perceptions of right and wrong are the object of immediate sense and feeling, not reason.
General rules of morality are formed by finding that one conduct pleases and another displeases the mind in many instances.
Reason cannot make any particular object agreeable or disagreeable for its own sake.
Reason can show that an object is a means to obtain something naturally pleasing or displeasing.
Nothing is agreeable or disagreeable for its own sake except by immediate sense and feeling.
If virtue pleases for its own sake and vice displeases, immediate sense and feeling reconcile us to virtue and alienate us from vice.
Pleasure and pain are the great objects of desire and aversion.
Pleasure and pain are distinguished by immediate sense and feeling, not by reason.
If virtue is desirable for its own sake and vice is an object of aversion, immediate sense and feeling originally distinguish these qualities.
Sentiments of approbation and disapprobation were long regarded as originally flowing from reason due to inattention.
Dr. Hutcheson was the first to distinguish precisely in what respect moral distinctions arise from reason and in what respect they are founded on immediate sense and feeling.
Dr. Hutcheson explained the moral sense fully and unanswerably in his illustrations.
If controversy about the source of moral distinctions continues, it is due to inattention to Dr. Hutcheson's writings or attachment to certain expressions.
Attachment to certain forms of expression is a weakness not uncommon among the learned, especially in deeply interesting subjects.
Systems that make sentiment the principle of approbation can be divided into two classes.
Some systems hold that the principle of approbation is founded on a peculiar sentiment, a particular power of perception exerted by the mind when viewing certain actions or affections.
According to these systems, some actions or affections affect this faculty agreeably and others disagreeably.
Actions or affections that affect this faculty agreeably are stamped with the characters of right, laudable, and virtuous.
Actions or affections that affect this faculty disagreeably are stamped with the characters of wrong, blamable, and vicious.
This peculiar sentiment is distinct from every other and is the effect of a particular power of perception.
This peculiar sentiment is called a moral sense.
Other systems argue that no new power of perception is needed to account for the principle of approbation.
These systems believe that nature produces many effects from one cause, and sympathy is sufficient to account for the effects ascribed to the moral sense.
Dr. Hutcheson argued that the principle of approbation is not founded on self-love.
Dr. Hutcheson demonstrated that the principle of approbation could not arise from any operation of reason.
Dr. Hutcheson supposed the principle of approbation to be a faculty of a peculiar kind endowed by nature to the human mind.
Dr. Hutcheson called this new power of perception a moral sense.
Dr. Hutcheson supposed the moral sense to be somewhat analogous to the external senses.

According to Dr. Hutcheson, the various affections of the human mind, by touching the moral sense in a certain manner, appear to possess qualities of amiable and odious, virtuous and vicious, right and wrong.
Dr. Hutcheson divided the senses or powers of perception into two kinds: direct or antecedent senses and reflex or consequent senses.
Direct senses are faculties from which the mind derives perception of things that do not presuppose the perception of any other.
Sounds and colours are objects of the direct senses.
Reflex senses are faculties from which the mind derives perception of things that presuppose the perception of some other.
Harmony and beauty are objects of the reflex senses.
To perceive harmony of a sound or beauty of a colour, one must first perceive the sound or colour.
The moral sense is considered a reflex internal sense.
Mr. Locke called the faculty from which we derive simple ideas of passions and emotions reflection, which Dr. Hutcheson considered a direct internal sense.
The faculty by which we perceive beauty or deformity, virtue or vice of passions and emotions is a reflex internal sense.
Dr. Hutcheson argued that the mind is endowed with other reflex senses similar to the moral sense.

Examples of other reflex senses include a sense of beauty and deformity in external objects, a public sense for sympathy with others' happiness or misery, a sense of shame and honour, and a sense of ridicule.
Dr. Hutcheson acknowledged consequences of his doctrine that some regard as confutations.
Qualities that belong to objects of any sense cannot be ascribed to the sense itself.
It is absurd to call the sense of seeing black or white, or the sense of hearing loud or low.
Similarly, it is absurd to call moral faculties virtuous or vicious, morally good or evil.
Virtuous or vicious qualities belong to the objects of moral faculties, not to the faculties themselves.
If a person approves cruelty and injustice as virtues and disapproves equity and humanity as vices, this constitution of mind might be inconvenient and strange but not morally evil.
If a man shouts admiration at a barbarous and unmerited execution, this behavior would be considered vicious and morally evil.
The sentiments of a spectator approving such an execution would appear without cause or motive and be detestable.
There is no perversion of sentiment more averse to the heart's sympathy than approval of barbarous executions.
Such a constitution of mind is considered the last and most dreadful stage of moral depravity.
Correct moral sentiments naturally appear laudable and morally good.
A man whose censure and applause accurately match the value or unworthiness of objects deserves some moral approbation.
The precision of a person's moral sentiments can excite wonder and applause.
Virtue requires habit and resolution of mind as well as delicacy of sentiment.
Delicacy of moral sentiment may be perfect even when habit and resolution are lacking.
A disposition with delicate moral sentiments is incompatible with grossly criminal behavior.
Such a disposition is the happiest foundation for building perfect virtue.
Many men who mean well and intend to do their duty are disagreeable due to coarseness of their moral sentiments.
It may be said that approbation is founded on a peculiar sentiment that answers this one purpose and no other.
Approbation and disapprobation may be feelings or emotions arising upon viewing different characters and actions.
Resentment might be called a sense of injuries, and gratitude a sense of benefits.
Approbation and disapprobation may properly be called a sense of right and wrong or a moral sense.
This account of approbation as a peculiar sentiment is exposed to objections different from those against the moral sense as a power of perception.
Any particular emotion preserves the general features that distinguish it as an emotion of a certain kind despite variations.
Anger is an emotion of a particular kind with general features more distinguishable than its variations.
Anger against a man differs somewhat from anger against a woman, and anger against a woman differs from anger against a child.
The general passion of anger receives different modifications from the particular character of its object.
The general features of anger predominate over its variations in different cases.
Distinguishing the general features of anger requires no delicate observation.
Discovering the variations of anger requires very delicate attention.
If approbation and disapprobation were emotions of a particular kind like gratitude and resentment, they would retain general features clear and easily distinguishable across variations.
In reality, the emotion felt when approving or disapproving varies greatly and no common features can be discovered between different cases.
The approbation felt for a tender, delicate, and humane sentiment is quite different from the approbation felt for a great, daring, and magnanimous sentiment.
Both types of approbation can be perfect and entire but produce different emotions such as softness or elevation.
According to the system described, approbation arises from sympathy with the emotions of the person approved.
When the emotions of the person approved are opposite, the approbation felt has no resemblance between occasions.
If approbation consisted of a peculiar emotion unrelated to the sentiments approved, the approbation would not vary as it does.
Disapprobation also varies such that horror for cruelty differs from contempt for mean-spiritedness.
The discord felt in disapprobation differs depending on the vice considered.
Proper and improper approbation appear morally good or evil to natural sentiments.
When a neighbor's approbation of a third person's conduct coincides with our own, we approve of that approbation and consider it morally good.
When a neighbor's approbation does not coincide with our own sentiments, we disapprove of it and consider it morally evil.
Coincidence or opposition of sentiments between observer and person observed constitutes moral approbation or disapprobation.
The principle of approbation as a peculiar sentiment distinct from every other has not been widely noticed or named in any language.
The word 'moral sense' is of very late formation and is not yet fully part of the English language.
The word 'approbation' has only recently been appropriated to denote a moral sentiment.
In common language, 'approve' is used for satisfaction with things like the form of a building or flavor of food.
The word 'conscience' does not immediately denote a moral faculty for approval or disapproval.
Conscience signifies consciousness of having acted agreeably or contrary to some directions.
Many passions such as love, hatred, joy, sorrow, gratitude, and resentment have names, but the supposed sovereign principle of approbation has not been named.
When we approve of any character or action, the sentiments felt derive from four sources.
The first source of approval is sympathy with the motives of the agent.
The second source is entering into the gratitude of those who receive the benefit of the agent's actions.
The third source is observing that the conduct agrees with general rules governing the two sympathies.
The fourth source is considering actions as part of a system promoting happiness, which gives them a beauty similar to a well-contrived machine.
After accounting for these four principles, any remaining sentiment may be ascribed to a moral sense or other peculiar faculty.
No instance has been alleged where the moral sense exerts itself alone and unmixed with other emotions or sympathies.
Another system accounts for moral sentiments from sympathy with the utility of qualities and the happiness of those affected.
This sympathy is different from sympathy with the motives of the agent and from sympathy with the gratitude of beneficiaries.
This sympathy is the same principle by which we approve of a well-contrived machine.
A machine cannot be the object of sympathy with motives or gratitude.
The author has given an account of this system in the fourth part of the discourse.
The rules of justice are the only rules of morality which are precise and accurate.
The rules of all other virtues are loose, vague, and indeterminate.
The rules of justice may be compared to the rules of grammar.
The rules of other virtues may be compared to those which critics lay down for attaining sublimity and elegance in composition.
Some authors have collected and digested the rules of morality into systems using a loose method.
Other authors have endeavoured to introduce accuracy into their precepts where possible.
The first set of authors wrote like critics.
The second set of authors wrote like grammarians.
Ancient moralists generally described virtues and vices in a general manner without laying down precise rules for all cases.
Ancient moralists aimed to ascertain the sentiment of the heart upon which each virtue is founded.
They also aimed to describe the general way of acting to which each sentiment would direct us.
Characterizing the sentiment of the heart for each virtue requires a delicate and accurate approach.
It is impossible to express all variations of each sentiment according to every possible circumstance.
The sentiment of friendship varies depending on the age and character of the person.
The general sentiment of friendship and familiar attachment can be ascertained with sufficient accuracy.
The general picture of friendship can be recognized and distinguished from similar sentiments like good-will, respect, esteem, and admiration.
Describing the ordinary way of acting prompted by each virtue is easier than describing the internal sentiment.
Internal sentiments are marked and distinguished by their external effects such as alterations in countenance, behavior, resolutions, and actions.
Cicero in his first book of Offices directs the practice of the four cardinal virtues.
Aristotle in his Ethics points out habits like liberality, magnificence, magnanimity, jocularity, and good humor as ways to regulate behavior.
Jocularity and good humor are considered virtues by Aristotle, though they may not seem to deserve the name.
Works describing virtues in this manner present agreeable and lively pictures of manners.
Such works inflame natural love of virtue and increase abhorrence of vice.
They help to correct and ascertain natural sentiments regarding propriety of conduct.
They suggest many nice and delicate attentions that form a more exact justness of behavior.
This manner of treating rules of morality is called Ethics.
Ethics does not admit of the most accurate precision but is highly useful and agreeable.
Ethics is the most susceptible of the embellishments of eloquence.
Eloquence can bestow new importance upon the smallest rules of duty.
Ethical precepts dressed with eloquence can produce noble and lasting impressions on youth.
Ethical precepts can inspire heroic resolutions in youth and help establish useful habits.
Whatever precept and exhortation can do to animate virtue is done by Ethics delivered in this manner.
The second set of moralists includes casuists of the middle and latter ages of the Christian church and natural jurisprudence writers.
The second set of moralists lay down exact and precise rules for every circumstance of behavior.
Justice is the only virtue for which exact rules can properly be given.
The two sets of writers treat justice in very different manners.
Writers on jurisprudence consider what a person to whom an obligation is due may exact by force.
They consider what an impartial spectator or judge would approve of exacting.
Casuists consider what the person who owes the obligation ought to think himself bound to perform from scrupulous regard to justice.
Jurisprudence prescribes rules for decisions of judges and arbiters.
Casuistry prescribes rules for the conduct of a good man.
Observing all rules of jurisprudence deserves freedom from external punishment.
Observing all rules of casuistry entitles one to considerable praise for exact and scrupulous delicacy of behavior.
A good man may feel bound by a sacred and conscientious regard to the general rules of justice to perform many things that it would be unjust to extort from him by force.
A highwayman can oblige a traveller to promise him a sum of money by the fear of death.
Whether a promise extorted by unjust force from a traveller to a highwayman is obligatory has been much debated.
From a jurisprudence perspective, it is absurd to suppose that a highwayman is entitled to use force to constrain another to perform a promise.
Extorting a promise by force is a crime deserving the highest punishment.
To extort the performance of a promise obtained by force would be adding a new crime to the former.
A person who has been deceived by someone who might justly have killed him can complain of no injury.
Judges ought not to enforce the obligation of promises extorted by force.
Magistrates ought not to allow promises extorted by force to sustain action at law.
The question of whether a good man is bound to perform a promise extorted by force is more doubtful from a casuistry perspective.
No regard is due to the disappointment of a robber who extorts a promise by force.
No injury is done to a robber by not performing a promise extorted by force.
Some regard may be due to the dignity and honour of the person who made a promise extorted by force.
The sacredness of a person's character that reveres truth and abhors falsehood may require some regard to promises extorted by force.
Cicero, Puffendorf, Barbeyrac, and Dr. Hutcheson determined that no regard is due to promises extorted by force.
Some ancient church fathers and eminent modern casuists judged promises extorted by force to be obligatory.
Common sentiments of mankind find that some regard is due even to promises extorted by force.
A man who easily makes and violates promises extorted by force would not be chosen as a friend or companion.
A gentleman who promises a highwayman five pounds and does not perform would incur some blame.
If the sum promised to a highwayman is very great, it is more doubtful what is proper to be done.
If payment of a promised sum would ruin the promiser's family, it would be criminal or extremely improper to pay it to a highwayman.
A man who beggars himself or throws away a large sum to observe a promise to a thief would appear absurd and extravagant.
Profusion in observing promises extorted by force is inconsistent with duty to oneself and others.
It is impossible to fix a precise rule for the degree of regard due to promises extorted by force.
The degree of regard due to promises extorted by force varies according to persons' characters, circumstances, solemnity of the promise, and incidents of the encounter.
If the promiser was treated with gallantry by the highwayman, more regard may be due to the promise.
Exact propriety requires observance of promises extorted by force when not inconsistent with more sacred duties.
More sacred duties include regard to public interest, gratitude, natural affection, and laws of proper beneficence.
There are no precise rules to determine what external actions are due from regard to such motives or when virtues are inconsistent with observance of promises extorted by force.
Violating promises extorted by force, even for necessary reasons, involves some degree of dishonour to the promiser.
After making a promise extorted by force, one may be convinced of the impropriety of observing it.
Making a promise extorted by force is a departure from the highest maxims of magnanimity and honour.
A brave man ought to die rather than make a promise he can neither keep without folly nor violate without ignominy.
Some degree of ignominy always attends situations where promises extorted by force are made and broken.
Treachery and falsehood are vices that are dangerous, dreadful, and easily indulged, causing jealousy in men.
Imagination attaches the idea of shame to all violations of faith in every circumstance.
Violations of faith resemble violations of chastity in the fair sex in terms of the delicacy of sentiments.
Breach of chastity dishonours irretrievably and cannot be excused or atoned for by sorrow or repentance.
Even rape dishonours, and innocence of mind cannot wash out the pollution of the body in imagination.
Fidelity is a necessary virtue due even to those to whom nothing else is due and whom it is lawful to kill and destroy.
A person who breaks a solemnly pledged promise appears to have some degree of shame inseparably connected to the action.
Breaking a solemn promise stains and pollutes character and affixes a ridicule difficult to efface.
No man who has gone through an adventure of making and breaking a promise extorted by force would be fond of telling the story.
The difference between casuistry and jurisprudence is shown in their consideration of obligations of the general rules of justice.
Jurisprudence and casuistry are two sciences with different ends but the same subject.
Many authors treat questions sometimes according to jurisprudence and sometimes according to casuistry without distinguishing between the two.
The doctrine of the casuists includes more than just what justice demands; it also covers other parts of Christian and moral duty.
The custom of auricular confession, introduced by Roman Catholic superstition, was a principal occasion for the cultivation of casuistry.
Auricular confession required revealing secret actions and thoughts suspected of deviating from Christian purity to a confessor.
The confessor informed penitents if and how they violated their duty and what penance they must undergo before absolution.
Consciousness or suspicion of wrongdoing causes anxiety and terror in those not hardened by iniquity.
People naturally seek to relieve mental oppression by confiding in someone they trust for secrecy and discretion.
The shame of confession is compensated by the alleviation of uneasiness through the sympathy of the confidant.
Confession relieves people by showing they are not entirely unworthy of regard and that their present disposition may be approved.
In times of superstition, clergy insinuated themselves into the confidence of almost every private family.
The clergy possessed all the little learning available at the time and had manners more polished than the general age.
Clergy were regarded as great directors of religious and moral duties.
Familiarity with clergy gave reputation, and their disapproval caused deep ignominy.
Clergy were considered great judges of right and wrong and were consulted about all moral scruples.
It was reputable to be known as someone who made clergy the confidants of all secrets and sought their advice.
Clergy established a general rule that they should be entrusted with secrets and moral direction.
Qualifying as confessors became a necessary part of the study of churchmen and divines.
Clergy collected cases of conscience, which are delicate situations hard to determine morally.
Books of casuistry originated from the collection of cases of conscience.
The moral duties considered by casuists were chiefly those circumscribed within general rules and whose violation causes remorse and dread of punishment.
The institution that gave occasion to casuists' works aimed to appease terrors of conscience from infringing such duties.
Not every virtue's defect causes severe compunctions, and people do not seek absolution for failing the most generous or magnanimous actions.
Rules violated in failures of generous or magnanimous actions are commonly not very determinate and usually do not expose one to blame or punishment.
Casuists regarded the exercise of such virtues as works of supererogation, not strictly exacted and unnecessary to treat.
Breaches of moral duty before the confessor and casuists were chiefly of three kinds: breaches of justice, chastity, and veracity.
Breaches of the rules of justice are express and positive and naturally cause consciousness of deserving and dread of punishment from God and man.
Breaches of chastity in grosser instances are real breaches of justice causing unpardonable injury to others.
Smaller breaches of chastity violate decorums in conversation between sexes and tend to bring ignominy and shame.
Breaches of veracity are not always breaches of justice but are always breaches of a plain rule causing shame.
Common lying may frequently do no harm and not expose to external punishment.
Young children have an instinctive disposition to believe whatever they are told.
Nature requires children to put implicit confidence in those caring for their childhood and early education.
Children's credulity is excessive and requires long experience to reduce to reasonable distrust.
In adults, degrees of credulity vary, with the wisest generally being least credulous.
Most people are more credulous than they ought to be and often believe false tales.
The natural disposition is always to believe, and only acquired wisdom and experience teach incredulity.
Even the wisest and most cautious frequently believe stories they later find false and are ashamed to have believed.
The man whom we believe is our leader and director in the things concerning which we believe him.
We look up to the man we believe with a certain degree of esteem and respect.
From admiring other people, we come to wish to be admired ourselves.
From being led and directed by other people, we learn to wish to become leaders and directors ourselves.
We cannot always be satisfied merely with being admired unless we persuade ourselves that we are in some degree really worthy of admiration.
We cannot always be satisfied merely with being believed unless we are conscious that we are really worthy of belief.
The desire of praise and the desire of praise-worthiness are distinct and separate desires.
The desire of being believed and the desire of being worthy of belief are distinct and separate desires.
The desire of being believed, persuading, leading, and directing other people is one of the strongest of all our natural desires.
The desire to lead and direct others is perhaps the instinct upon which the faculty of speech is founded.
No other animal possesses the faculty of speech.
No other animal shows any desire to lead and direct the judgment and conduct of its fellows.
Great ambition and the desire of real superiority, of leading and directing, seem to be altogether peculiar to man.
Speech is the great instrument of ambition, real superiority, and leading and directing the judgments and conduct of other people.
It is always mortifying not to be believed.
It is doubly mortifying when we suspect that we are supposed to be unworthy of belief and capable of seriously and wilfully deceiving.
To tell a man that he lies is of all affronts the most mortal.
Whoever seriously and wilfully deceives is conscious to himself that he merits the affront of being called a liar.
A person who wilfully deceives forfeits all title to the credit from which he can derive ease, comfort, or satisfaction in the society of his equals.
A man who imagines that nobody believes a single word he says would feel himself the outcast of human society and dread presenting himself before it.
It is probable that no man ever had just reason to believe that nobody believed a single word he said.
The most notorious liar tells the fair truth at least twenty times for every deliberate lie.
In the most cautious, the disposition to believe prevails over that to doubt and distrust.
In those most regardless of truth, the natural disposition to tell it prevails on most occasions over that to deceive or alter it.
We are mortified when we unintentionally deceive other people due to having been deceived ourselves.
Involuntary falsehood may not mark a want of veracity or love of truth.
Involuntary falsehood is always in some degree a mark of want of judgment, memory, improper credulity, precipitancy, or rashness.
Involuntary falsehood diminishes our authority to persuade and brings suspicion upon our fitness to lead and direct.
A man who sometimes misleads from mistake is widely different from one who wilfully deceives.
A man who sometimes misleads from mistake may safely be trusted on many occasions.
A man who wilfully deceives can very seldom be trusted on any occasion.
Frankness and openness conciliate confidence.
We trust a man who seems willing to trust us.
We think we see clearly the road by which a frank man means to conduct us.
We abandon ourselves with pleasure to the guidance and direction of a frank man.
Reserve and concealment call forth diffidence.
We are afraid to follow a man who is going where we do not know.
The great pleasure of conversation and society arises from a correspondence of sentiments and opinions and a harmony of minds.
This harmony cannot be obtained unless there is free communication of sentiments and opinions.
We desire to feel how each other is affected and to observe the sentiments and affections which really subsist in each other's bosoms.
The chief subjects of the works of the casuists were the conscientious regard due to the rules of justice.
The casuists addressed how far we ought to respect the life and property of our neighbour.
The duty of restitution was a subject of the works of the casuists.
The laws of chastity and modesty were topics in casuist writings.
The casuists discussed what they called the sins of concupiscence.
The rules of veracity and the obligation of oaths, promises, and contracts were covered by casuists.
The works of the casuists attempted to direct by precise rules what belongs only to feeling and sentiment.
It is difficult to ascertain by rules the exact point where a delicate sense of justice becomes frivolous scrupulosity.
It is difficult to determine when secrecy and reserve grow into dissimulation.
It is difficult to determine how far agreeable irony may be carried before it degenerates into a lie.
The highest pitch of freedom and ease of behaviour that is graceful and becoming is hard to define precisely.
What constitutes propriety and happiness of behaviour varies with the smallest variety of situation.
Books of casuistry are generally as useless as they are commonly tiresome.
Casuist books could be of little use even if their decisions were just because exact parallel cases are rare.
A person anxious to do his duty would have little occasion to consult casuist books.
The style of casuist writings is unlikely to awaken negligence to more attention.
Casuist writings do not tend to animate generosity or nobility.
Casuist writings do not tend to soften people to gentleness and humanity.
Many casuist writings tend to teach chicanery with one's own conscience.
Casuist writings authorize evasive refinements regarding essential articles of duty.
The frivolous accuracy attempted by casuists led to dangerous errors.
Casuist works are dry and disagreeable, abounding in abstruse and metaphysical distinctions.
Casuist works are incapable of exciting emotions which books of morality principally aim to excite.
The two useful parts of moral philosophy are Ethics and Jurisprudence.
Casuistry ought to be rejected altogether.
Ancient moralists did not affect nice exactness but described general sentiments on justice, modesty, and veracity.
Several philosophers attempted something like the doctrine of the casuists.
Cicero's third book of Offices endeavours to give rules for conduct in many difficult cases.
Several philosophers before Cicero had attempted similar work on conduct in difficult cases.
Neither Cicero nor others aimed at giving a complete system of such rules.
They meant to show how situations may occur where it is doubtful whether to observe or recede from ordinary rules of duty.
Every system of positive law may be regarded as an imperfect attempt towards a system of natural jurisprudence.
The violation of justice is something men will never submit to from one another.
Public magistrates must employ the power of the commonwealth to enforce the practice of justice.
Without magistrates enforcing justice, civil society would become a scene of bloodshed and disorder.
Magistrates in governments with considerable authority undertake to do justice to all and promise to hear and redress every complaint.
In well-governed states, judges are appointed to determine controversies of individuals.
Rules are prescribed to regulate the decisions of judges in well-governed states.
These rules generally coincide with those of natural justice.
Sometimes the constitution or interests of government or particular orders warp positive laws from natural justice.
In some countries, rudeness and barbarism hinder natural sentiments of justice from attaining accuracy and precision.
In such countries, laws are gross, rude, and undistinguishing like their manners.
In other countries, the constitution of courts hinders regular jurisprudence despite improved manners.
No country’s positive law decisions coincide exactly in every case with natural justice rules.
Systems of positive law deserve great authority as records of mankind’s sentiments in different ages and nations.
Systems of positive law can never be regarded as accurate systems of natural justice rules.
Reasonings of lawyers on law imperfections and improvements might have led to inquiry into natural rules of justice.
It was very late before any general system of natural jurisprudence was thought of.
Philosophy of law was treated by itself late and without regard to particular national institutions.
Ancient moralists did not attempt particular enumeration of rules of justice.
Cicero in his Offices and Aristotle in his Ethics treat justice generally as with other virtues.
The laws of Cicero and Plato are laws of police, not of justice.
Grotius was the first to attempt a system of principles foundational to laws of all nations.
Grotius’s treatise of the laws of war and peace is perhaps the most complete work on this subject to date.

The author will discuss revolutions in law and government concerning justice, police, revenue, arms, and other law objects.

The assignation of particular names to denote particular objects, that is, the institution of nouns substantive, would probably be one of the first steps towards the formation of language.
Two savages who had never been taught to speak but had been bred up remote from the societies of men would naturally begin to form a language by uttering certain sounds to denote certain objects.
The objects most familiar to the savages and which they had most frequent occasion to mention would have particular names assigned to them.

The particular cave sheltering the savages, the particular tree whose fruit relieved their hunger, and the particular fountain whose water allayed their thirst would first be denominated by words such as cave, tree, and fountain.
When the savages' experience enlarged and they observed other caves, trees, and fountains, they would bestow upon each new object the same name as the similar object they were first acquainted with.
The new objects had no names of their own but resembled other objects which had names.
The savages could not behold new objects without recollecting the old ones and the names of the old ones would present themselves to memory.
Words originally proper names of individuals would insensibly become common names of a multitude.
A child just learning to speak calls every person who comes to the house its papa or its mama, bestowing those names on the whole species.
A clown who did not know the proper name of the river by his door called it 'the river' and never heard any other name for it.
The clown's experience had not led him to observe any other river, so the general word river was, in his acceptance, a proper name signifying an individual object.
If the clown had been carried to another river, he would have readily called it a river.
An Englishman describing a great river in a foreign country naturally says it is another Thames.
The Spaniards, upon arriving at the coast of Mexico, called it 'New Spain' because it reminded them of Spain.
We say of a hero that he is an Alexander, of an orator that he is a Cicero, and of a philosopher that he is a Newton.
This way of speaking, called Antonomasia by grammarians, shows mankind's natural disposition to give one object the name of another which resembles it.
The application of the name of an individual to a multitude of objects resembling it seems to have given occasion to the formation of classes and assortments called genera and species.
A species is constituted by a number of objects bearing a certain degree of resemblance to one another and denominated by a single appellation.
When most objects had been arranged under classes distinguished by general names, most individuals under each species had no peculiar or proper names distinct from the general name.
To mention a particular object under a general name, it became necessary to distinguish it by its peculiar qualities or by its peculiar relation to other things.
Nouns adjective are words that express quality considered as qualifying some particular subject.
The word green expresses a certain quality considered as qualifying a particular subject.
Words expressing quality may serve to distinguish particular objects from others under the same general appellation.
The phrase green tree might serve to distinguish a particular tree from others that were withered or blasted.
Prepositions are words that express relation considered in concrete with the co-relative object.
Prepositions such as of, to, for, with, by, above, and below denote some relation subsisting between the objects expressed by the words they connect.
Words expressing relation serve to distinguish particular objects from others of the same species when peculiar qualities cannot properly mark them.
The phrase the green tree of the meadow distinguishes a particular tree by both its quality and its relation to another object.
Quality and relation cannot exist in the abstract.
Words denoting quality and relation considered in concrete would be of much earlier invention than words expressing them in the abstract.
Words like green and blue would probably be invented sooner than greenness and blueness.
Words like above and below would probably be invented sooner than superiority and inferiority.
Inventing abstract terms requires a much greater effort of abstraction than inventing concrete terms.
Abstract terms are generally derived from concrete terms.
The invention of nouns adjective requires a considerable degree of abstraction and generalization.
Those who first invented the words green, blue, red, and other color names must have observed and compared many objects.
Inventors of color words must have noticed resemblances and dissimilarities in the quality of color among objects.
Inventors must have mentally arranged objects into different classes based on color resemblances and dissimilarities.
An adjective is by nature a general and somewhat abstract word.
An adjective presupposes the idea of a species or assortment of things to which it applies equally.
The word green could not have originally been the name of an individual and then become a species name.
The word green denotes a peculiar quality of a substance, not the name of a substance.
The word green must have been a general word from the beginning, applicable to any substance with that quality.
The first person to call an object green must have observed other objects that were not green.
The invention of the name green supposes comparison.
The invention of the name green supposes some degree of abstraction.
The inventor of the name green must have distinguished the quality from the object and conceived the object as capable of existing without the quality.
The invention of even the simplest nouns adjective required metaphysical mental operations.
The mental operations of arrangement, comparison, and abstraction were employed before the names of different colors could be instituted.
When languages began to be formed, nouns adjective were not the words of the earliest invention.
Another way to denote different qualities of substances is to vary the noun substantive itself according to the qualities it has.
In many languages, qualities of sex and the absence of sex are expressed by different terminations in nouns substantive.
In Latin, lupus and lupa denote male and female qualities in animals and persons without needing adjectives.
Latin words forum, pratum, and plaustrum denote the absence of sex by their peculiar terminations.
Sex and the absence of sex are naturally considered qualities modifying and inseparable from particular substances.
It was natural to express sex qualities by modifying the noun substantive rather than by a general abstract word.
The expression of sex qualities by noun modification bears a more exact analogy to the idea or object denoted than by adjectives.
The quality and the subject are blended together in the expression when sex is expressed by noun modification.
The origin of masculine, feminine, and neutral genders in ancient languages comes from this noun modification.
The distinctions of substances into animated and inanimate, and animals into male and female, were marked without adjectives by these genders.
There are no more than three genders in the languages known to the author: masculine, feminine, and neutral.
Nouns substantive alone can express only the qualities of male, female, or neither male nor female.
The author is not surprised if other languages express many other qualities by different noun substantive formations.
Diminutives in Italian and some other languages sometimes express a variety of modifications in the substances denoted by nouns.
Nouns substantive could not undergo enough variations to express the almost infinite variety of qualities needed to specify and distinguish substances.
